Acetabular Fractures

Trauma · 1 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence~4 / 100,000 / yr

Bimodalyoung + high energy (MVC) · elderly + low energy (fall from standing)

Elderly volume~4,000/yr in USA → may become the commonest age group

Age group Commonest patterns
Young Posterior wall · transverse "family" (transverse, T-type, transverse + PW) · associated both column
Elderly Anterior wall · anterior column (quadrilateral plate) · anterior column posterior hemitransverse (ACPHT) · associated both column

Elderly low-energy fall onto greater trochanteranterior column + "medial wall" (quadrilateral plate) ± intrapelvic head dislocation
✗ Wrong options: PC + PW · transverse · T-type · T + PW → young, high energy

Associated injuries

Associated injury Rate
Lower extremity injury 36% (commonest)
Head injury 19%
Chest injury 18%
Nerve palsy 13% (3–33% in OB)
Abdominal 8%
Genitourinary 6%
Spine 4%

Nerve palsy patternsciatic, peroneal division → foot drop; highest with transverse + posterior wall

Nerve-injury share by pattern (OB)PW 9.5–23% · ABC 15.6% · PC + PW 12.5–23% · isolated PC rarely

Root most often involvedL5 (→ tibialis anterior, EHL, EDB)
✗ Wrong options: L4, S1, S2, S3

Isolated peroneal-division injurycommoner than complete sciatic injury

Posterior hip dislocation + decelerationthink traumatic thoracic aortic rupture; CXR may be normal → chest pain + hypotension + new leg weakness (cord ischaemia) → CT angiography of chest
✗ Wrong options: CT head · CT pelvis · CT L-spine · leg angiogram

Anatomy – column theory

Columnsinverted Y, linked to sacrum through the sciatic buttress

Anterior column Posterior column
Parts Anterior ilium (gluteus medius tubercle), anterior wall + dome, iliopectineal eminence, lateral superior pubic ramus Quadrilateral surface, posterior wall + dome, ischial tuberosity, greater/lesser sciatic notches
Radiographic line Iliopectineal line Ilioischial line
Best Judet Obturator oblique Iliac oblique

TO anatomy (TO)anterior column = anterior ½ iliac crest, iliac spines, anterior ½ acetabulum, pubis · posterior column = ischium, ischial spine, posterior ½ acetabulum, dense sciatic-notch bone

Acetabular orientationlateral inclination 40–48° · anteversion 18–21°

Corona mortis & vascular anatomy

Corona mortis ("crown of death")anastomosis external iliac (inferior epigastric) ↔ obturator (internal iliac system) behind superior pubic ramus

Prevalence (Tornetta)84% have an anastomosis · arterial 34%, venous 70%, both 20%

Distance from symphysismean 6.2 cm (range 3–9 cm) → "brisk bleeding ~5 cm from midline along superior ramus"

At riskilioinguinal (laceration 10–15%) + modified Stoppa (must be exposed + ligated); retracts into pelvis → hard to control

✗ Vessel trapssuperior gluteal + pudendal · internal iliac + MFCA · external iliac + deep femoral · femoral branch

2Mechanism

Pattern determined byforce vector + femoral head position at impact + bone quality (age)

Dashboard / posteriorly directed forceposterior wall ± posterior dislocation

Crescent fracture (posterior iliac wing on CT)lateral compression (laterally directed force on anterior iliac wing)
✗ Wrong options: APC · VS · combined

3Presentation

Foot drop / ↓ dorsiflexion after acetabular fractureperoneal division of sciatic → most likely pattern transverse + posterior wall

Hip flexed, adducted, IRposterior dislocation ± posterior wall

Os acetabuli marginalis superioraccessory ossification centre at superior acetabular rim in adolescents; mimics fracture / AVN; usually fuses by age 20
✗ Wrong options: fovea capitis · myositis ossificans · AVN · fracture

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Shows / use
AP pelvis Screening; 6 landmarks: iliopectineal line (AC), ilioischial line (PC), anterior wall, posterior wall, teardrop, weight-bearing roof (+ Shenton's line)
Obturator oblique (Judet) Obturator foramen in profile → anterior column + posterior wall ("OOPWAC", TO)
Iliac oblique (Judet) Iliac wing in profile, obturator foramen perpendicular → posterior column + anterior wall
Inlet / outlet Only if pelvic ring involvement suspected
CT Gold standard: pattern orientation, fragment size + position, marginal impaction, loose bodies (post-reduction), gap / step-off, surgical planning; 3D recon for planning
CT not for Pre-existing degenerative change (EXCEPT answer)
Post-op CT Most accurate for PW reduction → best correlation with outcome
EUA (dynamic fluoroscopy) Best test of posterior wall stability
Duplex US Delayed presentation → rule out DVT

Judet = 45° obliquesipsilateral iliac oblique = contralateral obturator oblique (same image)

"Best view of LEFT posterior column?"left iliac oblique (= right obturator oblique)
✗ Wrong options: left obturator oblique · right iliac oblique

Judet trapsPW on obturator oblique · OO does not show SI joint well
✗ Wrong options: iliac oblique · inlet · outlet · AP

Interobserver reliability (Beaulé)Letournel substantial (κ > 0.70) with or without CT → CT not essential for classification, but adds impaction + loose bodies

Sign / measure Meaning View
Spur sign Intact ilium (most caudal part of intact ilium / posteroinferior ilium) exposed as acetabulum medialises → pathognomonic for associated both column Obturator oblique (also AP)
Gull (seagull) sign Superomedial dome impaction → poor prognosis (Orthobullets) Iliac oblique (Orthobullets)
Gull sign – TO wording (TO) Anteromedial dome impaction; "pathognomonic for posterior column fractures" → needs surgery Obturator oblique (TO)
Roof arc angle (Matta) Vertical line through head centre vs line to fracture; stable if > 45° on AP + both Judets (fracture exits outside weight-bearing dome) AP + Judets
CT subchondral arc (Olson & Matta) Superior 10 mm of acetabulum intact = equivalent to 45° roof arc (TO) CT
Articular incongruity > 2 mm = unstable CT
Medial clear space widening on EUA Posterior wall instability Obturator oblique under stress

Gull sign viewiliac oblique (Orthobullets) · obturator oblique (TO) — read the options

Roof arc NOT applicableposterior wall + associated both column (no intact acetabulum to measure)

Spur sign absentnondisplaced ABC → use CT to confirm acetabulum–axial skeleton continuity

Letournel & Judet classification

Structure5 elementary + 5 associated = 10 types

Elementary Lines / views Key fact
Posterior wall PW outline broken on OO Commonest overall; check superior gluteal NV bundle; only ~30% single large fragment
Posterior column Ilioischial line only broken on AP; IO shows break, anterior wall intact; OO iliopectineal intact Superior gluteal NV bundle; isolated PC rarely injures nerve
Anterior wall — Very rare; geriatric
Anterior column Iliopectineal line broken on OO with undisturbed posterior acetabulum 3–5% of fractures; may extend to quadrilateral plate without exiting PC
Transverse Iliopectineal + ilioischial both broken; single line crossing acetabulum Only elementary to involve both columns; axial CT: vertical (sagittal) A→P line; articular surface still attached to intact ilium
Associated Key fact
Associated both column (ABC) All articular segments detached from intact ilium (which stays on sacrum via SI joint) → no articular surface attached to axial skeleton · spur sign · may show secondary congruence
Transverse + posterior wall Commonest associated · highest nerve injury · high DJD risk
T-type Transverse + vertical split into obturator ring · high DJD risk
ACPHT Commonest in elderly
PC + PW Only associated type NOT involving both columns

Column vs transverse on axial CTtransverse = vertical (sagittal) line · column = horizontal (coronal) line

"Only one column involved?"PC + PW
✗ Wrong options: ABC · transverse · T + PW

Line-pattern trapsboth lines + iliac wing + obturator ring = ABC or ACPHT · both lines + obturator ring = T-type · iliopectineal only = AC · ilioischial only = PC

Distinguishing ABC from ACPHT / T / T + PWthose keep part of articular surface on intact ilium

Posterior wall size & stability

PW involvement Stability Action
< 20% Generally stable Protected WB — but EUA if fracture exits superiorly (cranial exit near dome)
20–40% Indeterminate EUA
> 40–50% Unstable ORIF

Fragment-size methods (less accurate than EUA)Keith (depth vs contralateral at fovea) · Moed (depth vs contralateral at greatest involvement) · Calkins (posterior arc length at greatest involvement)

EUA techniquehip flexion + adduction + axial load, obturator oblique view → ↑ medial clear space = unstable

History of dislocationnot predictive of instability (Grimshaw & Moed: stable on stress exam → nonop fine)

Not instability predictorsfragment size alone, dislocation history, PW comminution, roof arc, MRI labral tear, iliac oblique

5Management

Acetabular fracture
  • Associated hip dislocation → urgent closed reduction (< 12 h)→CT
    • incarcerated fragment → traction pin→ORIF ASAP
  • Stable / minimally displaced / high-risk patient→protected WB 6–8 wk
  • Displaced roof > 2 mm, unstable, impaction, loose body→ORIF < 3 wk
    • elderly + impaction / comminution / head injury→ORIF + acute THA
Posterior wall fracture (post-reduction CT)
  • < 20%, exits low→protected WB
  • < 20% exiting near dome, or 20–40%→EUA (obturator oblique)
    • unstable→ORIF
  • > 40–50% or intra-articular fragment→ORIF

Nonoperative criteria

Patient factors Fracture factors
High operative risk (elderly, DVT) Minimally displaced < 2 mm
Morbid obesity < 20% posterior wall (EUA best test)
Open contaminated wound Head congruent with roof out of traction
Late presentation > 3 wk ABC with secondary congruence
Roof arcs > 45° on AP + Judets

Nonop regimenprotected WB 6–8 wk; skeletal traction NOT needed if stable outside dome; DVT prophylaxis; serial X-rays

Elderly ABC with secondary congruencenonop
✗ Wrong options: ORIF + THA

Operative criteria

Patient factors Fracture factors
< 3 wk from injury Roof displacement > 2 mm
Physiologically stable Unstable pattern (PW > 40–50%)
Adequate soft tissue Marginal impaction
No local infection Intra-articular loose bodies
Pregnancy is NOT a contraindication Irreducible fracture-dislocation

Absolute surgical indication after dislocationosseous loose body in weight-bearing joint
✗ Wrong options: sciatic palsy · labral tear · PW fracture per se · chondral defect

Fracture-dislocation – reduction, traction & ORIF

Posterior dislocation + small PW fracturereduce hip now, test stability
✗ Wrong options: CT first · MRI · open reduction · transfer before reduction

After reductionCT mandatory even if no fracture on X-ray → incarcerated osteochondral fragments · sciatic palsy ~10%
✗ Wrong options: exploration of nerve · EMG · traction

Reduction timing< 12 h (Orthobullets; > 12 h delay = poor result, OB) · < 6 h to minimise AVN (one OB explanation) — read the options

Incarcerated fragment after reductiondistal femoral traction pin + ORIF ASAP (offloads cartilage)
✗ Wrong options: knee immobiliser + delayed ORIF · nonop

Incarcerated fragment + shock / unresuscitated + knee laxitydistal femoral pin
✗ Wrong options: proximal tibial pin with knee ligament injury · emergent ORIF · binder · EUA with intra-articular fragment

Marginal impaction on CTmust be elevated + bone grafted + buttress plated; otherwise incongruent joint → poor result

Loose fragmentsremove, but incorporate large articular fragments into fixation

Pregnancy (12 wk, normal fetal HR, unstable hip)acute ORIF
✗ Wrong options: wait till 15 wk · traction 6–8 wk

Fetal mortality ↑ withinjury severity, mechanism of injury, maternal haemorrhage
✗ Wrong options: trimester · approach · classification · fetal position

Timing of surgery

Worse outcome if fixed> 3 wk from injury
✗ Wrong options: 48 h · 5 d · 1 wk · 2 wk

Delay > 11 days↓ rate of anatomic reduction (OB)

↑ Time to surgery↓ chance of anatomic reduction · infection trend ↑ · no effect on HO or neuro injury

Early fixation → ↓ LOS, ↓ organ dysfunction, ↑ function, ↑ discharge home, ↑ reduction quality (EXCEPT trap: "greater organ dysfunction")

Surgical approach selection

Approach Indications Risks
Kocher-Langenbeck (posterior) PW, PC, PC + PW, most transverse + T Sciatic nerve (2–10%), MFCA (head blood supply), ↑ HO vs anterior
Ilioinguinal (anterior) AW, AC, ABC (standard), ACPHT Femoral nerve, LFCN, femoral vessel thrombosis, corona mortis 10–15% · lowest HO
Modified Stoppa (anterior intrapelvic, AIP) Quadrilateral plate buttress (medial wall comminution, ABC); ± lateral window ≈ ilioinguinal access Corona mortis must be ligated
Extended iliofemoral Only single approach to see both columns directly; T-type / transverse with posterior comminution, transtectal T, ABC with posterior column comminution, SI joint involvement, > 3 wk delay Massive HO (highest), gluteal muscle necrosis
Iliofemoral High anterior column only Not ABC
Modified Gibson Gluteus max–TFL interval ± trochanteric flip; PW/PC, selected T + transverse —
Trochanteric flip osteotomy + surgical dislocation PW + femoral head fracture (Pipkin IV) —

Stöckle (extended iliofemoral)80% anatomic (< 1 mm) · loss of reduction 8% · HO grade 3 13% · AVN 4%

ABC with spur sign, intact SI + PW, acuteilioinguinal
✗ Wrong options: extended iliofemoral · iliofemoral · KL · Gibson

74-yo, anterior columnilioinguinal
✗ Wrong options: Watson-Jones = hip · Hardinge = lateral THA

Transverse + PWKL (✗ Wrong options: trochanteric flip · extended iliofemoral) · LC2 crescent — anterior or posterior (✗ Wrong options: extended)

Approach does not affect outcome (Matta)

Sciatic nerve – positioning & injury

Least sciatic tension during KLhip extended + knee flexed (90°)
✗ Wrong options: hip flexed · knee extended · ilioinguinal (that risks femoral + LFCN)

Highest intraneural pressurehip flexed 90° + knee extended (excursion from sciatic notch to leg)

Percutaneous column screws – fluoroscopic views

View Shows
Obturator outlet ("teepee" / teardrop) Joint penetration · cranial–caudal position · supra-acetabular start point (AIIS pin)
Iliac inlet (inlet iliac oblique) Anterior–posterior position in pubic ramus → screw not exiting posterior ramus / not intrapelvic
Obturator inlet Supra-acetabular screw between inner + outer iliac tables
Iliac oblique Trajectory above sciatic notch · posterior column screw
Inlet SI joint penetration
IO / OO with hip + knee flexed Posterior column screw

Teardrop on obturator outletcolumn of bone AIIS → PSIS (ex-fix pins / screws)
✗ Wrong options: ASIS · sciatic buttress · roof

Antegrade AC screwstart gluteal pillar → toward pubic tubercle · retrograde = ramus → iliac wing

Elderly – acute THA with / without ORIF

Acute THA indicationselderly + osteopenia / comminution, pre-existing arthritis, marginal impaction (gull sign), PW comminution, femoral head fracture / damage, superomedial dome impaction, dislocation, delayed presentation

Elderly PW + dislocation + impaction / comminution / head damageacute ORIF + immediate THA (single stage) → superior function vs ORIF + delayed THA

THA constructwall fractures → buttress plate + multi-hole cup · column fractures → cage + cup · columns must be stable first

78-yo, posterior column + femoral head fracturePC ORIF + THA same sitting
✗ Wrong options: cup screws alone → cup migration, LaFlamme · staged · cup-cage (only for protrusio / discontinuity)

74-yo neglected insufficiency fracture, 4 mo, head damagehip reconstruction (THA, flanged / custom cup)
✗ Wrong options: ORIF · traction

Fracture-dislocation + articular injury + head impaction + loose bodies, ORIF alone~50% convert to THA; THA → better function, fewer complications

Kreder> 50 yr + marginal impaction + PW comminution → 54% early THA; residual displacement > 2 mm → arthritis

THA after acetabular fracture> 60 yr: ~30% late conversion · 10-yr implant survival 75–80%

Acute ORIF + THA not foryoung patients · isolated AC · small (10–20%) PW · transverse with good bone · ABC with secondary congruence

Postoperative weight bearing & hip contact pressures

Activity Hip contact force
Rising from chair on affected leg Highest (> walking); posterosuperior acetabulum
Full WB gait High
Isometrics, bed pan Approach walking, not exceed
Cane ~60% of walking
Toe-touch WB + passive abduction Lowest (< NWB — muscles contract in NWB)

Touch WB10–15 kg (< 20% BW) · partial WB = 20–25 kg (30–50% BW) → after transtectal transverse PW ORIF

6Complications

Complication Fact
Post-traumatic DJD Commonest; 80% native-hip survival at 20 yr after ORIF; ~20% need THA by 20 yr; risk: age > 40, T + PW and T-type, femoral head injury, marginal impaction, malreduction → THA or fusion
Heterotopic ossification Highest extended iliofemoral · KL intermediate · lowest ilioinguinal / Stoppa; ~25% incidence
Osteonecrosis 6–7% overall · 18% posterior patterns
Nerve injury Highest T + PW; sciatic (KL 2–10%), femoral / LFCN (ilioinguinal)
DVT / PE, infection, bleeding —
Intra-articular hardware Check obturator outlet
Abductor weakness —

Prognostic factors

Poor outcomemulti-system trauma · ↑ age · poor articular congruency / malreduction · marginal impaction · femoral head injury · post-traumatic arthritis · intra-op complications · delay > 3 wk

Strongest risk for THAarticular malreduction (linear relationship)
✗ Wrong options: > 50% THA at 20 yr · op time ↓ infection · delay ↓ malreduction · anterior column highest arthritis (PW is)

Protective vs early THAage < 40, simple pattern, initial displacement < 20 mm, anatomic reduction, no head injury
✗ Wrong options: gender · approach

PW + age > 50 + non-anatomic reductionhighest THA conversion
✗ Wrong options: AC · PC · AW · ABC

NOT a negative factorinvolvement of both columns (EXCEPT answer) · surgical approach

Matta resultsexcellent 40% · good 36% · fair 8% · poor 16%; clinical result tracks radiographic reduction

Young, simple transverse, anatomic, no head injury — 20-yr native hip survival> 75%

PROs after PW ORIFcorrelate with hip muscle strength + gait restoration
✗ Wrong options: age · arc of motion · immediate WB

Heterotopic ossification

Brooker classificationused to grade HO

Prophylaxisindomethacin ×1 wk, low-dose radiation, debride gluteus minimus (Orthobullets)

OB updateonly radiation 700–800 cGy within 72 h clearly effective · indomethacin unproven in acetabulum + prolonged use → ↑ nonunion · gluteus minimus debridement now questioned

Natural history~85% asymptomatic; ~15% disabling stiffness → excision (even early if sciatic compression); low symptomatic recurrence (technical ~30%); expect ↑ blood loss

✗ HO trapsgenerous gluteus medius debridement (→ Trendelenburg) · "most need excision" · "high symptomatic recurrence" · ISS / fracture pattern as cause · radiation causing HO

T-type via extended iliofemoral, HO at 3 mo despite radiationcause = surgical approach

Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome

Trauma · 2 / 67

1Basics

Definition

ARDSacute lung injury after polytrauma / long-bone fracture → progressive respiratory distress, refractory hypoxaemia, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema

Causes – acute endothelial damage

Triggersaspiration, infection, pancreatitis, multiple transfusions, lung injury, sepsis / shock, major trauma, large burns, fat emboli, thromboembolism, MOF

Cascadenon-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema → respiratory distress → refractory hypoxaemia → ↓ lung compliance

Genes & lab markers

IL-6 (interleukin 6)inflammatory marker most closely tied to systemic inflammatory response after orthopaedic injury (femur fracture) and its treatment (IM nailing)
✗ Wrong options: IL-1 · IL-10 (no correlation with treatment) · TNF-α · D-dimer (↑ after trauma but don't track treatment)

Statusresearch marker, not yet clinically applicable

Phases

Phase Timing Histology
Exudative Initial Hyaline membranes (fibrin)
Proliferative ~3 days Alveolar exudate resolves or organises
Fibrotic 3–4 weeks Alveolar ducts + spaces fibrose

3Presentation

Onsetacute, 12–48 h after injury

Symptomsdyspnoea, fever, mottled / cyanotic skin

Examresistant hypoxia, intercostal retractions, rales / crackles, rhonchi, tachypnoea

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnostic criteria

PaO₂ / FiO₂ Grade
< 300 mm Hg Mild (= acute lung injury, ALI)
< 200 mm Hg Moderate — ARDS threshold
< 100 mm Hg Severe

Other thresholdsrespiratory compliance < 40 mL/cm H₂O · PEEP > 10 cm H₂O · corrected expired minute volume > 10 L/min

Hallmarkhypoxaemia refractory to O₂

Key radiology findings

CXRdiffuse bilateral infiltrates, patchy air-space oedema, normal-sized heart (→ CHF less likely)

Serial CXRsearly identification in at-risk patients

Differential

Mimicscardiogenic pulmonary oedema (CHF, MI), bilateral pneumonia, SARS

5Management

Preventionearly stabilisation of long-bone (femur) fractures · monitor PEEP in at-risk patients · serial CXR

TreatmentPEEP ventilation + steroids · treat underlying cause

6Complications

Pneumothoraxbarotrauma from high-PEEP ventilation

Mortality~50% even with ICU care

X vs Y

ARDS Cardiogenic oedema
Oedema Non-cardiogenic Cardiogenic

Amputations

Trauma · 3 / 67

1Basics

Goals & epidemiology

Goalspreserve functional length + useful sensibility · prevent symptomatic neuroma + adjacent joint contracture · early prosthetic fitting · early return to work

Prevalence1.7 million amputees in USA · 80% for vascular insufficiency

Commonest causeupper limb = trauma · lower limb = vascular disease

Wound healing predictors & level selection

Predictor Threshold for healing
Serum albumin > 3.0 g/dL — best lab predictor (✗ Wrong options: total protein · Ca · CRP · ESR)
Total lymphocyte count > 1500 /mm³
ABI > 0.45
Ischaemic index > 0.5 (Doppler pressure at level ÷ brachial systolic)
TcPO₂ > 30 mm Hg (ideally 45)
Toe pressure > 40 mm Hg; will not heal < 20

TcPO₂ cut-offs> 30 healing (Orthobullets, OB) · > 40 normal healing, < 20 → amputation is end result (TO) — read the options

Wound healing depends onvascular supply + nutrition + immune status

Hyperbaric oxygen

Indicationcrush injury / acute open fracture (✓ NOT a contraindication)

HBO contraindication Why
Chemo (bleomycin) / radiation Bleomycin + O₂ → life-threatening pneumonitis
Pressure-sensitive implanted device AICD, pacemaker, dorsal column stimulator, insulin pump → malfunction
Undrained pneumothorax Gas embolism, tension PTX, pneumomediastinum
COPD Air trapping / blebs → PTX

Energy expenditure by amputation level

Level ↑ Energy over baseline
Syme 15%
Transtibial — traumatic 25% (long BKA 10%, short BKA 40%)
Transtibial — vascular 40%
Bilateral transtibial 40% (41%, OB)
Through-knee Between BKA and AKA (habitus dependent)
Transfemoral — traumatic 68% (Orthobullets) · 65% (Miller, OB)
Transfemoral — vascular 100%
AKA + BKA 118%
AKA + AKA > 200%

Ruleenergy ↑ with more proximal level; inversely proportional to residual length → amputate at lowest possible level

ExceptionSyme more efficient than midfoot despite being more proximal

Vascular > traumatic at the same level

Unilateral AKA > bilateral BKA in energy cost

Walking speed, fastest → slowesttrauma BKA → vascular Syme → trauma AKA → vascular BKA → vascular AKA (slowest, highest cost)

Childrenthrough-knee = most proximal level keeping normal walking speed without ↑ energy
✗ Wrong options: AKA · BKA · Chopart · Girdlestone

4Diagnosis & Classification

Stump closure techniques (TO)

Technique (TO) Description Key fact
Myofascial closure Fascial envelope over muscles Minimal stabilisation; used in severe ischaemia
Myoplasty Muscle sewn to opposing muscle over bone end Bursa, crepitus, pain → not recommended alone
Myodesis Muscle attached directly to bone / periosteum Recommended; contraindicated in severe ischaemia (wound breakdown)
Tenodesis Tendon fixed to bone Most secure + most physiologic; used in disarticulations (knee: patellar tendon → cruciate origin)

Landmine / blast zones (TO)

Zone (TO) Injury
Zone I Nearest blast: traumatic amputation, widespread destruction + contamination → nonviable
Zone II Focal muscle micro-lacerations + haemorrhage along NV bundles / fascial planes
Zone III Arteriole avulsion, impaired venous return, axonal reactive change

Amputation level after landmine (TO)border of zone II and III (muscle contracts, minimal oedema)

5Management

Upper-extremity amputation

Indicationsirreparable blood supply loss, severe soft-tissue loss, malignant tumour, smouldering infection, congenital

Upper vs lowermangled UE has far greater functional impact than LE amputation; nerve repair better in UE; replantation > UE amputation for function (worse more proximally, esp. around elbow)

UE salvage vs amputation (civilian + METALS)no significant difference in function or psychological outcome; no broadly accepted indications; MESS is a poor predictor in UE (MESI more reliable)
✗ Wrong options: blast = contraindication to salvage

Level Key facts
Transcarpal Divide finger flexors / extensors; anchor wrist motors to carpus
Wrist disarticulation Longer lever arm + better pronation / supination; preserve radial styloid flare (suspension); needs intact DRUJ; children — preserves distal radial + ulnar physes; harder to fit high-function prosthesis
Transradial Middle third ideal; better cosmesis; easier myoelectric fit; ≥ 5 cm ulna needed for elbow motion (little pronosupination)
Transhumeral Max length; ideal 4–5 cm above elbow; ≥ 5–7 cm residual for GH mechanics
Elbow disarticulation Children — avoids bony overgrowth of transhumeral
Shoulder disarticulation Retain humeral head for contour → shoulder hiking (unopposed girdle muscles) · child → scoliosis

Techniqueidentify + preserve named motor + sensory branches (myoelectric signal, TMR) · myodesis recommended

Return to work after UE amputationoffer psychological counselling
✗ Wrong options: FCE · wait for final prosthesis · full elbow ROM

Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)

Concepttransfer amputated major nerves into expendable remaining muscles → new discrete myoelectric signal

Proven forpost-amputation neuroma pain + better myoelectric prosthesis control
✗ Wrong options: brachial plexus neurapraxia · Parsonage-Turner · SCI · CTS

Transfemoral – adductor myodesis

Levelideal cut ~12 cm (10–15 cm) above knee (room for prosthetic knee; resect condylar flare)

Alignment5–10° adduction ideal

Adductor myodesisadductor magnus → drill holes at distal femur end (Gottschalk) → most important step

Benefitsdynamic muscle balance (vs unopposed abductors + flexors) · soft-tissue envelope / cushion · better prosthetic (suction) fit · efficient femur position

NOT a benefitpreserving femoral length (extra femur is actually resected) (EXCEPT answer)

Missed adductor myodesisfemur drifts into abduction / subcutaneous lateral thigh → side lurch, ↑ energy, persists despite good prosthesis
✗ Wrong options: flap length · failure to bevel · abductor myodesis

Transfemoral flapsusually equal anterior + posterior

Gritti-Stokesthrough femur at adductor tubercle; excise synovium; patella arthrodesed to femur end (end-bearing); better outcomes than transfemoral

Osseointegration

Conceptimplant in residual bone → transcutaneous stoma → prosthesis (transfemoral, transtibial)

Benefits↑ prosthesis wear, mobility, QoL, proprioception vs socket

Commonest complicationlow-grade soft-tissue infection, managed without surgery (oral antibiotics)
✗ Wrong options: failed integration · deep infection · peri-implant fracture

Knee disarticulation vs other levels

Indicationsambulatory patients who cannot have BKA · non-ambulatory patients

Techniquepatellar tendon sutured to cruciates in notch (tenodesis) · gastrocnemius padding

vs Transfemoral vs Transtibial (LEAP)
Less energy Slower walking speed
End-bearing limb, proprioception, sitting, lever arm Worse SIP (worst function at 2 yr of all levels)
↓ hip flexion contracture, thigh muscles preserved Physicians less satisfied (cosmesis, function — lost gastrocnemius padding)
Children — no overgrowth More dependence in transfers
Asymmetry of prosthetic knee (sitting + gait), limited knee components, cosmesis Decreased prosthesis use
No difference in prosthesis fitting Pain similar to AKA + BKA

Through-knee in zone of injurypoorest outcome of LE amputations; AKA ≈ BKA outcome (BKA faster); gender, prosthesis sophistication, muscle anchoring don't affect outcome

Transtibial – flaps

Level12–15 cm below joint (10–16 cm residual tibia); more distal → Achilles region (poor blood supply, padding); need 8–12 cm from ground for modern prostheses

Flaps (TO)non-ischaemic → equal anterior + posterior flaps · ischaemic → long posterior flap (better vascularity)
✗ Wrong options: long anterior flap

Dog earsleave in place in long posterior flap → preserve saphenous + sural arteries (posterior flap supply)
✗ Wrong options: ATA · PTA · peroneal

Fish-mouth (equal coronal) flaps in diabetics / PVD↑ anterior flap necrosis (Manoli)

Burgess (modified)standard long posterior flap; fibula cut 1–2 cm shorter than tibia; gastrocnemius fascial closure

Ertl bone bridge & osteomyoplasty

Ertltibia–fibula bone bridge (original = corticoperiosteal flap; modified = fibular strut) → stable platform for load transfer / end-bearing; prevents "chopsticking"

Modified Ertl vs Burgess Fact
Op + tourniquet time Longer
Reoperation Higher (hardware, nonunion, bone-bridge dislocation)
Wound / deep infection Equivalent
Flaps Any tension-free flap (posterior, skew, fish-mouth, medial, sagittal)
Function No definitive improvement (small retrospective series; TAOS pending)
Early fitting / immediate WB Contraindicated (needs union)

Osteomyoplasty vs myodesisenhanced end-bearing · fibular abduction = complication of myodesis (syndesmotic instability)
✗ Wrong options: early fitting · immediate WB · less morbidity

✗ Wrong option: fibula-pro-tibianot an amputation; fibular centralisation for tibial defects

Syme amputation – heel pad & contraindications

Syme = ankle disarticulation
✗ Wrong options: "hindfoot amputation"

Requirementspatent posterior tibial artery + stable, viable heel pad (most important)

ContraindicationABI < 0.5 in PT artery (diabetic)
✗ Wrong options: albumin 3.4 · osteomyelitis unless hindfoot / tibia · TcPO₂ 45 · neuropathy

Techniquemalleoli removed flush with tibial plafond + flares bevelled · heel pad secured to anterior tibia · tibialis anterior + EDL tenodesed to anterior heel pad (stop posterior migration)

Problemsskin slough (vascular) + heel-pad migration / hypermobility

Usesforefoot gangrene in diabetics; tumour, trauma · equinus is not its complication

Hindfoot & partial-foot amputation

Amputation Level Deformity / key fact
Pirogoff Remove forefoot + talus → calcaneotibial arthrodesis; calcaneus rotated 50–90° Walk without prosthesis
Chopart / Boyd Talonavicular + calcaneocuboid Equinus (equinovarus) → TA lengthening / tenotomy + tibialis anterior → talar neck
Lisfranc Tarsometatarsal (2nd MT osteotomised to keep medial cuneiform stable) Equinovarus — unopposed gastroc-soleus + tibialis posterior → keep peroneus brevis insertion (5th MT base) + TA lengthening; walking cast 4 wk
Transmetatarsal MT shafts Almost all need TA lengthening; appeals to patients refusing BKA; rocker-sole shoe + toe filler + carbon plate
Great toe Keep 1 cm of proximal phalanx base Preserves plantar fascia, sesamoids, FHB → ↓ transfer ulcers

Chopart (TO)forefoot gangrene to navicular in smoker → Chopart: preserves heel support, shoe + AFO, little shortening, heel-skin end-bearing, muscle balancing possible (tibialis anterior transfer + TA lengthening) — easier than Syme / Pirogoff

Tibialis anteriorinnervated by deep peroneal nerve

Not Chopart preventionposterior capsule release · TA → cuboid (cuboid removed) · FHL / peroneus brevis → calcaneus · Achilles shortening

Lisfranc supination preventionpreserve PB, peroneus tertius + plantar fascia around 5th MT base
✗ Wrong options: release tib post · TA → cuneiforms · Achilles lengthening alone

Lisfranc varusTA + tib post overpower peroneus brevis · equinus from loss of EDL + EHL · fixes: TAL / gastroc recession, STATT, 4th–5th flexor-to-extensor tenodesis, PB → PL

Lisfranc energy≈ BKA

Soft-tissue balancing requiredLisfranc
✗ Wrong options: Gritti-Stokes · transtibial · TMA · knee disarticulation

Commonest deformity after midfoot amputationequinovarus

Only partial-foot amputation functional in a shoetransmetatarsal (others need ankle-controlling prosthesis)

Hindquarter amputation (TO)

Standard hemipelvectomy (TO)posterior (gluteal) flap; disarticulates symphysis pubis + SI joint + limb

Anterior flap hemipelvectomy (TO)buttock / posterior thigh lesions; quadriceps myocutaneous flap on superficial femoral vessels

Extended hemipelvectomy (TO)+ sacrum / lumbar spine

Mortality (TO)once > 50% → now < 10%

Limb salvage vs amputation – decision factors

Highest impact on decision (LEAP)severity of soft-tissue injury
✗ Wrong options: reduction quality · smoking · insurance · time to debridement

2nd highestabsent plantar sensation — not an absolute contraindication; often recovers

High late-amputation riskhigh-energy foot trauma with 1st MT fracture or all 5 metatarsals (up to 20% at 1 yr)
✗ Wrong options: CRPS commonest

Late amputation after salvage associated withfracture nonunion, LE periarticular fracture, limb dysfunction, chronic pain
✗ Wrong options: UE injury (lower rate) · nerve injury · flap failure · diaphyseal

Limb salvage vs amputation – outcomes

Study Finding
LEAP (civilian) SIP + return to work not different at 2 yr; ~50% return to work; infection 25%; salvage → longer to full WB + more rehospitalisation
LEAP — mangled foot / ankle with free flap or ankle fusion Worse (higher) SIP than BKA (✗ Wrong options: faster walk · more RTW)
METALS (military) Amputation → slightly better PROs, lower PTSD, more return to vigorous sport / activity; depression, pain, RTW same

Strongest predictor of patient satisfaction / PROs after LE amputationability to return to work (+ no depression, faster walking, less pain)
✗ Wrong options: age · gender · graft · plantar sensation · amputation vs salvage · cosmesis · counselling

Higher SIP (Sickness Impact Profile)= more disability

Psychological counsellingimproves outcomes (rehab team incl. psychiatrist, social worker)

6Complications

Complication Fact
Wound healing See predictors
Contracture Adjacent joints → early mobilisation, positioning
HO More common in trauma amputations
Infection ~34% in trauma amputations
Neuroma 20–30%; prevent with nerve handling; treat with TMR
Phantom limb pain 53–100% of traumatic amputations → mirror therapy
Terminal bone overgrowth Commonest paediatric complication (up to 50% of transosseous)

Paediatric amputation – terminal bone overgrowth

Mechanismdisorganised appositional growth at cut bone end (periosteal, endosteal, heterotopic) → tapering spike → skin ulceration, pain

Preventiondisarticulation (articular-cartilage-covered end never overgrows) · epiphyseal / osteochondral cap

Treatmentrevision with bone-end capping or Ertl
✗ Wrong options: HO + NSAIDs · neuroma + TMR · remodelling · osteomyelitis

Knee disarticulation in child avoidsbone overgrowth; costs proximal tibial physis → shorter limb
✗ Wrong options: neurogenic pain · contractures

Phantom & neuroma pain

Mirror therapyfor phantom pain: visual feedback corrects proprioceptive mismatch
✗ Wrong options: proprioception training · flexor tendon · plumbism · ACL

Ankle Fractures

Trauma · 4 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence187 / 100,000 adults / yr

Bimodalyoung men 15–24 yr · elderly women 75–84 yr

Pattern splitisolated malleolus 70% · bimalleolar 20% · trimalleolar 7%

Risk factorsmale, younger age, obesity, smoking, alcohol

Associatedopen 2% · syndesmotic injury 10% · chondral injury · peroneal tendon tears 4%

Anatomy – ligaments

Complex Components Key fact
Deltoid Superficial (MM → navicular, sustentaculum, talus) — resists hindfoot eversion · Deep (MM → talus) — resists talar ER Deep deltoid = primary restraint to anterolateral talar displacement; inserts on posterior colliculus
Lateral ATFL — restrains anterior displacement, IR, inversion; most often injured · CFL — deep to peronei; 2nd · PTFL — strongest, least injured —
Syndesmosis AITFL · PITFL · IOL · interosseous membrane · inferior transverse ligament See below

Syndesmotic ligament anatomy

Ligament Tibial origin Fibular insertion
AITFL Chaput tubercle (anterolateral tibia) Wagstaffe tubercle (anterior fibula)
PITFL — strongest Volkmann (posterior malleolus / posterolateral tibia) Posterior lateral malleolus
IOL Distal continuation of interosseous membrane —
Inferior transverse Runs with PITFL to posterolateral plafond —

Pilon fragmentsChaput (anterolateral) = AITFL · Volkmann (posterolateral) = PITFL
✗ Wrong options: ATFL · IOL · ITL · tibionavicular (deltoid)

Avulsion eponymsTillaux–Chaput = AITFL off tibia · LeFort–Wagstaffe = AITFL off fibula (with SER)

Anatomy – tendons & nerves at risk

Structure Location At risk with
Peroneal tendons (PL, PB) Posterior fibular groove Posterolateral (antiglide) fibular plate
Tibialis posterior Posteroinferior to MM Posteriorly placed MM screws
ATA + deep peroneal n. Between EDL + EHL Anterior approach
PTA + tibial n. Behind MM, between FDL + FHL Posteromedial approach
Superficial peroneal n. Crosses fibula posterior → anterior ~5–7 cm above tip (3–12 cm) Proximal direct lateral, posterolateral, anterior / anterolateral
Sural n. Posterolateral Posterolateral + lateral approaches

SPN factsL4–S1 · branches off CPN at fibular neck · motor to PL + PB (eversion) · subcutaneous in lower third of leg · two terminal branches (medial + intermediate dorsal cutaneous)
✗ Wrong options: 1st web space = deep peroneal · dorsiflexors = deep peroneal

Biomechanics

Talustrapezoidal, wider anteriorly → dorsiflexion = fibula ER + lateral translation; plantarflexion → narrow posterior talus, talar IR

Fibulalateral buttress against talar shift

1 mm lateral talar shift↓ tibiotalar contact area 42% (40–42%)

2Mechanism

Usualtwisting injury

Lauge-Hansen classification

Namefirst word = foot position, second = force on foot relative to tibia; predicts MRI ligament injury in < 50%

Type Stages Fibula pattern
Supination–adduction (SAD) 1 talofibular sprain / distal fibular avulsion (tip) → 2 vertical MM + anteromedial plafond impaction Low transverse, infrasyndesmotic
Supination–external rotation (SER) — commonest 1 AITFL sprain → 2 short oblique fibula (anteroinferior → posterosuperior) → 3 PITFL rupture / posterior malleolus → 4 transverse MM or deltoid At syndesmosis (Weber B)
Pronation–abduction (PAB) 1 transverse MM / deltoid → 2 AITFL → 3 transverse comminuted fibula above syndesmosis (butterfly) Comminuted, above / at syndesmosis
Pronation–external rotation (PER) 1 transverse MM / deltoid → 2 AITFL → 3 short oblique / spiral fibula (anterosuperior → posteroinferior) above joint → 4 PITFL / posterior malleolus High spiral (Weber C); Maisonneuve

PAB failure sequencemedial → AITFL → lateral (medial-to-lateral disruption)

✗ Wrong options: "pronation-adduction" / "supination-abduction"do not exist

Supination–adduction specifics

SAD = 5–20% of ankle fractureshighest talar / hindfoot injury (talar OCD + medial plafond impaction) → PTOA up to 80%

Vertical MM fracture on axial CTSAD

Hyperdorsiflexion associationSAD with plafond impaction

3Presentation

Symptomssevere pain, unable to bear weight

Examswelling, ecchymosis; medial tenderness / swelling / ecchymosis NOT reliable for deltoid competence (Tornetta) · palpate proximal fibula (Maisonneuve) · fracture blisters, tenting, open wounds · PVD, diabetic neuropathy

On-field obvious fracture-dislocation in athlete (TO)after ABC → splint limb in situ as it lies; assessment < 60 s; reduce after leaving field of play
✗ Wrong options: reduce on field · immediate shift · oral analgesic

Pulseless foot with fracture-dislocationreduce + splint → re-evaluate pulses
✗ Wrong options: vascular consult · CTA · angiogram first

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

View / study Use
AP, lateral, mortise Ankle series
Mortise (TO) AP in 15° internal rotation (clears fibular shadow) — best for articular surfaces
ER stress (manual) Mortise view, foot dorsiflexed + ER, tibia stabilised → deltoid competence; more sensitive than tenderness / ecchymosis
Gravity stress Lateral decubitus; = manual stress
Full-length tib-fib Rule out Maisonneuve (any medial injury / isolated posterior malleolus / widened MCS without fibula fracture)
CT Trimalleolar (posterior malleolus size + morphology — axial + sagittal; 25% of surgeons change plan) · SAD (anteromedial impaction, talar cartilage) · loose bodies, comminution · suspected syndesmotic malreduction post-op · occult nonunion
MRI Deltoid, syndesmosis (lambda sign), lateral ligaments, peroneals, talar OCL — utility controversial

Radiographic parameters

Parameter Normal Abnormal / meaning
Medial clear space ≤ 4 mm (mortise or stress) > 5 mm with ER stress on dorsiflexed ankle → deep deltoid tear · > 4 mm or ≥ 1 mm more than superior clear space = deltoid incompetent (SER-4)
Tibiofibular clear space < 6 mm on AP + mortise, measured 1 cm above joint Widened → syndesmotic injury (fixation if > 5 mm on AP, treatment section)
Tibiofibular overlap > 6 mm on AP, > 1 mm on mortise ↓ → syndesmotic injury / malreduction → CT (e.g. 2 mm overlap on AP)
Talocrural angle 83 ± 4° (OB) · 75–86° (one OB explanation) Fibular shortening → ↑ angle → lateral talar tilt
Talar tilt < 5° —
Talar tilt / asymmetry — > 2 mm = instability marker
Ball / dime sign (TO) Unbroken curve from recess at fibular tip to lateral talar process Absent → fibula shortened / malreduced (✗ Wrong options: deltoid tear · ATFL · syndesmosis)

Talocrural angleline ⟂ plafond (or tibial axis) vs line between malleolar tips; not 100% reliable for fibular length

Weber B stable fracture on APtibiofibular clear space < 4 mm
✗ Wrong options: overlap < 3 mm · Weber C · PER · MCS > 5 mm

Posterior malleolus signsdouble contour, misty mountains, spur sign

Spur sign (hyperplantarflexion variant)double cortical density at inferomedial tibial metaphysis; 79% sensitive, 100% specific; pathognomonic

Fleck sign (TO)cortical avulsion off lateral malleolus → superior peroneal retinaculum injury → peroneal subluxation
✗ Wrong options: ATFL avulsion · Tillaux · Wagstaffe

Stability assessment – stress radiographs & deltoid competence

Best test of deltoid competenceER stress radiograph (manual or gravity)
✗ Wrong options: anterior drawer = ATFL · IR / inversion stress · palpation · squeeze · Canale view

ORIF indication in isolated fibula fractureMCS widening on gravity stress (= SER-4 / bimalleolar equivalent)
✗ Wrong options: medial tenderness / swelling · squeeze test · Cotton (intra-op)

Deep deltoid intact even with 8–10 mm stress widening (recent MRI studies) — MRI role controversial

Danis-Weber / AO-OTA 44 Level Note

Type Fragment

Differential

Mimic Clue

5Management

Rotational ankle fracture
  • Stable (no talar shift on stress)→splint / boot, early WBAT
  • Talar shift / bimalleolar / Maisonneuve / Bosworth / open→ORIF
    • after fixation → stress syndesmosis→fix if unstable
Syndesmosis after malleolar fixation
  • Posterior malleolus fractured→fix PM first (restores PITFL)
  • Cotton / ER stress still widens→open reduction + screw or suture button

Operative criteria

Nonoperative ORIF
Stable isolated MM (no talar shift), avulsion tips Any talar displacement
Stable isolated LM (stress negative) Bimalleolar / bimalleolar-equivalent
PM < 25% and < 2 mm step-off, stable syndesmosis PM > 25% or > 2 mm step-off, syndesmotic instability, posterior talar subluxation
Unfit for surgery Maisonneuve · Bosworth · open · symptomatic malleolar nonunion
— LM > 3 mm displacement

Stable fractures – nonoperative management

Stable Weber B (stress negative, < 3 mm, TCA 83°)below-knee splint 2–4 wk → WBAT in boot
✗ Wrong options: TCC · MRI · CT · ORIF

Stable LMremovable walking boot + progressive WB
✗ Wrong options: strict NWB cast · fibula ORIF ± medial repair

Isolated MM, no talar shiftNWB 4–6 wk; > 95% union

Unstable fractures in elderlyoperate on same indications as young; cast for unstable (esp. PAB) → 48–73% malunion / nonunion

Medial malleolus fixation

Technique Indication
Lag screws ⟂ fracture Transverse MM
Antiglide / buttress plate + lag screws, screws parallel to joint Vertical shear MM (SAD) — biomechanically superior to screws alone
Tension band Fragment too small, poor bone

Bicortical 3.5 mm fully threaded (lag by technique) > unicortical 4.0 mm partially threaded

Supination–adduction – marginal impaction & fixation

Unique, must-recognise featureanteromedial plafond marginal impaction

Unaddressed impactionmalunion with anteromedial pain → surgical correction

Lateral malleolus fixation

Construct Fact
Lateral plate (1/3 tubular / anatomic) Distal bicortical screws may be intra-articular
Posterolateral antiglide plate Biomechanically stronger than lateral; screws exit anteriorly; peroneal (brevis) irritation — hardware removal up to 43%
Locking plate Stiffest / most rigid (✗ Wrong options: fibular nail · antiglide · non-locked bridge · lag screws alone); risks prominence, excess stiffness
Retrograde IM fibular nail Poor soft tissue / wound-healing risk

Plate modesneutralisation protects a lag screw · buttress = under-contoured plate + axilla screw (compression vs shear) · antiglide = uncontoured plate fixed at fracture apex (posterolateral in SER) · bridge = relative stability · tension band = tension side of eccentric load

Absolute stabilityarticular fractures: PM > 25% / large PM 45% → ORIF with absolute stability

BimalleolarORIF any displacement; ORIF > closed; early WB → better ROM, earlier return

Syndesmosis – diagnosis & intra-operative testing

Incidence by fibula levelWeber A < 10% · Weber B 40–50% · Weber C > 80%; fixation usually not needed if fibula fracture within 4.5 cm of plafond

Most unstable directionanterior–posterior → lateral stress view more reliable

Cotton (hook) testbone hook pulls fibula laterally under fluoro after fixation → most reliable intra-op test; best done in sagittal plane, 100 N, lateral view (van den Bekerom)

ER stress after fibular fixation widenssyndesmosis injured → open reduction + fixation of syndesmosis
✗ Wrong options: arthrotomy · close · revise fibula · ex-fix

Cotton test without wideningno further fixation

Syndesmosis – reduction technique, fixation & outcomes

Most important for outcomeanatomic syndesmotic reduction
✗ Wrong options: immediate WB · OCD debridement · medial repair · neutral casting

Malreduction rate16–51% (> 50% reported; up to 30% with screws / flexible fixation on CT)

✗ Wrong options: radiographic parameters · incisura view

Open reductionshown to guide anatomic reduction
✗ Wrong options: clamp 2 cm too proximal · bump + IR · plantarflexion = ER → malreduction · dorsiflexion (no effect)

Clamp rule Detail
Lateral tine Directly on lateral fibular (malleolar) ridge (✗ Wrong options: posterior to ridge → sagittal malreduction)
Medial tine Mid-medial tibia = anterior third of tibia on true lateral
Axis Parallel to trans-syndesmotic angle / joint line
Level 1–2 cm above plafond (incisura)
Force Judicious — avoid over-compression
No Clamp on malleolar tips

Fibular shorteningfirst causes syndesmotic malreduction (lengthening → impingement; gap → nonunion) → restore length, alignment, rotation (dime sign / Shenton line)

Ankle positionreduce at neutral; full dorsiflexion not required
✗ Wrong options: "complete dorsiflexion" → stays widened

Fixation fact Value
Implant 1–2 screws or suture button, 2–4 cm above joint
Angle 20–30° posterior → anterior (fibula posterior to tibia)
Cortices / size 3 or 4 cortices, 3.5 or 4.5 mm — no proven difference
Suture button Lowest malreduction + reoperation
Screw retention ≥ 8–12 wk (Orthobullets) · ≥ 12 wk (OB) — NWB, screws can't take gait loads

Retained intact screwmay be worse than loosened / broken screw; broken ≈ loose; removing broken screw doesn't help · remove intact screw if painful prominence + dorsiflexion < 10° (~9 mo)

Posterior malleolus fixationrestores PITFL (strongest syndesmotic ligament) → 70% stiffness vs 40% with syndesmotic screw alone → obviates syndesmotic fixation in most cases; outcomes ≥ screw fixation; still stress-test after

Definition (TO)proximal-third fibula fracture + distal syndesmotic disruption + MM fracture / deltoid → pronation–external rotation

Neuropathyindependent risk factor for complications after ankle fracture (✗ Wrong options: DR · patella · metatarsal · distal femur) · most important predictor (✗ Wrong options: BMI · CKD III · age · sex)

Complication ratesabsent pulses 83% · neuropathy 92% → neuropathy > absent pulses · surgical complications up to 40% · deep infection up to 20% · cast skin breakdown up to 50%

Brachial Plexus Injuries

Trauma · 5 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Traumatic BPI pattern Share
Complete (all roots, supraclavicular) 75–80% — commonest
C5–C6 upper trunk (Erb) 20–25%
C8–T1 (Klumpke) 0.6–3%

Causehigh-speed vehicle, mostly motorcycle (83%)

Spectrumtraumatic · obstetric (Erb, Klumpke) · burners / stingers · Parsonage-Turner

Plexus anatomy – cord / trunk innervation & lesion localisation

Level Branches
Roots Dorsal scapular (rhomboids, C5) · long thoracic (serratus anterior, C5–7) · phrenic contribution (C3–5)
Upper trunk (C5–6) Suprascapular (SS, IS) · nerve to subclavius
Lateral cord Musculocutaneous · lateral root of median (FCR, PT) · lateral pectoral (clavicular pec major)
Medial cord Medial pectoral · medial brachial + antebrachial cutaneous · ulnar · medial root of median
Posterior cord Upper + lower subscapular (subscapularis, teres major) · thoracodorsal (latissimus) · axillary (deltoid, teres minor) · radial (triceps, BR, wrist + finger extensors)

✗ Wrong options: long thoracic (does not meet there)

✗ Wrong options: C4 · middle trunk · lateral cord · axillary nerve

Posterior cord lesionspares supraspinatus (suprascapular, upper trunk) (EXCEPT answer) · clavicle fragment on posterior cord → radial numbness + weak abduction, IR, wrist extension

Subscapularisupper subscapular nerve consistently from posterior cord (lower subscapular variably from axillary)
✗ Wrong options: biceps = lateral cord · pec major = medial + lateral · rhomboid = C5 root · supraspinatus = upper trunk

✗ Wrong options: C5–7 / lateral cord = musculocutaneous · C5–6 / upper trunk = suprascapular · C5–7 roots = long thoracic · C8–T1 / medial cord = ulnar

Cord lesion (TO) Deficit

Posterior Subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary, radial → can't IR, elevate, extend; sensory loss over deltoid

Can't flex fingers + no ulnar-side sensation (TO)C8

Key radiology findings

Study Finding / use
CXR (PA + lat) 1st / 2nd rib fracture → plexus injury · old rib fractures matter for intercostal transfer · inspiration / expiration → paralysed diaphragm (upper root)
C-spine AP + lateral Transverse process fracture → root avulsion
Scapula / shoulder (AP + axillary) Scapulothoracic dissociation → root avulsion + major vascular injury
Clavicle Fracture may signal BPI
CT myelography Gold standard for root level; avulsion → meningocele; do at 3–4 wk (clot dissipates, meningocele forms)
MRI Lesions distal to roots; pseudomeningocele (T2), empty root sleeves (T1), cord shift away from midline (T1), neuromas

Electrodiagnostics

Test Fact
EMG Fibrillations 10–14 d proximal muscles, 3–6 wk distal; test rhomboids, serratus, cervical paraspinals for pre vs post
NCV / SNAP SNAP preserved proximal to DRG → preganglionic
NAP (intra-op) Across lesion; detects reinnervation months before EMG; NAP negative = neurapraxic · NAP positive = axonotmetic (Orthobullets wording)
SSEP / MEP More sensitive than EMG / NCV for root–cord continuity; at 4–6 wk (Wallerian); stimulate Erb's point, record scalp

5Management

Traumatic brachial plexus injury
  • Sharp / open / iatrogenic / vascular / expanding haematoma→explore < 1 wk
  • Near-total, high energy (avulsion likely)→early surgery 3–6 wk
  • Partial upper plexus, low energy / GSW→observe
    • plateau at 3–6 mo→delayed surgery (not > 6 mo)

Operative criteria (timing)

Timing Indication
Immediate (< 1 wk) Sharp penetrating (not GSW), iatrogenic, open, progressive deficit, vascular injury / expanding haematoma
Early (3–6 wk) Near-total plexus, high energy · preganglionic → explore + reconstruct within 6 wk (OB)
Delayed (3–6 mo) Partial upper plexus, low energy, plateaued recovery · postganglionic: wait 6 wk–6 mo
Observe Most; GSW without vascular injury → 3 months

Techniques

Technique Fact
Direct repair Rare — acute sharp injuries only
Nerve graft Common for postganglionic traction; upper + middle trunk best; donors sural, medial brachial cutaneous, MABC; vascularised ulnar (superior ulnar collateral a.) if C8–T1 avulsed
Neurotisation (nerve transfer) Expendable motor nerve → important denervated muscle; reduces high injury to low injury, faster reinnervation
Extraplexal donors Spinal accessory (CN XI), intercostals, contralateral C7, hypoglossal (CN XII)
Intraplexal donors Phrenic, median / ulnar fascicles, pectoral
Muscle / tendon transfer Isolated adult C8–T1 (too far to reinnervate intrinsics) · late presentation · gracilis = commonest free muscle

Oberlin / double fascicular transferulnar fascicle → biceps branch + median fascicle → brachialis branch → elbow flexion

Calcaneus Fractures

Trauma · 6 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest tarsal fracture~65% of tarsal fractures (OB)

Intra-articular60–75% (Orthobullets) · 75% (OB) · tuberosity fractures 1–3% · avulsion + tongue-type < 15%

Open17% (15–20%) → no ↑ infection, ↑ wound complications

Tuberosity fracturespeak in women, 7th decade

Associated injuries

Association Rate
Calcaneocuboid joint extension 63%
Vertebral fracture 10%
Contralateral calcaneus 10%
Peroneal tendon instability (SPR tear) ~20% — commonest acute concurrent pathology
Foot compartment syndrome 10% (Orthobullets) · 3–10% (TO)

Fracture anatomy – constant fragment, sustentaculum & FHL

Facetsposterior = largest, main weight-bearing · middle on sustentaculum (anteromedial) · anterior often confluent with middle · sinus tarsi = calcaneal interosseous sulcus + talar sulcus

Constant (superomedial / sustentacular) fragmentsustentaculum tali; stays attached to talus by interosseous + medial talocalcaneal ligaments (+ deltoid); lateral fragments + tuberosity are reduced to it
✗ Wrong options: held by Achilles · by navicular · displaces superolateral

FHLwraps inferiorly around sustentaculum in a groove · medial to posterior facet, inferior to middle facet; origin inferior ⅔ posterior fibula + interosseous membrane

FHL problem Cause Sign
Iatrogenic Lateral → medial drill / screws too long into constant fragment Fixed flexed hallux post-op
Stenosis / tear Sustentaculum tali fracture Pain / popping with great-toe flexion
Entrapment Marked posterior facet displacement Limited hallux motion

✗ FHL trapsbeak / tuberosity (Achilles) · lateral wall · FDL runs superior to sustentaculum (lesser-toe flexion) · plantar paraesthesia = medial plantar nerve · spring ligament

Bifurcate ligamentdorsal anterior process → cuboid + navicular; resists plantarflexion–inversion; EDB also originates there

Blood supply

Extensile lateral flaplateral calcaneal branch of peroneal artery (± lateral malleolar + lateral tarsal)
✗ Wrong options: branch of ATA · lateral malleolar a.

Heel padmedial calcaneal branch of posterior tibial artery
✗ Wrong options: lateral calcaneal · sinus tarsi a. · tarsal canal a. (those feed talus)

2Mechanism

Intra-articularaxial load (fall from height, MVC)

Primary fracture lineoblique shear → superomedial (constant) + superolateral (posterior facet) fragments · secondary line decides tongue vs joint depression

Tuberosity (avulsion)osteoporosis + violent triceps surae contraction with forced dorsiflexion / knee extended · tight gastroc · neuropathy

Anterior processinversion + plantarflexion → bifurcate ligament avulsion

Stress↑ activity with relative energy deficiency; runners, military recruits, female athlete triad, obesity, after hip / knee arthroplasty

3Presentation

Heelswollen, shortened, widened, apparent varus

Posterior heel skintenting, blanching, ecchymosis with tuberosity / tongue fractures → urgent fixation

Fracture blistersmust epithelialise before surgery · wrinkle sign (Langer lines) = skin ready

Checkcompartments, nerves, pulses (severe PVD may preclude surgery), Achilles continuity, plantarflexion strength

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

View / study Use
AP, lateral, oblique foot Standard
Broden Posterior facet; ankle neutral, ~45° IR, beam 40, 30, 20, 10° cephalad; intra-op reduction check
Harris (axial) Tuberosity widening, shortening, varus; max dorsiflexion, beam 45°
AP ankle Lateral wall extrusion → fibular impingement
CT (2–3 mm) Gold standard · 30° semicoronal = posterior + middle facets (Sanders) · axial = CC joint · sagittal = tuberosity · axial CT shows peroneal dislocation
MRI Only for stress fracture with normal X-ray: T2 oedema first, later T1 low-signal fracture line
Sign / angle Normal Fracture
Böhler angle 20–40° ↓ (posterior facet collapse)
Crucial angle of Gissane 120–145° ↑
Double-density sign — Lateral portion of posterior facet depressed / rotated ~90° into body, separated from sustentaculum → subtalar incongruity
Calcaneal shortening, varus tuberosity — Present

Böhler angleline anterior process top → posterior facet top vs line along superior tuberosity (lateral view)

Gissaneline along lateral posterior facet vs line anterior to calcaneal beak

Essex-Lopresti classification

Type Secondary line
Tongue-type Axial plane beneath facet, exiting posteriorly — posterior facet stays attached to tuberosity → Achilles pulls fragment up
Joint depression Behind posterior facet

Sanders classification (coronal CT, widest posterior facet)

Type Posterior facet Treatment
I Non-displaced (any number of lines) Nonop
II 1 line → 2 fragments ORIF
III 2 lines → 3 fragments ORIF
IV > 3 lines, comminuted (≥ 4 fragments) ORIF + primary subtalar arthrodesis

Sanders III vs II6.5× PTOA, 4× subtalar fusion

Beavis classification (tuberosity)

Type Fracture
1 Sleeve — small cortical shell avulsed
2 Beak — oblique line from superior posterior facet running posteriorly
3 Infrabursal — from mid-tuberosity

Anterior process fracture types

Type Description
I Non-displaced avulsion
II Displaced, no CC joint
III Displaced, involves CC joint

Extra-articular (25%)anterior process (bifurcate), sustentaculum, tuberosity (Achilles avulsion)

5Management

Calcaneus fracture
  • Tongue-type / tuberosity + skin threatened → splint 30° PF→urgent fixation
  • Sanders I, small extra-articular, comorbid→NWB cast 10–12 wk
  • Sanders II–III→ORIF at 10–14 d (wrinkle sign)
  • Sanders IV→ORIF + primary subtalar fusion

Operative criteria

Nonoperative (NWB cast 10–12 wk) Operative
Small extra-articular < 1 cm, Achilles intact, < 2 mm Displaced tongue-type > 1 cm, threatened skin, open
Sanders I Sanders II + III: facet > 2–3 mm, flattened Böhler, varus tuberosity
Near-normal Böhler (20–40°) Large extra-articular, > 10° varus / valgus
Anterior process < 25% CC joint Anterior process > 25% CC joint
Smoker, diabetes, PVD (avoid wound complications) Displaced sustentaculum
Elderly low-demand tuberosity < 1 cm, skin OK Sanders IV → primary subtalar arthrodesis

Stress fractureNWB short-leg cast 6 wk (well-padded heel) / CAM boot + NWB

Cast technique (10–12 wk)mild equinus, posterior heel window, weekly cast changes (skin complications)

Timing of ORIF10–14 days (swelling + blisters resolve, wrinkle sign) · no benefit to early surgery · except displaced tuberosity / tongue with skin compromise → urgent

Goals (TO)posterior facet congruity · restore height, width, length, Böhler angle · correct hindfoot varus (TO)
✗ Wrong options: correct talar declination (that's talar neck)

Tongue-type / tuberosity fracture – urgent fixation

Why urgentAchilles pulls fragment proximal + posterior → posterior skin necrosis (> 20%)
✗ Wrong options: subtalar arthrosis · nonunion · AVN · compartment syndrome · better reduction

Splint30° plantarflexion (max PF) to relax skin

Fixationimmediate, minimally invasive / percutaneous lag screws posterosuperior tuberosity → inferior + distal (perpendicular to fracture) · ORIF bone-to-bone if large · ± gastrocnemius recession (Strayer)

✗ Tuberosity trapscast in equinus · excise fragment + reattach Achilles (large fragment, tension lost) · percutaneous K-wires (too weak vs triceps) · extensile lateral approach with swelling · delayed ORIF · primary arthrodesis (beak is extra-articular)

Posterior approach (tuberosity)prone, midline; lag screws / tension band / Krackow through tunnels; restricted WB 6 wk + 6 wk progression

Approaches & techniques

Technique Key facts
Closed reduction + percutaneous pinning Minimally displaced tongue-type, severe PVD / soft-tissue compromise; Essex-Lopresti manoeuvre; pins out 8–10 wk; ± distracting ex-fix (tuberosity, cuboid, tibia)
Extensile lateral (L-shaped) Vertical limb between fibula + Achilles, horizontal toward 5th MT base; full-thickness flap (lateral calcaneal a.); high wound complications; sural nerve + peroneals in flap; bone graft adds nothing
Sinus tarsi Tip of fibula → 4th MT base, 2–4 cm; EDB up, peroneals back; sees posterior facet, anterolateral fragment, lateral wall; ↓ wound complications, ↓ infection, ↓ op time, better Maryland foot scores; same Böhler restoration; ↑ radiation; sural nerve at greatest risk (identify inferiorly)
Arthroscopic-assisted Anterolateral + posterolateral portals; ↓ dissection; ↑ swelling, demanding
Primary subtalar arthrodesis Sanders IV; restore height + fuse; avoids second surgery

Post-op (sinus tarsi)NWB 6–8 wk; ankle ROM from 2 wk

Positive prognostic factor (Sanders II, 2 fragments)Sanders classification
✗ Wrong options: sex · age 40 · labourer job · approach

Surgery reducesPTOA / subtalar fusion ~6× (5.5–6×)
✗ Wrong options: faster RTW · ↑ subtalar ROM · ↓ nonunion (nonunion is rare)

Sanders II, young healthy non-smokerORIF
✗ Wrong options: cast · fusion · percutaneous (tongue only) · ex-fix

68-yo healthy, blistersdelayed ORIF (age > 50 no longer absolute contraindication; comorbidities matter more)

Open calcaneus fractures (TO)

Medial wound < 4 cm, closeable, stable (TO)serial I&D → standard ORIF when swelling settles (Sanders III)
✗ Wrong options: percutaneous · ex-fix

Lateral wounds / medial > 4 cm / not closeable / unstable after 7–10 d (TO)open reduction through wound + percutaneous fixation

✗ Wrong options: 3–5× infection · ex-fix only

6Complications

Complication Fact
Wound complications 10–25% (Orthobullets) · 10–35% (OB) · delayed wound healing / dehiscence = commonest (up to 25%) · deep infection 1–4% closed
Subtalar arthritis ↑ with nonop; commonest complication of nonop
Sural neuroma Extensile lateral / sinus tarsi
FHL injury Long lateral→medial screws at sustentaculum
Compartment syndrome 10% → claw toes
Peroneal tendinitis / impingement Lateral wall blowout; typical after nonop
Malunion Loss of height, widening, varus, impingement
Overall ~40% complication rate

Wound complications, approach & sural nerve

Risk factors (TO)smoking · diabetes, open fracture, single-layer closure, higher Sanders, long op, ↑ EBL, many people in OR, delay to surgery, ↑ BMI, less surgeon experience
✗ Wrong options: RA · steroids · alcohol

Not wound risk factors (OB)workers' comp, allograft, contralateral fracture, male sex

Prevention (TO)tourniquet, no smoking, full-thickness flap, drain, two-layer closure ends → middle, sutures 2–3 wk, no ROM during that time, keep hardware away from incision corner

Superficial dehiscence after sinus tarsi in smokerstop PT, immobilise, local wound care (± oral antibiotics) · deep / purulent → serial debridement
✗ Wrong options: I&D · hardware removal

Sural neuroma (burning lateral pain, 7 cm above heel)excise + bury sural nerve in muscle or vein
✗ Wrong options: SPN neuroplasty · subtalar fusion · hardware removal at 6 mo

Nerve by approachsinus tarsi / extensile = sural · direct lateral fibula + anterolateral ankle = SPN · posteromedial = tibial nerve + PTA

Malunion triad↓ height (talus dorsiflexed, talar declination < 20°), ↑ width (lateral wall exostosis), varus

Sequel Cause
Anterior tibiotalar impingement / ↓ dorsiflexion Loss of posterior facet height → dorsiflexed talus (talar declination < 20°)
Subfibular / peroneal impingement, peroneal tendinitis Lateral wall blowout + widening (✗ Wrong options: hindfoot valgus (uncommon))
Shoe-wear problems ↑ width

Malunion type (Stephens–Sanders) Features Treatment
I Lateral exostosis, no subtalar arthritis Lateral wall resection (exostectomy)
II Exostosis + subtalar arthritis Lateral wall resection + subtalar fusion

✗ Wrong options: ASO lace-up · UCBL · medial wedge

Capitellum Fractures

Trauma · 7 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequency1% of elbow fractures · 6% of distal humerus fractures

Associatedradial head and / or LUCL injury in up to 60%

Anatomy

Radiocapitellar jointkey static stabiliser: longitudinal + valgus stability; capitellar excision → coronal instability if medial structures are torn

LUCL relationshipintegral to posterolateral complex → don't destabilise LUCL during fixation

Blood supplyenters posterolateral → preserve during exposure

2Mechanism

Mechanismlow-energy FOOSH; axial compression through radial head with elbow semi-flexed → shear of anterior capitellum

3Presentation

Symptomselbow pain, swelling, ± wrist pain

Exammechanical block to flexion / extension and / or rotation; instability; NV exam

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Best viewlateral elbow (+ AP, radiocapitellar view)

Double-arc signpathognomonic on lateral: subchondral bone of displaced capitellum + lateral trochlear ridge → coronal shear fracture extending into trochlea · also called "double bubble"
✗ Wrong options: sagittal lateral epicondyle · coronal medial condyle · olecranon · trans-olecranon dislocation

CTlow threshold; delineates anatomy, trochlear involvement, posterior comminution

Bryan & Morrey classification (McKee modification)

Type Description Treatment
I — Hahn-Steinthal Large osseous capitellar fragment, may involve trochlea Displaced > 2 mm → ORIF
II — Kocher-Lorenz Articular cartilage shear with little subchondral bone Displaced → excision
III — Broberg-Morrey Comminuted / multifragmentary Displaced → excision (or TEA elderly)
IV — McKee Coronal shear including capitellum + trochlea ORIF

5Management

Capitellum fracture
  • Non-displaced (< 2 mm) type I / II→posterior splint < 3 wk
  • Displaced type I or IV→ORIF, headless screws
    • posterior comminution / medial injury→posterior ± olecranon osteotomy
  • Displaced type II / III→fragment excision
  • Elderly, unreconstructable + medial column instability→TEA

Treatment choice – ORIF vs arthroplasty

Indication Treatment
Non-displaced I + II (< 2 mm) Posterior splint < 3 wk
Displaced type I (> 2 mm), type IV ORIF
Isolated type I with good bone (experienced arthroscopist) Arthroscopic-assisted ORIF (70° scope; proximal anterolateral portal trocar reduces; flex past 90° to lock; screws P→A)
Displaced type II, III Fragment excision
Elderly, unreconstructable + medial column instability TEA

Healthy 33-yo coronal shear (double bubble)ORIF
✗ Wrong options: excision (large fragment excision → arthritis / instability with MCL tear) · sling · capitellar replacement

Displaced capitellum, no dislocation (diabetic 41-yo)ORIF
✗ Wrong options: MRI for ligaments (unlikely injured without dislocation) · cast · splint + motion · radial head replacement

88-yo comminuted low distal humerus (capitellum + trochlea), poor boneTEA · TEA = choice for comminuted DHF > 70 yr; lifting limit 10–15 lb; interposition arthroplasty for young who can't comply
✗ Wrong options: ORIF · nonop · excise capitellum + fix trochlea

5Management

Distal femur fracture
  • Unstable polytrauma / bad soft tissue / contamination → spanning ex-fix→staged
  • Extra-articular or simple articular→retrograde nail or lateral locked plate
    • intra-articular→reduce + lag articular block first
  • Partial articular (33B)→lag screws + buttress plate (medial approach for B2/B3)
  • Elderly + OA / unreconstructable→distal femoral replacement (immediate WB)

Treatment options

Option Indications Key facts
Hinged knee brace (rare) Stable non-displaced, non-ambulatory, prohibitive risk 6–8 wk; ROM 3–4 wk; stiffness, wounds
Ex-fix Temporising (polytrauma, soft tissue, contamination); definitive for severe open / comminuted Definitive union 92–100% at 4–6 mo; keep pins out of plate zone; narrow anterior safe zone
ORIF Displaced, intra-articular, osteoporotic periprosthetic, nonunion Fixed-angle for metaphyseal comminution (non-fixed → varus collapse); nonunion up to 18%
Retrograde IMN Extra-articular, simple intra-articular, periprosthetic with open-box femoral component ≥ 4 cm intact distal femur (traditional); more symmetric callus, ↓ malunion, ↑ satisfaction
TKA / DFR Pre-existing OA, unreconstructable, loose TKA, low demand Immediate WB, better ambulation, ↓ nonunion; same complications + reoperations; ↓ longevity

Up to 20% wheelchair-bound at 1 yr after internal fixation (elderly)

Locked plating principles & implant choice

Locking platesscrew–plate interface (angular stability), no bone–plate contact needed → comminuted metaphyseal / diaphyseal, short segments, osteoporotic periprosthetic
✗ Wrong options: simple diaphyseal · displaced articular unless lagged first

Lag first, then locklocked screws can't reduce or compress → reduce + lag articular block, then attach to shaft

Osteoporotic 68-yo, metaphyseal comminution + sagittal splitlag screws then locking plate
✗ Wrong options: non-locking plate · retrograde nail · ex-fix

Lateral locking plate NOT for33B partial articular (isolated medial condyle) → medial approach, lag + buttress plate

Implant Fact
Locking compression plate Best control of coronal-plane + small distal segments; multiplanar screws for Hoffa; may be too stiff → nonunion / failure
95° angled blade plate Precise insertion needed; greater torsional strength than LCP but more subsidence, lower load to failure; not C3 or Hoffa; poor in osteoporosis
Dynamic condylar screw Sagittal alignment forgiving (rotates on barrel); removes most bone
Dual plating (lateral + medial) Greatest axial + torsional stiffness — best for medial comminution in osteoporosis
Nail-plate combination ↓ reoperation vs lateral plate alone (LLP nonunion ~20%); same infection; allows immediate WB

Plate failure riskshort working length, plate-screw density > 0.5, short plates, non-locked diaphyseal screws, stainless steel may be worse than titanium, improper bridging
✗ Wrong options: early ROM · bridging · density < 0.5

Percutaneous submuscular precontoured locking plate↓ infection + nonunion, preserves perfusion, but ↑ malreduction (rotational)

Intercondylar screw lengthAP in 30° internal rotation
✗ Wrong options: ER view · full extension AP

Approach Use

Startsuperior margin of Blumensaat line (lateral), centre of notch (AP); knee flexion ≥ 70°

Nonunion without instabilitydoes not worsen outcome (least likely to affect function)
✗ Wrong options: DRUJ instability · step-off > 3 mm · radial shortening · workers' comp (all worsen)

Operativedisplaced base fracture + instability, sigmoid notch fracture, Galeazzi, TFCC avulsion with unstable DRUJ → ORIF or excision preserving TFCC ulnar attachment

Non-displaced, proximalcast

Acute traumaticimmobilisation + NSAIDs first → arthroscopic / open debridement or repair if persistent

Degenerative (type II)debride TFCC + treat impaction: ulnar shortening osteotomy (no DRUJ arthrosis) or wafer resection

Ulnar impaction syndrome

Causeradial shortening → positive ulnar variance → lunate chondromalacia + degenerative TFCC tear

SurgeryTFCC debridement, radial osteotomy, ulnar shortening, wafer (preserve TFCC attachment)

Forearm stabilisers – Essex-Lopresti

Essex-Lopresti (longitudinal radioulnar dissociation)radial head fracture + interosseous membrane tear + DRUJ disruption → proximal radial migration → DRUJ pathology + ulnocarpal abutment

Acutefix / replace radial head (restore radiocapitellar contact + length) + pin DRUJ 6 wk in neutral; failed pinning / missed → radial head replacement

Chronicrestore radial length, level DRUJ, reconstruct central band of IOM

Ipsilateral radial head / neck + Galeazzi (functional Essex-Lopresti)treatment causing chronic instability = radial head excision
✗ Wrong options: temporary ex-fix · radial head ORIF · arthroplasty · DR ORIF + cross-pinning

Procedure Key fact

Distal Radius Fractures

Trauma · 14 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest orthopaedic injury17.5% of adult fractures; lifetime risk 15% women, 2% men; F:M 2–3:1

Bimodalyoung high energy (MVC) · elderly low energy (FOOSH) = fragility fracture → DEXA

Pattern65% extra-articular, 10% partial articular, 25% complete (Orthobullets) · ~50% intra-articular (OB)

Predictor of later fracturesosteoporosis, women > 50

Associated soft-tissue injury (70%)TFCC 40%, SL 30%, LT 15% · DRUJ injury · radial styloid fracture (higher energy)

Abbreviations

Tendons / nervesEPL = extensor pollicis longus · EIP = extensor indicis proprius · FPL = flexor pollicis longus · EDC = extensor digitorum communis · PIN = posterior interosseous nerve · CTR = open carpal tunnel release

Anatomy

Loadradius carries 80% of axial load

Column Contents Roles
Radial Styloid (volar structure) + scaphoid fossa BR insertion, long radiolunate + radioscaphocapitate (blocks ulnar carpal translation); buttress; ulnar-deviation load
Intermediate Lunate fossa Load transfer; short radiolunate origin (radiocarpal stability)
Ulnar TFCC + distal ulna DRUJ stability, rotation

Lister tubercledorsal, ~1 cm above joint; EPL just ulnar → long volar screws rupture EPL

Watershed linemost volar prominent rim (lunate portion highest; short radiolunate) → keep volar plate proximal

Volar-ulnar ("critical") corner / volar lunate facetradiolunate ligaments → loss → volar carpal subluxation

2Mechanism

FOOSH (elderly) · MVC (young)

Chauffeur (Hutchinson) (TO)radial styloid fracture from scaphoid impacting styloid
✗ Wrong options: ulnar styloid

3Presentation

Exampain, swelling, dinner-fork deformity if displaced; median nerve check

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Measure Normal Acceptable (post-reduction)
Radial height (PA) 13 mm (Orthobullets) · 11 mm (TO) < 5 mm shortening
Radial inclination (PA) 23° (22° TO text) < 5° change
Articular step-off Congruous < 2 mm
Volar tilt (lateral) 11° Dorsal angulation < 5° or within 20° of contralateral (Orthobullets, TO) · dorsal tilt < 10° in healthy < 65 (OB)
Ulnar variance Slightly negative —

TO EXCEPT trap (TO)"dorsal tilt up to 7°" is not acceptable

Radial length (TO)radial styloid ~1 cm distal to ulnar head

CTarticular involvement, planning · MRI — TFCC, SL (DISI), LT (VISI)

Classifications & eponyms

SystemsFernandez (mechanism) · Frykman (radiocarpal / DRUJ ± ulnar styloid) · Melone (4 intra-articular types by displacement) · AO (comprehensive, cumbersome)

Eponym Description
Colles Dorsally angulated, extra-articular
Smith Volarly angulated, extra-articular
Volar Barton Radiocarpal fracture-dislocation with volar lip fragment
Dorsal Barton Radiocarpal fracture-dislocation with dorsal lip fragment
Chauffeur (Hutchinson) Radial styloid (transverse / oblique)

✗ Wrong options: gunstock deformity (supracondylar humerus)

5Management

Distal radius fracture
  • Reduce + rigid splint → meets criteria→cast
  • Unstable / > criteria, young→ORIF (volar locked plate)
    • volar-ulnar corner fragment→fragment-specific fixation
  • Elderly > 60–65→closed treatment acceptable (function equal)
  • Open / highly comminuted / unwell→ex-fix ± pins, or dorsal bridge plate

Instability & indications for fixation

LaFontaine instability predictorsradial shortening (most predictive), then dorsal comminution; dorsal comminution > 50%, palmar / intra-articular comminution, dorsal angulation > 20°, initial displacement > 1 cm, shortening > 5 mm, severe osteoporosis, associated ulnar fracture; ≥ 3 criteria → ↑ loss of reduction

Redisplacement after closed reductionseverity of initial displacement (esp. shortening), age, metaphyseal comminution
✗ Wrong options: TFCC tear · open · radial head · time to reduction

Best stability predictorpre-reduction radiographs

Repeat closed reduction< 50% satisfactory

ORIF indications
Dorsal angulation > 5° / > 20° vs contralateral
Intra-articular displacement > 2 mm
Radial shortening > 5 mm
Volar or dorsal comminution · associated ulnar fracture (not styloid) · severe osteoporosis
Barton (articular margin) fractures · Smith (comminuted) · die-punch
Progressive loss of tilt / length in cast

Young, large dorsal articular fragmentORIF
✗ Wrong options: casts · ex-fix · CRPP

Young high-energy metaphyseal comminutionORIF of radius (locking resists shortening + dorsal angulation)
✗ Wrong options: cast · ex-fix + pins · styloid repair (only if DRUJ unstable / base displaced)

Closed reduction & casting

Techniqueanaesthesia, traction + volar / dorsal pressure; below-elbow cast / splint (rigid / sugar tong)

Avoid Cotton-Loder positionextreme flexion + ulnar deviation → CTS

Within criteria (65-yo)rigid splint + clinic follow-up
✗ Wrong options: admit · ORIF · soft splint

75-yo dorsally angulated extra-articular — initial treatmentclosed reduction + splint

Complicationsacute CTS, EPL rupture

Elderly / osteoporotic – closed vs operative

Meta-analysesno functional difference closed vs operative in > 65 (Orthobullets) / ≥ 60 (OB); radiographic results better with surgery

Osteoporotic, failed closed treatmentperi-articular locked plate

Volar comminution in 65-yo — contraindicatedKapandji intrafocal pinning alone
✗ Wrong options: cast · pinning + ex-fix · dorsal bridge plate · volar plate

Dorsal bridge plateligamentotaxis for comminuted fractures; polytrauma / elderly needing walker → immediate platform (front-wheel) walker WB (~22% BW) · must be removed
✗ Wrong options: crutches ~50% BW · NWB wheelchair · no device

CRPP

Indicationextra-articular with stable volar cortex; 82–90% good

TechniquesKapandji intrafocal (pins lever fracture) · Rayhack (arthroscopic)

Complicationsradial sensory nerve injury, pin-tract infection

Volar plating & volar (Henry) approach

Volar plating preferred over dorsal; locked plates support subchondral bone

Classic Henrybetween BR and radial artery (radial to artery) · modified (FCR) Henry — ulnar (medial) to radial artery, through FCR sheath (TO)

Distal third (TO)FCR medial + radial artery lateral → sweep FPL ulnarward with a finger, protecting palmar cutaneous branch → PQ incised along its RADIAL border and elevated with periosteum

TO FALSE statement (TO)"PQ elevated from ulnar side"
✗ Wrong options: true: FPL swept ulnarly, modified Henry medial to artery, Thompson more cosmetic for middle / distal-third shaft

Proximal third (TO)full supination moves PIN away; incise supinator medially · middle third — pronate, partially detach pronator teres

Palmar cutaneous branch of median nerveleaves median 4–6 cm above wrist crease, between median nerve + FCR → thenar base hyperaesthesia from retraction
✗ Wrong options: CRPS · Wartenberg · CTS · C7

Bone voidcalcium phosphate incorporates by ~1 yr
✗ Wrong options: calcium sulfate (resorbs 4–12 wk) · TCP (osteolysis) · OP-1 · freeze-dried allograft (not synthetic)

Volar-ulnar corner fragment→ volar carpal translation
✗ Wrong options: die-punch · radial styloid (ulnar translation) · extra-articular

✗ Wrong options: non-locking plate · volar tilt · styloid column · 3 shaft screws
