External fixation

Indicationsopen, highly comminuted, unwell · cannot reliably restore 10° palmar tilt alone → add pins / plate

Spanning (small articular fragments) vs non-spanning (large fragments)

Ligamentotaxistraction restores length + inclination; volar translation of lunate restores volar tilt (multiplanar, Agee)

Rulesopen placement of radial pins (superficial radial nerve at "bare area" ~4 finger-breadths above styloid, dorsal to BR — commonest nerve injured); avoid over-distraction (< 5 mm), flexion, ulnar deviation; ≤ 8 wk; aggressive finger OT

✗ Wrong options: thumb UCL · ulnolunate / ulnotriquetral

Rehabilitation & outcomes

Formal therapy vs home programmeno long-term difference (Wakefield-McQueen); better DASH + ROM early (6 wk) in women > 40 — improves early, not late PROMs

Poor outcomeworkers' comp, ↓ SES, ↓ education, ↓ BMD

Good outcomearticular reduction accuracy, restored anatomy, early finger + wrist motion

Distal Radius Malunion

Trauma · 15 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Most common complication of distal radius fractures

Rates17% overall · 11% after operative · 24% after definitive casting

Risk factorspost-reduction malalignment, osteoporosis

Anatomy – three columns

Distal radiuscarries 80% of wrist axial load

Column Contents Role
Radial Radial styloid, scaphoid fossa Buttress vs radiocarpal translation; load in ulnar deviation; anchors radioscaphocapitate (vs ulnar translation)
Intermediate Lunate fossa Main load transfer carpus → forearm
Ulnar TFCC + distal ulna DRUJ stability

Biomechanics

Deformity Effect
↓ volar tilt (dorsal tilt) Limits flexion + supination
↑ volar tilt Limits extension + pronation
↓ radial inclination ↓ flexor mechanical advantage → hand weakness
Radial shortening ↑ positive ulnar variance; load shifts to ulnocarpal joint; largest change in DRUJ kinematics
Volar tilt change DRUJ incongruity → IOM tightens → ↓ rotation + flexion–extension arc

Volar-angulated malunion (OB stem)↓ supination + extension, dorsal subluxation of radius in supination (OB) vs ↑ volar tilt limits extension + pronation (Orthobullets) — read the options

Dorsal malunion carpal instability(1) adaptive midcarpal DISI · (2) dorsal radiocarpal subluxation with maintained midcarpal alignment

2Mechanism

Howinitial displacement · secondary loss of reduction in cast · failed fixation

Pattern Note
Dorsally angulated (apex volar) Most common; DISI-like collapse
Volarly angulated (apex dorsal) —
Radial shortening DRUJ kinematics
Intra-articular With initial intra-articular displacement > 2 mm

3Presentation

Symptomspain (localise radial vs ulnar side → guides ulnar procedures), grip weakness, ↓ motion with pronation / supination worst

Examdeformity, tenderness map, ROM all planes, bilateral grip dynamometry, DRUJ shuck test (pain with instability), Allen test, CTS, CRPS

Late DRUJ instability in adult (longshoreman)from untreated childhood distal radius fracture malunion
✗ Wrong options: supracondylar (cubitus varus / valgus) · medial epicondyle · both-bone forearm (DRUJ preserved) · elbow dislocation

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Measure Normal
Radial height (PA) 8–14 mm
Radial inclination (PA) 21–25°
Articular step-off Congruous
Volar tilt (lateral) 7–15°
Ulnar variance Neutral (< 1 mm change)

Viewsbilateral PA, lateral, oblique · anatomic (tilted) lateral for lunate facet

CTintra-articular malunion, axial rotation, DRUJ instability (> 50% translation vs other side)

MRITFCC

5Management

Symptomatic distal radius malunion
  • Low demand / CRPS / can't comply→therapy, NSAIDs, splint
  • No arthritis→corrective osteotomy ± graft + plate
    • ulnar positive with good radial alignment→ulnar procedure
  • Arthritis→salvage (wrist fusion, etc.)
  • Pain only, low demand, good function→PIN / AIN neurectomy

Corrective osteotomy for symptomatic malunion

Indicationssymptomatic after failed casting or failed fixation with mechanical symptoms, ↓ grip, ↓ ROM, instability on stress; Fernandez: active patient, extra-articular > 25–30° angulation, no degenerative change

Ballet dancer, dorsal angulation, joint space preservedcorrective osteotomy · arthritis → salvage
✗ Wrong options: wrist arthrodesis · PRC · SLAC procedures · interposition

Nonop outcomesage 18–65 → more adverse outcomes when untreated

Approach Pros Cons
Dorsal (2nd–4th compartments) Easy osteotomy; tension-side fixation; for dorsal subluxation Extensor tendon irritation
Volar (extended FCR) Align volar cortex → stability, may avoid graft; for volar subluxation; volar malunions Flexor tendon irritation
Osteotomy Fact
Opening wedge Needs bone graft
Closing wedge Bone contact + compression; ↑ ulnar variance → often needs ulnar shortening
Intra-articular Arthroscopy-aided; outcomes ≈ extra-articular osteotomy; push-pull screw restores height

Graftstructural bicortical ICBG → union ~7 wk, better supination · cancellous distal radius ≈ structural ICBG · allograft, DBM, calcium phosphate options

Complication rateextra-articular correction ~50%; higher with distraction osteotomy

Denervation

PIN ± AIN neurectomydebilitating pain + infection, low demand, preserved function; dorsal incision proximal to DRUJ; PIN on radial floor of 4th compartment; AIN after dividing IOM (1 cm excised)

Ulnar-sided procedures

Indicationsulnar-positive with preserved radial alignment, DRUJ instability, TFCC tear, styloid nonunion

Procedure Rule
Ulnar shortening osteotomy (Milch) Isolated radial shortening; not with DRUJ arthrosis
Wafer (Feldon) Intact TFCC; angular deformities
Hemiresection-interposition (Bowers) Intact TFCC; DRUJ arthrosis / instability
Sauvé-Kapandji Younger, incongruity + degeneration; keeps rotation
Darrach Salvage; don't over-resect
Ulnar head / DRUJ arthroplasty Salvage
One-bone forearm Ultimate salvage; no rotation

TFCCcentral perforations usually settle; irreparable + unstable DRUJ → Adams reconstruction (palmaris graft) or BR wrap; confirm reparability arthroscopically

Styloid nonunionsmall + stable → excise · large + unstable → repair (headless screw, TBW, or excise + foveal TFCC repair)

6Complications

Complication Fact
Tendon irritation / rupture 20% of complications; EPL commonest; rupture ~10 wk; risk: distraction osteotomy, dorsal callus, volar plate, dorsal osteophyte, prominent hardware
Others Nerve injury, CRPS, nonunion, infection, PTOA

X vs Y

↓ volar tilt (dorsal malunion) ↑ volar tilt (volar malunion)
Lost motion Flexion + supination Extension + pronation (Orthobullets)
Carpus DISI / dorsal subluxation —
Opening wedge Closing wedge
Graft Needed Not needed
Ulnar variance Restores length ↑ positive → ulnar shortening

1Basics

IPV epidemiology

Fact Value

DV = commonest cause of non-fatal injury to women

Scale~2 million Americans / yr; 1 in 25 over 65; widely under-reported; forms: physical, mental, neglect, financial, abandonment

Injuriesinconsistent with history, long delay to treatment, repeat injuries, multiple injuries of varying ages, multiple providers / EDs, unusual patterns

Behaviour

✗ Wrong options: malingering · CRPS · anxiety · fibromyalgia

Barriersfear of retaliation, shame, embarrassment, reluctance with male physicians, custody fears, downplaying

4Diagnosis & Classification

No skeletal survey in competent adults (or pregnancy)

Documentationexact quotes, abuser's name, body maps / drawings, photographs with consent, demeanour, opinion if injuries don't fit story

5Management

Suspected abuse
  • Child→report (all states)
  • Elder → report (almost all states); in danger→admit / transfer to ED
  • Adult IPV→interview alone, screen, document, social work, resources
    • report only per state law / with consent

Screening & management

First step in suspected IPVspeak with patient alone, privately, non-judgementally → resources
✗ Wrong options: confront partner · treat + discharge · mandatory psych referral · call police first

Pregnant, inconsistent history, bruisesafter treating fracture → social work consult

Elbow Dislocation

Trauma · 17 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Rank2nd commonest major joint dislocation (after shoulder); commonest dislocation in children

Share10–25% of elbow injuries · posterolateral 80% · peak age 10–20

Simple vs complexsimple (no fracture) 50–60% · complex 40–50%

Associatedshoulder / wrist injuries 10–15% · radial head fracture up to 10%

Anatomy – stabilisers

Type Structures
Primary static Ulnohumeral joint, anterior bundle MCL (key valgus), LCL complex incl. LUCL (primary varus + posterolateral rotatory)
Secondary static Radiocapitellar joint, capsule, common flexor + extensor origins
Dynamic Anconeus, brachialis, triceps (+ biceps) — compression

LCL (TO)radial collateral, annular, lateral ulnar collateral · MCL (TO) — anterior bundle (valgus), posterior bundle (secondary valgus + ulnar rotation) · extensors resist varus, flexors resist valgus

2Mechanism

Posterolateral dislocationaxial load + forearm supination / ER + valgus posterolateral force (O'Driscoll) · varus posteromedial mechanism also reported

Circle of Horii (lateral → medial)LCL fails first → capsule → MCL last (energy dependent); some recent work suggests failure may start medially (TO)

LUCL failure modeavulsion from humeral (lateral epicondylar) origin · McKee: proximal avulsion 32, midsubstance 18, bony humeral 5, ulnar 3 / 62
✗ Wrong options: ulnar insertion · midsubstance (less common) · bony avulsion

MRI of torn LCLavulsed off lateral epicondyle (MCL + flexor origin intact)

3Presentation

Exampain, swelling, deformity; skin (open?); compartments; wrist + shoulder; NV

Commonest nerve injury (TO)ulnar nerve (stretch) · median rare (with brachial artery) · brachial artery (rare; open)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

AP + lateralcongruency esp. post-reduction · obliques — periarticular fractures · CT — complex patterns, fractures, loose bodies

"Drop sign" (TO)↑ static ulnohumeral distance on post-reduction lateral → residual posterolateral subluxation

Classification

Basis Types
Anatomic (olecranon vs humerus) Posterolateral (commonest) · posteromedial
Simple No fracture
Complex With fracture: terrible triad (dislocation + LUCL + radial head + coronoid tip) · varus PMRI (LCL + anteromedial coronoid; radial head spared)

5Management

Elbow dislocation
  • Simple, stable after reduction → splint 5–10 d→early active ROM
    • residual subluxation (drop sign)→active ROM pronated, avoid varus
  • Unstable (needs > 50–60° flexion) / irreducible→open, repair LCL ± MCL
  • Complex→fix coronoid / radial head / olecranon + LCL ± MCL
  • Chronic→open reduction, release, hinged ex-fix

Simple dislocation – reduction & early motion

Reductionanalgesia + relaxation → in-line traction (coronal) + forearm supination (coronoid under trochlea) + flex elbow with pressure on olecranon → "clunk"

Post-reduction testunstable in extension + valgus; test valgus with forearm pronated (locks lateral side)

Splintposterior splint ≥ 90° flexion, rotation of maximum stability: LCL torn → pronation · MCL torn → supination (O'Driscoll: reduce in supination, immobilise in pronation) · neutral acceptable

Duration5–10 days (5–7 d, OB) → early active ROM through stable arc; hinged brace with extension block 3–4 wk; light duty at 2 wk; full extension by 6–8 wk · avoid varus / valgus loading until 12 wk (TO)

Stable after reduction — start motion~1 week
✗ Wrong options: immediately · 3 wk · 6 wk · after LCL repair

Best outcome predictormobilisation within 5–10 days (> 10 days → arthrofibrosis, pain) · immobilisation > 3 wk → poor final ROM

Avoidimmobilisation 4 wk
✗ Wrong options: vs active motion, 90° neutral splint, extension-limited early rehab, light duty (all OK)

Simple dislocation, can't move elbowclosed reduction, splint, early ACTIVE ROM
✗ Wrong options: passive ROM · hinged ex-fix · acute LCL repair · open reduction

Residual posterolateral subluxation (drop sign) (TO)splint 1 wk → active motion with forearm PRONATED through full range; elbow at side (no varus / shoulder abduction); supinate only at ≥ 90° flexion
✗ Wrong options: LCL reconstruction · splint 1 month

Recurrent instability after simple dislocationrare (< 1–2%)

Operative criteria

Indication Treatment
Irreducible (soft tissue / osteochondral fragment) Open reduction
Persistent instability — needs > 50–60° flexion to stay reduced (Orthobullets, OB) · redislocates at < 30° flexion (TO) Repair LCL ± MCL
Complex (coronoid, radial head, olecranon) ORIF / arthroplasty + LCL ± MCL
Open, vascular injury, recurrent Surgery
Throwers ± MCL repair
Chronic dislocation Open reduction + capsular release + dynamic hinged ex-fix
Still unstable after all repairs Hinged external fixator

Highly unstable after closed reductionopen reduction + LCL repair ± MCL repair
✗ Wrong options: 6 wk splint · ex-fix alone · internal joint stabiliser alone · reconstruction + 6 wk immobilisation

Essential lesion in persistent instabilityLUCL
✗ Wrong options: MCL (repaired only if still unstable) · coracohumeral · capsule

Structure needing repairLUCL
✗ Wrong options: radial collateral · MCL bands · accessory collateral

Approaches

Kocher (ECU–anconeus)LCL, extensor origin, coronoid, capitellum, radial head; incise anterior to radial head midline to spare posterior LCL fibres; careful retractors → PIN

MedialMCL, flexor-pronator, comminuted coronoid; protect ulnar nerve

Complex dislocation – fixation

Coronoidtip fractures rarely need ORIF (proximal to brachialis); lateral or medial approach

Radial head ORIFsafe zone ≈ 90° non-articulating arc (between Lister tubercle + radial styloid lines) (Orthobullets, OB) · ~110° in original dissections · 69% of head articulates with ulna

Radial head arthroplastyif unreconstructable; anatomic size / length → restores varus + ER stability only once LCL repaired · excision → varus / ER instability without LCL

Dislocation + comminuted radial head (55-yo)open reduction, LCL repair, radial head ORIF or metallic replacement
✗ Wrong options: cast 4 wk · brace + immediate ROM · silastic implant (contraindicated) · excision

Complex dislocation – coronoid & PMRI

Varus PMRILCL rupture (humeral) + anteromedial coronoid facet fracture + ulnohumeral subluxation / dislocation; radial head usually spared

Dislocation + anteromedial coronoid fracture on APhighest risk varus PMRI
✗ Wrong options: AIN / PIN palsy · PLRI · chair-rise instability

Fixation preventing PMRIanteromedial coronoid facet · failure to fix / malunion → poor function + arthrosis (Doornberg & Ring)
✗ Wrong options: radial head · coronoid tip · olecranon tip · medial capitellum

Transolecranon fracture-dislocation (TO)anterior dislocation with intact PRUJ, mainly bony, usually no ligament injury, coronoid fracture common → NOT a Monteggia variant (EXCEPT) · type I simple / II complex · restore ulnar length, alignment, rotation + sigmoid notch; missed coronoid = failure

Complication Fact

Stiffness / contracture Immobilisation > 3 wk

Varus PMRI LCL + anteromedial facet

Brachial artery Rare, open dislocations

Post-traumatic stiffness – release & HO excision

Functional arc30–130°

Arc 30–95° (flexion-limited) + HOexcise HO + release posterior bundle of MCL + ulnar nerve decompression (flexion < 100° → decompress)
✗ Wrong options: supracondylar osteotomy + anterior MCL release · anterior capsule release (helps extension) · LCL release → instability

MCL release orderposterior bundle → transverse → (posterior half of anterior bundle)

Extension loss 80° with mature anterolateral HO, no ulnar symptomsopen resection + capsulectomy via lateral approach (access anterior + posterior)
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopic (risky with tight capsule) · anterior approach (no posterior access) · indomethacin + radiation (too late once visible) · manipulation (contraindicated)

HO maturationfluffy → sharp margins over 3–6 months; labs + bone scan not prognostic; prophylaxis (NSAID, 700 cGy) ineffective once visible

1Basics

Trimodal death after trauma

Peak Share Cause
Minutes 50% Massive bleeding, neurological injury
Hours 30% Shock, hypoxia, neurological injury
Days–weeks 20% MOF, infection

Golden hour~60% of preventable deaths

Airbags (head-on)↓ head injury, facial fractures, thoraco-abdominal injury (splenic rupture, flail chest), extraction · pelvic ring injuries NOT reduced

PsychologicalPTSD ~50% after orthopaedic trauma (females 4×; LE / pelvic injuries 2× UE) · depression 33%

PTSD risk factorhigh ISS (> 15 = polytrauma)
✗ Wrong options: social history · timing of surgery · tobacco · rehab duration

Female sex is linked toPTSD
✗ Wrong options: nonunion · malunion · infection · fat embolism

Genes & lab markers

IL-6most reliable marker of systemic inflammatory response; correlates with injury severity, complications, mortality · > 500 pg/dL → DCO
✗ Wrong options: IL-8, IL-10, CRP, TNF-α (too variable)

Elevated IL-6↑ mortality · also sensitive for PJI
✗ Wrong options: osteomyelitis, rhabdo, compartment syndrome

Lactatenormal < 2–2.5 mmol/L (0.6–1.7 in one OB explanation); most sensitive marker of occult hypoperfusion; last to normalise; clearance within 12–24 h predicts survival

Base deficitnormal −2 to +2; global hypoperfusion; most predictive of mortality (incl. normotensive elderly); confounded by saline (hyperchloraemia), renal failure, DKA, CO₂ retention

Gastric mucosal pHnormal > 7.3 (7.30–7.35); regional endpoint

SIRS criteria (≥ 2)

Parameter Threshold
Temperature > 38 °C or < 36 °C
Heart rate > 90 / min
Respiration RR > 20 or PaCO₂ < 32 mm Hg
WBC > 12,000, < 4000, or > 10% bands

Lactate is NOT a SIRS criterion

Adults vs childrenadults: robust systemic response, lungs fail first (day 2–3) · children: dampened systemic, robust local, all organs simultaneously

2Mechanism

Two-hit theory1st hit (hypoxia, hypotension, soft tissue, fractures) + 2nd hit (surgery, ischaemia-reperfusion, compartment syndrome, infection) → SIRS → ARDS / MOF

Compensated shocknormal vitals with ongoing hypoperfusion (up to 85%) → "primed" immune system → exaggerated SIRS to a 2nd hit
✗ Wrong options: "no risk" · ↑ nonunion / infection after staged fixation

Lethal triad (TO)hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy
✗ Wrong options: haemorrhage · hypoxia · hypotension

HBV — highest viral risk 1 in 205,000 (Orthobullets)

Damage control vs early total care

ETC (1980s)fix everything at once ("too sick not to operate") → 2nd hit in unstable, head, chest injuries

DCO (2000)temporary stabilisation (ex-fix, traction, splints, I&D) → definitive once physiology improves

EAC (2013)definitive fixation of spine, pelvis, acetabulum, femur within 36 h once any ONE of: lactate < 4.0 mmol/L, pH ≥ 7.25, base excess ≥ −5.5 (BD ≤ 5.5) → ↓ delay, ↓ complications (ARDS, MOF, death), ↓ LOS, ↑ revenue; main delay = surgeon decision

Femoral Head Fractures

Trauma · 19 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Rare12% of hip dislocations; rising (more MVAs, better resuscitation)

With posterior dislocation5–15% (Orthobullets) · ~15% (TO) · 95% of head fractures accompany a dislocation (TO)

Blood supply

Vessel Fact
MFCA (from profunda) Main supply to weight-bearing head; runs posteromedially → endangered by posterior approach
Artery of ligamentum teres (obturator or MFCA) 10–15%; perifoveal area

2Mechanism

Mechanismimpaction, avulsion, shear; dashboard injury (knee on dash, hip flexed + adducted + IR), falls, sport, industrial

Posterior dislocationhead shears against posterior acetabular rim → fracture (usually anteromedial / anteroinferior fragment)

Anterior dislocationimpaction / indentation fractures of head

Associatedfemoral neck fracture, acetabular (posterior wall) fracture, sciatic neurapraxia, AVN, ipsilateral knee ligament injury

3Presentation

Posterior dislocationflexed, adducted, IR, shortened (little rotation with large wall fractures)

Anterior dislocationflexed, abducted, ER

Checksciatic nerve, ipsilateral knee stability

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
AP pelvis + hip series (pre + post reduction) —
Judet Acetabular fracture
Inlet / outlet Pelvic ring
Post-reduction CT Loose bodies / incarcerated fragments, fragment size, plane, comminution, impaction, acetabulum

Pipkin classification

Type Definition Key fact
I Below fovea (infrafoveal), non-weight-bearing, small Nonop or excision (excision > ORIF)
II Above fovea (suprafoveal), weight-bearing, larger; ligamentum stays on inferior fragment → may block reduction ORIF if displaced (ORIF > excision)
III I or II + femoral neck fracture Highest AVN → catastrophic ORIF failure
IV I or II + acetabular fracture (usually posterior wall) Treat by acetabular injury

Chiron classification (TO)

Type (TO) Extent
1 Osteochondral injury
2 ¼ of head
3 ⅓ of head
4 ½ of head
5 Cartilage impaction of weight-bearing dome (superior collapse)

Subtypes (TO)A pure head · B + acetabulum · C + neck · Brumback — more prognostic than Pipkin (TO)

5Management

Femoral head fracture
  • Dislocated → reduce < 6 h→post-reduction CT
  • Pipkin I, or II with < 1 mm step-off, stable, no fragments→TDWB 4–6 wk
  • Pipkin II > 1 mm / loose bodies / irreducible→ORIF (anterior)
    • Pipkin IV→TFO surgical dislocation (head + posterior wall)
  • Pipkin III or older / comminuted / osteoporotic→arthroplasty

Nonoperative Operative

Approach Facts

Kocher-Langenbeck ± digastric (trochanteric) osteotomy Posterior wall (Pipkin IV); gluteus max split (no internervous plane); plain KL → worse outcomes, more AVN

✗ Wrong options: minimally invasive · minimal stripping · better union

✗ Wrong options: 3.0 mm cannulated screws with washers → poor results

✗ Wrong options: HO uncommon (~15–20%) · KL optimal · excision better · 2 mm cut-off

1Basics

Epidemiology

Rate10–30% after femoral neck ORIF

Risk factor Note
Vertical fracture (Pauwels III) Shear > compression

Why the neck fails to heal

Intracapsularno periosteum / extraosseous supply, bathed in synovial fluid, intra-osseous healing only (no callus) → anatomic reduction essential

Neck-shaft angle130 ± 7° · anteversion 10 ± 7° · tensile + compressive trabeculae

AssociatedAVN, malunion, hardware failure, septic nonunion, low BMD

3Presentation

Symptomspersistent groin / buttock pain, pain on WB + hip extension, referred to medial thigh / knee

Exam↓ internal rotation, antalgic gait, pain with log-roll, pain on straight-leg raise; check old incision, sciatic + femoral nerves

Nonunion signalpersistent pain + no radiographic healing at 3 months → consider revision

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
AP pelvis + hip, cross-table lateral, full femur Lucent line, settling, hardware backing out, head perforation, > 10 mm change in position, collapse, calcar comminution, varus

MRI Head AVN
Bone scan Uptake at nonunion; helps exclude AVN

Classification (descriptive)

Type Description
1 Inadequate fixation / non-anatomic reduction
2 Loss of fixation with displacement
3 Fibrous nonunion, no displacement, intact fixation

Femoral neck nonunion
  • Young, viable head→valgus intertrochanteric osteotomy
    • aligned but posterior bone loss→vascularised graft
  • Older / active→THA (long stem past screw holes)
  • Older / low demand / cognitive decline→hemiarthroplasty
  • Non-ambulatory, comorbid→observe

Treatment options

Option Indication Fact
Observation Non-ambulatory, comorbid Poor function
Revision ORIF Not recommended Bone loss, LLD, high failure
Valgus intertrochanteric osteotomy Young, viable head, varus collapse, nonunion > 3 mo Commonest salvage; turns vertical → ~30° (horizontal) line → compression; restores length + abductor lever; 80–90% union; not with bone loss, incongruity, age > 65 (relative)
Vascularised graft (quadratus femoris pedicle, free fibula) Aligned nonunion with posterior bone loss, failed fixation Up to 90% union; not if malalignment is the cause
Hemiarthroplasty Low demand, comorbid, cognitive decline Lower dislocation than THA; cemented > uncemented; bipolar ≈ unipolar; risk of acetabular erosion
THA Older, active, cognitively intact; acetabular degeneration ~90% 10-yr, 75% 20-yr survival

✗ Wrong options: primary tapered stem · hardware removal · valgus osteotomy · IM revision

Valgus osteotomylateral approach; blade plate or sliding hip screw; risks: malrotation, over-medialisation of shaft → ↓ offset + abductor weakness (longer blade avoids)

Conversion THAlonger stems past screw holes (intra-op fracture risk), gentle cup impaction ± screws, dual-mobility / large heads vs dislocation; loosening ↑ if age < 65 + BMI > 30

Dual mobility vs fixed bearing (< 55 yr)lower dislocation (same HHS, loosening, infection, op time)

Failed hemi → THAworse than primary THA

Acetabular cartilage wear → THA

Conceptturns vertical shear line into horizontal compression; corrects varus; works even with non-collapsed AVN

Femoral Shaft Fractures

Trauma · 22 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence37.1 / 100,000 / yr

Whohigh energy in young (MVC) · low energy in elderly · gunshot

Associated injuries

Association Fact
Ipsilateral femoral neck fracture 2–6% (Orthobullets) · ~5% · 1–9% / 2.5–9% / 0–15% (OB) · 7.5% (Tornetta); basicervical, vertical, non-displaced; missed 19–31% (~30%)
Bilateral femur fractures ↑ mortality (5.6% vs 1.5%), initial hypotension, head + pelvic injuries (✗ Wrong options: not ↑ rib fractures); pulmonary complications
Ipsilateral tibia (floating knee), acetabulum —
Pulmonary injury Early fixation → ARDS ~2% if under-resuscitated
Head injury Intra-op hypotension → ↓ cerebral perfusion

Blood lossclosed femur 1000–1500 mL · closed tibia 500–1000 mL · open ≈ double · bilateral closed femur 2000–3000 mL

Anatomy

Femurlargest, strongest; anterior bow (radius of curvature 120 ± 36 cm); linea aspera = posterior compressive strut

Compartmentsanterior (sartorius, quads) · posterior (hamstrings) · adductor (gracilis, adductors)

Blood supply after fractureperiosteal + soft-tissue supply predominates; reaming disrupts endosteal but stimulates periosteal

Deforming forces

Fragment Deformity Muscle
Proximal Abducted Gluteus medius + minimus
Proximal Flexed (+ ER) Iliopsoas (+ short rotators)
Distal Varus Adductors
Distal Extension Gastrocnemius

2Mechanism

Force Pattern
Pure bending Transverse
Rotation Spiral
Uneven bending Oblique
4-point bending Segmental
High-speed crush / torsion Comminuted

3Presentation

Examtense swollen thigh, shortened, tender; hip exam unreliable (neck fracture easily missed); document distal NV status

Adequate resuscitationHR < 100, SBP > 100, DBP > 70, temp > 35 °C, urine 0.5–1 mL/kg/h, lactate < 2.5, BD −2 to +2, IL-6 < 500 pg/dL, gastric pH > 7.3

Compensated shock cluesnormotensive, afebrile tachycardia, cool limbs, narrow pulse pressure, weak pulses, slow refill

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
AP + lateral whole femur, ipsilateral hip + knee Standard
AP hip in ~10° internal rotation Neck in profile (✗ Wrong options: ER view)
Fine-cut (2 mm) CT of hip Best pre-op study for occult neck fracture; CT capsular sign = > 1 mm more capsular distension than uninjured side
Intra-operative fluoroscopy of neck Still needed even after negative 2 mm CT
Post-op hip X-ray in OR + follow-up AP hip in 15–20° IR New groin pain after nailing → hip X-ray first

Neck protocol10° IR AP hip + 2 mm CT + intra-op fluoro + post-op film
✗ Wrong options: bone scan · traction views · MRI routinely · frog-leg (too painful)

Septic nonunion labsCRP most sensitive for occult infection, ESR, WBC

Winquist classification

Type Comminution
0 None
I Insignificant
II > 50% cortical contact
III < 50% cortical contact
IV Segmental — no contact between main fragments

AO / OTA 32

Type Subtypes
A — simple A1 spiral · A2 oblique > 30° · A3 transverse < 30°
B — wedge B1 spiral · B2 bending · B3 fragmented
C — complex C1 spiral · C2 segmental · C3 irregular

5Management

Femoral shaft fracture
  • Resuscitated→reamed, statically locked IMN < 24 h (WBAT)
    • antegrade = gold standard
    • retrograde: neck fracture, floating knee, acetabulum, bilateral, obese, pregnant, polytrauma
  • Unstable / head injury with ICP problems / vascular / severe open → ex-fix→IMN within 2–3 wk
  • Ipsilateral neck fracture→fix NECK first (open if displaced), then retrograde nail / plate

Treatment options

Option Indication Fact
Spica / long leg cast Children (< 5 yr spica), unfit adults —
Antegrade reamed IMN Gold standard 98–99% union, infection ~2%; < 24 h → ↓ ARDS, VTE, LOS, cost
Retrograde IMN Ipsilateral neck fracture, floating knee, acetabular fracture, bilateral femurs, polytrauma, morbid obesity, pregnancy (1st trimester), infra-isthmal Not with skeletal immaturity, knee sepsis, knee soft-tissue injury
Ex-fix → IMN within 2–3 wk Unstable polytrauma, vascular injury, severe open Union + infection = acute nailing; infection ↑ if ex-fix > 28 days; ↓ ARDS / fat embolism; knee stiffness
Plate Neck fracture needing screws, distal meta-diaphyseal fracture, no canal access ↑ infection, nonunion, hardware failure

Immediate (retrograde / antegrade) nailingsafe for GSW femur fractures

WB after statically locked appropriately sized nailimmediately (even comminuted)

Antegrade vs retrograde nailing

Antegrade Retrograde
Union Equal Equal
Pain Hip pain, abductor weakness, abductor HO Knee pain, symptomatic distal locking screws
Setup Fracture table / lateral Supine, all limbs accessible, compare rotation + length
Bilateral femurs Reposition Shorter op — no re-prep

Retrograde preferred becauseless hip pain
✗ Wrong options: union · infection · time · less knee pain

Long-term weakness after antegrade nailhip abduction + knee extension (quads + abductors weaker)

Stable, floating knee + open ankleretrograde femur nail + tibial nail + ankle I&D + ORIF
✗ Wrong options: ex-fix

Femur + ipsilateral open tibia, stablereamed retrograde nail, static locking
✗ Wrong options: unlocked · unreamed · dynamic locking (length unstable)

Bilateral femurs, resuscitated (lactate 1.2)reamed retrograde nailing of both
✗ Wrong options: traction · ex-fix · plates · unreamed antegrade

Antegrade technique & entry points

Positioningfracture table (perineal post, well-leg lithotomy) or sloppy lateral

Entry Pros Cons
Piriformis fossa Colinear with shaft Hard in obese; most damage to piriformis tendon, abductors, MFCA (→ AVN in children)
Trochanteric Less abductor injury, easier Not colinear → trochanteric-design nail required; too lateral → varus

Trochanteric startdepends on trochanter position relative to shaft axis + nail geometry (tip or just medial)
✗ Wrong options: "always at the tip"

Varus causestrochanteric start too lateral · straight (piriformis) nail through trochanteric portal · wrong-side trochanteric nail · (trochanteric nail through piriformis → valgus)

Too ANTERIOR start (≥ 6 mm)↑ hoop stress → iatrogenic proximal femur fracture ("bursting") (esp. piriformis nail); over-ream ≥ 0.5 mm to reduce · 3 mm anterior improves cephalic screw position in CMN

Too POSTERIOR start + straight nail (larger radius of curvature) + short / bowed femuranterior cortical perforation of distal femur / anterior thigh pain → prevent: more anterior start, smaller radius of curvature (more curved) nail, anterior blocking screws, smaller nail, notched tip
✗ Wrong options: larger nail · posterior blocking screw · straighter nail

Insertionnail inserted rotated 90° internally then rotated back (uses bow, avoids medial comminution)

Piriformis nailsingle sagittal bow (either side) · trochanteric nail — double bow, side-specific (twist on insertion); 3-point fit

Reamed vs unreamed nailing

Reamed↑ union, ↓ time to union, no ↑ pulmonary complications, no ↑ infection in open; unreamed → 4.5× nonunion (Canadian RCT)

Why reaming helpsreaming debris ≈ iliac crest autograft (osteogenic cells) · stimulates periosteal flow · larger nail (stiffness ∝ r⁴) · more isthmic contact · fluted nails ↓ marrow pressure (greatest at nail insertion)

Unreamedconsider only with bilateral pulmonary injury; biggest nonunion risk factor among options
✗ Wrong options: open reduction · cerclage · retrograde · staged ex-fix

Nail diameter10 mm ≈ larger nails for union
✗ Wrong options: bigger canal needs bigger nail

Retrograde technique

Startcentre of notch (AP) + extension of Blumensaat line (lateral) (posterior → cruciate injury); medial condylar start needs curved nail (else valgus) · knee flexed 30–50°

Stepsreduce before reaming (F-tool, bumps, Schanz joysticks); ream 1–1.5 mm over nail; nail ~1 cm deep to cartilage; guidewire proximal to lesser trochanter; long nail to LT

Proximal interlockssafe above lesser trochanter; A→P screws below LT → femoral nerve branches + deep femoral artery at risk

Periprosthetic (CR TKA)start more posterior → hyperextension (recurvatum); arthrotomy needed; PS box may need burr; backup = locking plates (multiple distal points)

Ipsilateral femoral neck + shaft

Priorityneck first (AVN / nonunion) → open reduction + screws if displaced → reamed retrograde nail (or plate) for shaft

Two implantslower malreduction than single cephalomedullary nail
✗ Wrong options: single CMN (highest malreduction; no faster neck healing, less pain)

Missed neck found after antegrade nailscrews anterior to nail (difficult)

Polytrauma & head injury

Head injuryearly stabilisation does not worsen neurological outcome if hypotension + hypoxia avoided; intra-op hypotension → lower GCS at discharge

Severe head injury with ↑ ICP (bifrontal contusion, ICP 30)ex-fix femur
✗ Wrong options: due to L4 burst, open tibia, LC1, rib fractures

SAH + femur — adverse outcome from?intra-operative hypotension (traction if ICP labile)

GCS 13, normal CT head, stableearly fixation, no neuro risk
✗ Wrong options: ↑ pulmonary risk · delay · DCO · chest injury always contraindicates

Unilateral contusion + chest tube, now stable (BD −2)reamed IMN

Shock, bilateral contusions, BD −10ex-fix
✗ Wrong options: plating · reamed / unreamed nails

Borderline after splenectomy, bilateral open femurs + pelvisbilateral femoral ex-fix + anterior pelvic ex-fix

BD −6, lactate 3.5, contusions, hip reducedbilateral temporising ex-fix

Distal interlocking

Perfect circleshole widened proximal–distal → adjust abduction / adduction · widened anterior–posterior → adjust internal / external rotation

Computer navigation↓ fluoroscopy time
✗ Wrong options: accuracy, time, image quality, length

Single distal screw failure4-point bending → screw shaft fractures inside the nail
✗ Wrong options: pull-out · head shear

Most associated factorfracture comminution (TO, OB) · also night-time surgery

Fracture table↑ internal malrotation (vs manual traction supine)

Direction by levelproximal fracture → INTERNAL malrotation (proximal fragment ER by iliopsoas, rotators, abductors) · distal fracture → EXTERNAL malrotation (gastrocnemius / plantaris ER distal fragment) · antegrade vs retrograde and entry type don't matter

Definitionno healing by 9 months or no progress over 3 months; broken distal locks = race lost

Aseptic, after reamed nail (smoker) Reamed antegrade exchange nailing (✗ Wrong options: graft in situ · stimulator · biopsy)

Upper tibial pin (sliding) traction (TO)counter-traction by raising foot end of bed (~1 inch per lb) with BB splint · Thomas splint = fixed traction (ring in groin)

Flail Chest

Trauma · 23 / 67

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Flail chestsegmental fractures of ≥ 3 consecutive ribs → hemothorax / pneumothorax

Incidence~300,000 / yr; ~10% of blunt thoracic trauma (OB); more ribs → ↑ morbidity + mortality

Whobimodal: young trauma · elderly osteopenic

Commonest ribs7–10

Mortalityup to 33% with flail chest · 2.5% with surgical stabilisation

Associated injuries

Ribs Association
1–3 Mediastinal injury (aorta, brachial plexus), worse mortality
1–4 (upper) Progressive displacement of ipsilateral clavicle fracture
9–12 Intra-abdominal injury — liver + spleen
Any Hemopneumothorax, pulmonary contusion, scapula + clavicle fractures

Anatomy

Ribs12 pairs; 11–12 = floating (no costal cartilage to sternum)

Intercostal neurovascular bundleposteroinferior, in costal groove → avoid when plating

2Mechanism

Mechanismdirect blunt / penetrating; fracture at impact or rib angle (posterolateral bend) = weakest point; pathological / metastatic

Pathophysiologynegative-pressure ventilation → paradoxical motion → pain → ↓ respiratory effort → pneumonia, ARDS, intubation

3Presentation

Symptomspain, chest-wall bruising, respiratory difficulty

Paradoxical respirationsegment sinks in on inspiration, expands on expiration

Study Fact

Dedicated rib series More sensitive (oblique views, higher energy)
CT Best for displacement, segmental injury, need for surgery + thoracic / abdominal injuries

Rib fractures
  • No respiratory compromise, no flail→O2, incentive spirometry, multimodal analgesia
  • Flail (≥ 3 consecutive segmental) / failure to wean / open / intractable pain→ORIF
    • haemodynamically unstable / spine or pelvis first→delay

Indication (ORIF) Contraindication
Flail segment (≥ 3 consecutive segmental ribs) Haemodynamic instability
Failure to wean from ventilator Spinal / pelvic fractures needing fixation first
Open rib fractures —
Displaced fractures with intractable pain —

Foot Compartment Syndrome

Trauma · 24 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology & causes

Pathophysiologytrauma → bleeding + oedema → ↑ interstitial pressure → vascular occlusion → myoneural ischaemia

Causesfractures 69% (5–17% of calcaneus fractures), crush, severe ankle sprain, GSW, tight casts / dressings, burns, post-ischaemic swelling, bleeding disorders, vascular injury

Foot compartment anatomy

Number9 (Orthobullets, TO; controversial) · 8 (OB: lateral, medial, central, 4 interosseous)

Compartment Contents
Medial Abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral Abductor + flexor digiti minimi brevis
Interosseous (× 4) Interossei — each in its own compartment
Central — superficial Flexor digitorum brevis
Central — middle Quadratus plantae
Central — deep (calcaneal / adductor) Adductor hallucis + posterior tibial NV bundle

Trap (TO)"adductor compartment = adductor hallucis + interossei" = wrong; interossei form 4 separate compartments

3Presentation

Symptompain out of proportion

Exampain on passive toe dorsiflexion (MTPJ) (stretches intrinsics; may be absent in foot) · tense swollen foot · ↓ 2-point discrimination

Pulsespresent pulses do not exclude; absent DP may be expected with severe foot trauma

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Radiographsrule out fracture only; diagnosis is clinical ± pressures

Compartment pressure measurement & thresholds

Indicationspolytrauma, obtunded / unreliable, children, equivocal exam (not needed when clinically unequivocal → straight to theatre)

Compartment Needle entry
Medial Base of 1st MT, 2 cm into abductor hallucis
Central Base of 1st MT, directed lateral + plantar through abductor hallucis (deeper than medial)
Interosseous 2nd, 3rd, 4th web spaces, plantar 2 cm through extensor fascia
Lateral Midshaft 5th MT, 1 cm medial + plantar

Diagnostic criteria

Fasciotomy if Observe if
Δp (diastolic − compartment) < 30 mmHg Δp > 30 mmHg
Absolute 30–45 mmHg (historic, controversial) Exam not consistent
Clinical diagnosis —

Intra-opanaesthesia lowers diastolic → compare to pre-op diastolic

5Management

Suspected foot compartment syndrome
  • Clinically unequivocal→emergent fasciotomy (no pressures)
  • Equivocal / obtunded / child→measure pressures

Gun Shot Wounds

Trauma · 27 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

GSW2nd leading cause of death in US youth (after MVA) · buttock GSW ≈ 8% of extremity GSWs

Ballistics — kinetic energy transfer

KE = ½ m v²velocity matters more than mass (m at 2v > 2m at v); injury rises exponentially with velocity

Damagemissile passage + secondary shock wave + cavitation; fractures possible without direct impact

Max energy transferpenetrating (no exit) > perforating (exits) · yaw 90° (sideways) > nose-on; yaw ↓ with longer travel

Thresholds (TO)50 m/s penetrates skin · 65 m/s fractures bone · larger calibre → slower (TO)

Contamination (TO)bullets are not sterile (heat + barrel friction insufficient); skin flora + clothing; civilian GSW infection risk is LOW

Associated conditions

Lead intoxication (plumbism)intra-articular missile; lead soluble in synovial fluid; blood lead peaks 4–6 months (TO) → neurotoxicity, anaemia, emesis, abdominal colic; local lead synovitis → chondrolysis, hypertrophic arthritis

GSW to hip / acetabulumbowel perforation > vascular > urogenital

Hip dislocation

    • incarcerated fragment / non-concentric→open reduction ± removal
  • Irreducible → urgent open reduction (posterior → KL · anterior→Smith-Petersen)

Reduction — urgency & technique (including children)

Hip before wristreduce hip first; CT after reduction
✗ Wrong options: CT / MRI first

Manoeuvre (TO) Dislocation Key steps

✗ Wrong options: ED sedation · no fluoroscopy · open first

Indication Treatment

Anterior / obturator & irreducible dislocations — recognition & open approach

Approachposterior → Kocher-Langenbeck · anterior → Smith-Petersen (or Watson-Jones)

✗ Wrong options: traction · excision · posterior ORIF

Humeral Shaft Fractures

Trauma · 31 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence3–5% of all fractures · 20% of humeral fractures · 7–11.3 / 100,000

Agebimodal; 60% > 50 yr · < 50: 70% men · > 50: 70% women

Locationproximal ⅓ 30% · middle ⅓ 60% (commonest) · distal ⅓ 10%

Mechanismground-level fall 60% · MVA ~30% · pathological 4.3% · open 3%

Risk factorsprevious fracture, smoking (men), age, osteoporosis

Level Mechanism
Proximal ⅓ FOOSH, elderly (impaction at surgical neck)
Middle ⅓ transverse Direct blow
Middle ⅓ spiral FOOSH / torsion (throwing, arm wrestling)
Distal ⅓ Fall on flexed elbow

Associatedfloating elbow (+ radius / ulna; commoner in children) · ipsilateral shoulder dislocation (posterior > anterior)

Surgical anatomy & approaches

Canalends 2–3 cm proximal to olecranon fossa

Deforming forcesfracture proximal to pectoralis major → deltoid abducts proximal fragment

Radial nerve courseexits axilla posterior to brachial artery → triangular interval → between medial + long heads of triceps → spiral groove (medial to long + lateral heads, 2 cm proximal to deep head) → pierces lateral intermuscular septum ~10 cm proximal to radiocapitellar joint (20 cm above medial, 14 cm above lateral epicondyle) → anterior ~7.5 cm from articular surface (safe zone — never posterior within 7.5 cm)

Radial nerve in contact with bone~6.5 cm of diaphysis in spiral groove

Ulnar nerveenters posterior compartment at arcade of Struthers, ~8 cm above medial epicondyle

Axillary nerve4–7 cm below acromion (limits proximal posterior exposure)

Posterior antebrachial / inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nervebranch of radial; trace proximally to find radial nerve (Gerwin modification, paratricipital)

Compartmentsanterior: biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis, brachial vessels, musculocutaneous, median, ulnar · posterior: triceps, radial nerve

3Presentation

Examshortening + varus; document radial nerve pre- and post-reduction (wrist + thumb IP extension, dorsal hand sensation)

Radial nerve palsy"A-OK" + finger crossing intact, ↓ wrist / finger extension, dorsal hand numbness → Holstein-Lewis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use
AP + lateral humerus, joint above + below Standard
Transthoracic lateral Sagittal (apex anterior) deformity; rotate patient, not distal fragment
Traction views Shortened / extension (not routine)
CT Intra-articular extension
CTA Vascular injury
EMG / NCS Nerve palsy follow-up — not acutely

Classification

System Categories
Descriptive Proximal / middle / distal ⅓ · spiral, transverse, comminuted
OTA 12 A simple · B wedge · C complex
Garnavos Location P / M / D (+ j = joint) · morphology S simple (T transverse / oblique, S spiral) · I intermediate (1–2 butterflies) · C complex (≥ 3 butterflies / comminution)
Holstein-Lewis Spiral distal ⅓ → radial nerve palsy 7–22% (Orthobullets) · 22% (OB); entrapment risk; 7.5% of shaft fractures

5Management

Humeral shaft fracture
  • Isolated, closed, acceptable alignment → coaptation splint 7–10 d→functional brace
    • radial nerve palsy alone→still brace (observe nerve)
  • Absolute indication (open, vascular, plexus, floating elbow, compartment syndrome)→ORIF
  • Polytrauma / lower-limb fractures → plate (WB through arm) · DCO→splint first

Functional bracing — indications, acceptable alignment & contraindications

Acceptable alignment (adult) Limit
Anterior (sagittal) angulation < 20°
Varus / valgus < 30°
Rotation < 30° (Orthobullets, TO) · < 15° (OB)
Shortening < 3 cm

TO trap (TO)"angulation < 30°" is NOT acceptable (must be < 20°) · shortening < 3 cm, rotation < 30°, angulation < 20° (TO)

Child (TO)20–30° varus, 20° apex-anterior, 15° IR, ≤ 2 cm shortening

Infant / toddlercoaptation splint + bandage arm to thorax
✗ Wrong options: hanging cast · flexible nails · ex-fix · plate

Techniquecoaptation splint / hanging cast 7–10 days → Sarmiento brace (2.5 cm below axilla → 2.5 cm above condyles); no sling (gravity reduction); valgus mould vs varus; weekly X-ray × 3 wk, then every 3–4 wk

Hanging castavoid in transverse fractures (distraction)

At 9 days, acceptablefunctional brace 6–8 wk
✗ Wrong options: continue splint (stiffness) · ORIF

Contraindications (absolute)severe soft-tissue injury / bone loss · vascular injury needing repair · brachial plexus injury (no muscle tone → nonunion)

NOT contraindicationsradial nerve palsy (closed) · comminution · 1 cm shortening · 20° varus

Outcomesunion 93.5% (Sarmiento < 2% nonunion); time 10.7 wk; malunion 12%; proximal ⅓ oblique / spiral nonunion 29% (Rutgers-Ring) · 54% proximal ⅓ (Orthobullets)

Varus malunioncommonest deformity (esp. distal / transverse) → no effect on function
✗ Wrong options: nonunion · pain · satisfaction · nerve recovery

Nonop nonunionhigher than all surgical techniques (contemporary literature); 33% nonunion in one series

Radial nerve palsy — natural history, recovery order, EMG timing, exploration & tendon transfer

Incidence12.3% (8–15%) (Orthobullets) · 11–11.8% (OB); distal ⅓ 22%; 10–20% secondary (develop during treatment, TO)

Fracture typetransverse 21.2% > spiral 19.8% > oblique 8.4% > comminuted 6.8% · level: distal > middle > proximal

Injury typeclosed → neurapraxia · low-velocity GSW → axonotmesis · open (high energy) → neurotmesis (laceration) · complete palsy 50–68% (TO)

Spontaneous recovery~70% by 7 weeks (OB, TO > 70%) · 77.2% (Orthobullets) · 85–90% within 3 months · full at ~6 months · 100% of low-energy by 4 months (TO) · 88.6% overall · iatrogenic 93.9%

At explorationin continuity 62.7% · lacerated 26.8% · incarcerated 10.5% · transected only 12% (Pollock, TO)

LastEIP → index MCP hyperextension

5Management

Humeral shaft nonunion
  • Rule out infection (ESR, CRP) + metabolic (vitamin D)
  • Symptomatic→compression plate (4.5 mm) ± autograft (gold standard)
    • after nail→remove nail + compression plate + graft
    • very proximal / distal, poor bone→dual plating
  • Low demand, high risk, asymptomatic→brace ± stimulator

Treatment options

Option Indication Fact
Brace ± bone stimulator Low demand, high risk, asymptomatic Stimulator not if pseudarthrosis, gap > 5 mm, poor blood supply
Compression plating + bone graft Symptomatic nonunion — gold standard Superior to IMN; ~100% union; ICBG donor morbidity 44%
Dual plating (orthogonal) Very proximal / distal, poor metaphyseal bone, micromotion after one plate 92–100% union at 16 wk
Cortical strut allo- / autograft (intramedullary or medial + lateral plate) Severe osteopenia, bone loss, recalcitrant 95–100% union
Free fibula Recalcitrant atrophic —
Induced membrane / fibula / cancellous allograft Bone loss —
BMP Limited role — no proven benefit —

Compression plating with bone graft (after nail or brace)

Techniqueanterior / anterolateral / posterior (radial nerve neurolysis); debride fibrous tissue + bone ends; maximal cortical contact; 4.5 mm compression plate

GraftICBG autograft if atrophic · DBM, RIA, local callus · graft in hypertrophic — controversial

✗ Wrong options: exchange nailing · dynamisation · MUA · nail removal + brace

✗ Wrong options: augmentative plate (hypertrophic only) · plate without graft · smoking cessation alone

✗ Wrong options: spacer · ex-fix · brace · retain implants

Intertrochanteric Fractures

Trauma · 33 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Share~50% of hip fractures · 150,000 / yr (US) · F 500 vs M 200 / 100,000 / yr

Whoaverage ~80 yr (older than neck fractures) · F:M 2:1 to 8:1

Risk factorsosteoporosis, age, comorbidities, ADL dependency, recurrent falls (dementia, Parkinson's, vision, drugs)

Osteoporosis — sentinel fractures & bisphosphonates

Sentinel fractureproximal humerus fracture → ↑ hip fracture risk (for 1 yr)
✗ Wrong options: sacral · radius · fibula · distal humerus

Early bisphosphonate after fragility hip fracturegreatest BMD gain in first year; no ↑ nonunion, delayed union or peri-implant fracture; oral ≈ IV

Anatomy

Neck-shaft130 ± 7° · anteversion 10 ± 7°

Calcar femoraledense vertical wall from posteromedial shaft → posterior neck; its involvement decides stability

Femoral radius of curvature114–120 cm; smaller (more bowed) in elderly, Asian, short stature

Fragment Deformity Muscles
Proximal Flexion Iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus, pectineus
Proximal External rotation Short external rotators
Proximal Abduction Gluteus medius + minimus, maximus, TFL
Distal Adduction + shortening → varus Adductors, gracilis

Blood supplyrich (trochanteric anastomosis: MFCA + LFCA ascending branches, superior + inferior gluteal) → nonunion < 2%

TrabeculaeWard's triangle = lowest BMD, bounded by primary compressive, principal tensile, secondary compressive trabeculae

3Presentation

Examshortened, externally rotated, GT tenderness, pain on log-roll, no straight-leg raise

Historypre-injury function (predicts outcome), antecedent pain (OA / pathological), anticoagulants, ASA

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use / fact
AP pelvis, AP hip, cross-table lateral, full-length femur Pattern; posterior comminution (lateral); subtroch extension, lesions, nail length, bow, canal
Traction internal-rotation view Better classification, assess reduction
MRI Occult fracture (best; T1 100% sensitive, T2 84%) · isolated GT fracture → MRI for IT extension (✗ Wrong options: CT · traction view · fix first)
CT (1–2 mm) Second line if no MRI: sens 86%, spec 98%
Bone scan Rare; false negative up to 72 h; sens up to 98%

MRI findingsmarrow oedema on STIR / fat-suppressed T2; low-signal T1 line

Stability classification

Stable Unstable
Definition Intact posteromedial cortex → resists medial compression Collapses into varus / shaft medialises
Examples 2-part; small LT fragment without medial comminution Large / comminuted posteromedial (LT) fragment · reverse obliquity (transtrochanteric) · subtrochanteric extension · lateral wall < 20.5 mm

Lateral wall thicknessmeasured 3 cm below innominate tubercle at 135° to fracture line; < 20.5 mm → postop lateral wall fracture → CMN, not SHS; 25 mm = not a risk

AO / OTA 31A Description
A1 Simple 2-part pertrochanteric, intact lateral cortex
A2 Separate posteromedial fragment, intact lateral cortex
A3 Through lateral + medial cortex (reverse oblique / transverse)
Evans Description
Stable Posteromedial cortex intact / minimal comminution
Unstable Greater posteromedial comminution — convertible to stable with medial cortical opposition
Reverse obliquity Unstable — adductors medialise shaft

Reduction quality — cortical support

Medial cortical support (TO) Proximal fragment
Positive — most acceptable Medial to shaft cortex
Neutral Anatomical
Negative Lateral — collapses

5Management

Intertrochanteric fracture
  • Stable (intact posteromedial + lateral wall ≥ 20.5 mm)→SHS or CMN (equal outcomes)
  • Unstable / reverse obliquity / subtroch extension / thin lateral wall→CMN
    • subtroch extension ≤ 3–4 cm → short CMN · more distal→long CMN
  • Comminuted + severe OA / bone won't hold→calcar-replacing arthroplasty

Treatment options

Option Indication Fact
Nonop (NWB, bed → chair) Non-ambulatory, too high risk, skin breakdown, incomplete fracture 1-yr mortality 84.4%; pneumonia, UTI, sores, DVT
SHS (most common ORIF) Stable Cheapest, spares abductors, dynamic compression; 2-hole side plate = 4-hole
CMN Stable or unstable — AAOS strong for unstable, reverse oblique, subtroch extension Load-sharing, shorter lever arm, intramedullary buttress limits medialisation, ↓ / = blood loss; violates abductors; dearer; ↑ use over last decade
Proximal femoral locking plate Young + unstable (rare) Surgeon-dependent; no early WB
95° blade plate / DCS Rare Acceptable for reverse oblique
Arthroplasty (long-stem, calcar-replacing) Salvage, severe comminution, pre-existing OA, very osteoporotic Fix GT; more blood loss, time, cost

Stable vs unstable patterns — implant choice (SHS vs cephalomedullary nail, reverse obliquity)

StableSHS = CMN outcomes; reduction quality > implant choice

Reverse obliquityNOT SHS (56% failure) → shear, shaft medialisation + cut-out → CMN (trochanteric or piriformis), blade plate, DCS, locking plate, ex-fix all acceptable

SHS advantages over CMNnone for DVT, blood loss, nonunion, biomechanics
✗ Wrong options: all

CMN preferred becausestability for the fracture pattern
✗ Wrong options: shorter LOS · less abductor damage · easier THA conversion · cheaper

Most cost-effective (stable)SHS
✗ Wrong options: cannulated screws · hemi

Spare abductorsSHS
✗ Wrong options: lateral position · lag screw vs blade · omitting distal lock

Short vs long CMNequal function, reoperation, peri-implant fracture, cut-out, mortality · long: ↑ OR time, ↑ blood loss, ↑ postop anaemia + transfusion, radiation, bow mismatch · short tolerates 3–4 cm subtroch extension

Distal locking screwprotective against peri-implant fracture (omitting ↑ refracture)

SHS contraindicatedreverse oblique, lateral wall comminution / < 20.5 mm, subtrochanteric fractures

Tip-apex distance & cut-out

TADsum of tip → apex distances on AP + lateral, corrected for magnification

GoalTAD < 25 mm · > 45 mm → 60% failure · 27 / 32 / 40 mm → ↑ cut-out

Strongest predictor of cut-outTAD
✗ Wrong options: age · stability · reduction · plate angle

Lag screw positioncentre–centre (TO); low-central AP + central lateral acceptable; never peripheral / posterior (head rotates → superior cut-out)
✗ Wrong options: posterior on lateral

Lag screw vs helical bladecontroversial · blade compacts bone, ↑ cut-out resistance (biomechanical), but much higher "cut-through"

Failure Definition
Cut-out Anterocranial perforation with varus collapse
Cut-through Central perforation without collapse — helical blade

Lateral wall integrity & sliding hip screw failure

Intra-op lateral wall fracture↑ collapse / sliding
✗ Wrong options: nail length · WB status

Predictor of postop lateral wall fracture with SHSlateral wall thickness
✗ Wrong options: reverse obliquity · T-score · calcar comminution

Highest SHS failurewall 18.5 mm + TAD 28.5 mm

DHS failure — EXCEPT2-hole side plate
✗ Wrong options: reverse oblique · TAD 27 / 32 · lateral wall comminution

Left-sided unstable fracture + DHSanterior spike (screw torque) → derotation wire first

SHS problems in unstable fracturesexcessive collapse, limb shortening, shaft medialisation

Anterior cortical perforation & nail technique

Causeradius-of-curvature mismatch (nail straighter / larger radius than bowed femur) + posterior start on GT
✗ Wrong options: anterior start · large implant · lateral position

Preventlateral view of distal femur while seating · avoid posterior start

Too-lateral start (> 3 mm)varus → collapse + cut-out

Guidewire stuck in nail (no fragment)remove nail, check guidewire bend
✗ Wrong options: insert lag wire · re-ream · smaller nail · tighten jig

PFN-A2 vs PFN-A (TO)all: less lateral cortex pressure (flat lateral surface), smaller proximal diameter (16.5 vs 17.0 mm), smaller blade; higher bend point, 5° ML bend — for Asian femora

PFN types (TO)conventional PFN (2 screws: lag + anti-rotation) → Z / reverse Z · PFN-A (single helical blade, unreamed, 2003)

6Complications

Complication Fact
Cut-out / implant failure Commonest after CMN; 4–20%, within 4 months (Orthobullets) · 3 months (OB)
Nonunion / malunion < 2%; diagnosis: pain + lucency 4–7 months; rule out infection
Peri-implant fracture 1–3% at 1 yr; short = long; short → at nail tip, long → around rod
Anterior perforation Long CMN, bow mismatch, posterior start
Anaemia > 30% transfused; threshold ≤ 8 g/dL if asymptomatic; TXA (strong)

Failed fixation — conversion to THA

Z effect (TO)lag screw migrates laterally, varus collapse, derotation screw perforates head

Reverse Z effect (TO)derotation screw migrates laterally + lag screw migrates medially (TO case answer)

Causeunstable calcar, deficient lateral buttress, no medial support; head vs neck compressive-strength mismatch

Failure Treatment
Elderly / joint damaged by cut-out THA (✗ Wrong options: NWB · valgus osteotomy · revision ORIF · resection)
Malunion + hardware into acetabulum THA with calcar-replacing stem bypassing hardware (✗ Wrong options: bipolar (acetabular erosion))
Active 72-yr, cut-out + acetabular erosion Conversion THA (✗ Wrong options: exchange CMN · osteotomy · proximal femoral replacement · hemi)
Young / intact head Valgus osteotomy ± graft / revision ORIF

Mortality, surgical timing & perioperative care

1-yr mortality15–30% (Orthobullets) · 20–30% (OB) · ~10% at 1 mo, 20% at 4 mo, 30% at 1 yr; nonop 84.4%

↑ Mortalitymale (25–30% vs 20%), IT > neck fracture, age > 85, ≥ 2 comorbidities, ASA III–IV, delay > 48 h (> 2 days, Orthobullets · ≥ 3 days, OB)

Recognised predictorASA class
✗ Wrong options: WB status · comminution · device · anaesthetic

Not associated with ↑ mortalitysurgery within 48 h, spinal vs general (REGAIN), nail length, interdisciplinary care (↓)

Delay > 48 h↑ 30-day mortality, ↑ pneumonia
✗ Wrong options: OR time · transfusion · infection

Timing24–48 h (AAOS moderate) · co-management (AAOS strong)

Dementia patientgeriatric co-management, avoid centrally-acting drugs (meperidine), rapid optimisation, surgery < 48 h
✗ Wrong options: neurology consult · routine echo · nephrology for normal CrCl (low muscle mass masks renal impairment)

Routine echodelays surgery without changing outcome (unless valve disease, arrhythmia, worsening CHF, CAD)
✗ Wrong options: hospitalist · fascia iliaca block · Foley · fluids cause delay

DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel)continue, proceed when optimised
✗ Wrong options: vitamin K (warfarin) · idarucizumab (dabigatran) · FFP · stop + wait 48 h

Function at 1 yr41% regain status · 40% more aids · 12% household · 8% non-functional · rule of thirds: ⅓ regain, ⅓ lose a level, ⅓ die

Post-opWBAT ↓ complications

Isolated Ulnar Shaft Fracture

Trauma · 34 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Rare< 1% of upper-limb fractures · men 10–20 yr, women > 60 yr

Associated conditions

Elbow / DRUJMonteggia, Essex-Lopresti → image wrist + elbow

Compartment syndromeup to 15%

Atypical (bisphosphonate-associated) fracture

Patternisolated transverse proximal ⅓ ulna, thickened posterior cortex, minimal comminution, prodromal ache → alendronate
✗ Wrong options: teriparatide · semaglutide · levothyroxine · methotrexate

Location20–45% of ulnar length from olecranon tip · ASBMR major / minor criteria (as for atypical subtrochanteric)

Outcomedelayed / nonunion ~50% → resect diseased bone + plate

Anatomy

Forearm axisradial head (proximal) → ulnar fovea (distal); radius rotates around ulna; ulnar malangulation → ↓ rotation

Interosseous membrane5 ligaments; central band = key part to reconstruct · accessory band, distal oblique bundle, proximal oblique cord, dorsal oblique accessory cord

2Mechanism

Direct blow ("nightstick") · indirect: MVA, fall from height (axial load)

3Presentation

Examdeformity, open wounds, tense compartments, pain on passive finger stretch; radial + ulnar pulses; median, radial, ulnar nerves

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral forearm ± obliques + ipsilateral wrist + elbow

Radial head aligned with capitellum on every viewexcludes Monteggia

OTA (ulna shaft) Subtypes
A — simple A1 spiral · A2 oblique · A3 transverse
B — wedge B2 intact · B3 fragmentary
C — multifragmentary C2 intact segmental · C3 fragmentary

5Management

Isolated ulnar shaft fracture
  • Distal ⅔, < 50% displacement + < 10° angulation→brace / Muenster cast / soft dressing
  • Displaced distal ⅔ or any proximal ⅓→ORIF (3.5 mm DCP, 6 cortices each side)
  • Gustilo I–IIIA open → primary ORIF · IIIB→ex-fix
  • Bone loss / nonunion→autograft, vascularised fibula, Masquelet

Operative criteria

Nonoperative Operative
Distal ⅔ (nightstick) Displaced distal ⅔
< 50% displacement Proximal ⅓
< 10° angulation Open (I–IIIA primary ORIF; IIIB ex-fix)
e.g. 20% translation, < 5° angulation Any adult radial shaft or both-bone fracture (even undisplaced)

Nonoperative management — outcomes & acceptable displacement

Minimally displacedequivalent clinical outcomes to surgery; slower union; union > 92%
✗ Wrong options: long-arm cast needed · 20° rotation loss · wrist / elbow stiffness

> 10° angulation or > 50% displacementloss of forearm rotation if treated nonop

Optionsfunctional brace, Muenster cast (interosseous mould), soft compression + immediate motion — all similar; above- vs below-elbow = no difference; review at ~1 wk; ≥ 6 wk

Operative technique

ORIFsubcutaneous approach; 3.5 mm DCP; compression mode; 6 cortices above + below; locking in osteoporosis; bridge if comminuted; 2.0 / 2.7 lag screws
✗ Wrong options: 4.5 mm — refracture after removal

Post-opearly ROM; NWB ~6 wk (secondary displacement)

Ex-fixGustilo IIIB; distal pins in 2nd + 3rd MC, ≤ 4 mm pins

IMNpoor soft tissue; through posterior olecranon; union ≈ ORIF; 7% nonunion forearm nailing (Street)

Graftingopen fracture with bone loss (delayed) / nonunion; autograft is critical (ICBG, proximal tibia, RIA); vascularised fibula — large defects, ↓ infection

Masquelet (induced membrane)stage 1: I&D + cement spacer + temporary fixation → stage 2: graft into membrane at 4–6 wk

6Complications

Complication Fact
Infection 3% after ORIF; open fractures
Compartment syndrome Up to 15%; crush, open, low-velocity GSW, vascular, DIC
Nonunion < 5% compression plate · up to 12% bridge plating of comminution
Malunion Radial bow restoration ∝ function
NV injury PIN with Monteggia, type III open → observe 3 months, explore if no return
Refracture Up to 10% with early removal; remove ≥ 1 yr (ulna, Orthobullets) · ≥ 18 months (Galeazzi note); 4.5 mm plates, comminution, lucency → brace 6 wk + protect 3 months after removal

Nonunion

Type Treatment
Atrophic ORIF (3.5 mm plate) + autogenous cancellous graft (✗ Wrong options: dynamic splint · graft alone · pinning · ultrasound)
Infected / atrophic with defect Masquelet
Hypertrophic Debridement + compression plating

Minimal displacement Nonop OK ORIF always
Risk if nonop Little Displacement, malunion, ↓ rotation
Nightstick Atypical (bisphosphonate)
Site Distal ⅔ Proximal ⅓

Union > 92% ~50% delayed / nonunion

Knee Dislocation

Trauma · 35 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence0.02% of orthopaedic injuries; under-reported — ~50% self-reduce before ED

WhoM:F 4:1 · morbid obesity → "ultra-low-energy" dislocation with ADLs + ↑ neurovascular injury

Mechanismhigh energy (MVC, dashboard → axial load on flexed knee, fall) · low energy (sport, walking) · hyperextension → anterior · posterior force on proximal tibia → posterior

Associatedvascular, common peroneal nerve (~25%), fractures 60%, patellar tendon rupture, avulsions, displaced menisci

Anatomy

Ligaments at riskACL, PCL, MCL, LCL, PLC (bony stability minimal)

Popliteal artery tetheredproximally at adductor hiatus (fibrous tunnel) + distally at soleus arch

Geniculate collateralscan give palpable pulses despite complete popliteal occlusion

KD classification & cruciate injury pattern

Kennedy (tibial direction) Share Key fact
Anterior 30–50% — most common Hyperextension; vascular injury = intimal tear (traction)
Posterior 30–40% — 2nd Highest vascular injury → complete popliteal artery tear
Lateral 13% Varus / valgus
Medial 3% Varus / valgus
Rotational (posterolateral) 4% Usually irreducible (buttonholed MFC)
Schenck Ligaments torn

KD II ACL + PCL only
KD III ACL + PCL + PMC (IIIM) or PLC / LCL (IIIL) — IIIL → highest peroneal nerve risk
KD IV ACL + PCL + PMC + PLC — highest vascular injury (5–15%)
KD V Multiligament + periarticular fracture

KD IV cruciate pattern (TO)ACL midsubstance + PCL femoral avulsion · ACL: midsubstance 45% > femoral 34% > tibial 21% · PCL: femoral avulsion 76% > midsubstance 17% > tibial 7%

✗ Wrong options: procurvatum

Test (TO) Positive means

Dial test at 30° AND 90° PLC + PCL

Valgus stress opens in full extension MCL + POL / posteromedial capsule + PCL

Incidence5–15% all (Orthobullets) · 10–40% / 18–45% / ~16% / ~25% (OB) · 40–50% anterior or posterior · low-velocity anterior ~40% (OB) — read the options

ABI = ankle systolic ÷ brachial systolic (normal 0.9–1.1) — < 0.9 → concern (e.g. 0.8) · < 0.85 (TO); ABI < 0.9: sens 87%, spec 97%; > 0.9 → NPV 100%

After reduction
  • Pulses absent / cool limb→emergent vascular exploration (no imaging delay)
  • Pulses present, ABI < 0.9 → CT angiography→vascular surgery if injury
  • Pulses present, ABI > 0.9→serial exams (2–4 hourly, 48 h)
  • Pulses absent pre-reduction, return after (TO)→CT angiography (intimal tear)

Trauma · 36 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology & causes

Commonest siteleg · anterior compartment most often (TO)

Fractures69% (Orthobullets) · 75% (TO) · tibial shaft = commonest cause (TO) · proximal tibia commonest overall (other TO) · plateau 12% vs shaft 3%, Schatzker VI high risk (TO)

Other causescrush, contusion, GSW, tight casts / dressings, IV extravasation, burns, post-ischaemic swelling, bleeding disorders / anticoagulants, arterial injury, osteotomy (Blount's), lithotomy position, snake bite, exercise

Risk factor Fact
Young age Highest 12–19 yr, then 20–29 (more muscle, less room)
Diaphyseal fracture More muscle than tendon
Open, segmental / comminuted Higher energy (Orthobullets, OB) · open not associated (one OB item) — read the options
Higher BMI (children) Most significant paediatric factor in OB
Paediatric Older (> 14 yr), male, MVC / motorbike, ipsilateral fibula fracture, IMN · < 12 yr protective
Polytrauma (TO) ↑ lactate / base deficit, transfusion, coagulopathy (warfarin)

Not associated (OB)male sex, BMI ≥ 30 (adult), open fracture, nicotine

Anterior compartment vulnerability (TO)type I (slow-twitch, oxidative) fibres → most sensitive to hypoxia

Pathophysiology — venous outflow obstruction

Cascadetrauma → bleeding + oedema → ↑ interstitial pressure → ↓ venous outflow relative to arterial inflow → myoneural ischaemia

Fasciotomy effect↑ venous outflow
✗ Wrong options: ↓ arterial inflow · ↑ interstitial pressure · ↓ perfusion · ↓ bleeding (may ↑ by losing tamponade)

Irreversible damagewithin 6 h

Deep posterior TP, FDL, FHL, popliteus Tibial nerve, posterior tibial artery Plantar foot numb + pain on passive toe EXTENSION
Superficial posterior Gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris Sural Plantarflexion

Lateral Just anterior to posterior fibular border
Superficial posterior Mid-calf

Technique Detail
Dual incision — 2 × 15–18 cm, 8 cm skin bridge Anterolateral: protect SPN; anterior fasciotomy 1 cm in front of septum, lateral 1 cm behind · Posteromedial: protect saphenous vein + nerve; superficial posterior; detach soleal bridge from tibia → deep posterior
Single lateral (perifibular) Fibular head → ankle; anterior + lateral, then superficial posterior; deep posterior via interosseous membrane behind fibula

Medial incision does NOT releaseEHL (anterior)
✗ Wrong options: TP, FDL, popliteus, soleus

Principles (TO)extensile incisions, release all involved compartments, protect vital structures, debride

Contraindicationmissed (established) compartment syndrome

Hyperbaric oxygen

Mechanism↑ oxygen diffusion gradient (100% O₂ at ↑ pressure)

Monteggia Fractures

Trauma · 37 / 67

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Monteggiaproximal ⅓ ulna fracture + radial head dislocation (PRUJ disruption)

Whorare in adults (high energy) · children 4–10 yr commoner, different protocol

Associatedolecranon fracture-dislocation, radial head (~5%), coronoid, LCL injury, terrible triad

Key ligamentannular ligament

4Diagnosis & Classification

Bado classification — direction of radial head dislocation

Ruleradial head dislocates toward the apex of the ulnar fracture (apex anterior → anterior)

Bado Share Pattern
I 60% Proximal / middle ulna, anterior dislocation — commonest in children + young adults
II 15% Posterior dislocation — 70–80% of adult Monteggia; worst prognosis
III 20% Ulnar metaphysis (distal to coronoid), lateral dislocation — most often irreducible (annular ligament)
IV 5% Ulna + radius fractures, dislocation any direction
Jupiter (type II) Ulnar fracture level
IIA Coronoid level
IIB Metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction
IIC Distal to coronoid (diaphysis)
IID Extends into distal half

Monteggia "variant"+ radial head / neck fracture → separate approach; ↑ OA, instability, nonunion, ↓ ROM

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral elbow, wrist, forearm; radiocapitellar line congruent on every view

CTcoronoid, olecranon, radial head involvement

3Presentation

PIN palsymost likely nerve injury; wrist extension in radial deviation (ECRL spared), weak thumb + MCP extension, sensation intact

5Management

Monteggia fracture
  • Child, stable ulna, reduced RC joint→closed reduction + cast (supination for Bado I / III)
  • Adult (almost all) → ORIF ulna (plate)→radial head usually reduces
    • radial head still out → check ulna (revise)→then open reduction (annular ligament)
  • Transverse / short oblique, easily reduced→closed reduction + IM fixation of ulna

Treatment options

Option Indication
Closed reduction + cast Children, stable transverse ulna; supination for Bado I + III; oblique / unstable → pinning
ORIF ulna + closed radial head reduction Adults, open, unstable (long oblique), comminuted
ORIF ulna + open radial head reduction Radial head won't reduce after correct ulnar ORIF, complex injury, variants
Closed reduction + IM ulnar fixation Transverse / short oblique, easily reduced

Techniquelateral decubitus; posterior incision lateral to olecranon tip; FCU / anconeus proximally, FCU / ECU distally; dorsal plating; dorsal cortex to judge length; distractor if comminuted; fluoroscopy through full motion

Radial head open reductionposterolateral (Kocher); separate lateral incision

Persistent radial head dislocation — ulnar malreduction / length

After ulnar fixation, radiocapitellar joint dislocatedrevise ulnar ORIF
✗ Wrong options: radial neck osteotomy first · radial head arthroplasty · splint in supination · shortening osteotomy

Commonest cause of persistent / recurrent dislocationfailure to restore ulnar length / anatomic alignment
✗ Wrong options: annular ligament not repaired · missed radial head fracture · LCL · fixation rigidity

Late (6 mo) subluxation + stiffnessulnar corrective osteotomy + open radial head reduction

Irreducible radial head — annular ligament interposition

Non-concentric after reduction (child, posterolateral)annular ligament interposed · Bado III most often
✗ Wrong options: LUCL · MCL bands · anconeus

How common"often found interposed" (Orthobullets) · "rare complication" in adults (OB) — read the options

Radial head excision — MCL competence

Chronic malunionulnar osteotomy + radial head reduction · or radial head excision (restores rotation)

Must be competent before excisionanterior bundle of MCL (primary valgus stabiliser)
✗ Wrong options: posterior bundle (secondary) · brachialis · RCL / LUCL (varus)

6Complications

Complication Fact
PIN palsy Up to 10% acute; blunt trauma from radial head → observe 2–3 months (usually resolves) → NCS if not
Radial head malunion / redislocation Ulnar malalignment
Stiffness Diagnosis delayed > 2–3 wk → complications ↑↑
Synostosis, nonunion, plate failure Type II: nonunion + plate failure

Outcomes & prognostic factors

Bado IIhighest complication rate, worst prognosis; nearly all lose some ROM
✗ Wrong options: full recovery · casting = surgery · nerve injury common · ulnohumeral instability

Worse DASHradial head / neck fracture
✗ Wrong options: age · radius injury type · treatment method

Morel-Lavallee Lesion

Trauma · 38 / 67

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Morel-Lavallée lesion (MLL)closed degloving: shear separates dermis + subcutaneous fat from deep fascia

Incidenceup to 8% of acetabular fractures (Orthobullets) · up to 10% (TO)

Siteproximal lateral thigh (peritrochanteric) — commonest; gluteal, lumbosacral, abdominal (hypermobile skin)

Riskhigh-energy shear; obese; with pelvic, acetabular, proximal femur fractures

Anatomy — plane of fluid collection

Layersepidermis → dermis → subcutaneous fat → [MLL] → deep fascia → muscle

Planedeep to subcutaneous fat, superficial to deep fascia
✗ Wrong options: dermis (seroma) · subcutaneous (oedema) · intramuscular (haematoma) · deep to muscle

Pathophysiology (4 stages)

Stagesshear separation → subdermal plexus lymphatics + vessels bleed → replaced by serosanguinous fluid → pseudocapsule (chronic, untreated)

Bacterial colonisationup to 46%

3Presentation

Missedup to 33% at index evaluation (distracting injuries, habitus)

Examecchymosis, swelling, fluctuance, skin hypermobility · discoloration may take days

Earliest indicator (TO)paraesthesia of overlying skin

Chronicdull pain, contour deformity, cosmesis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Use / finding
Radiographs Underlying fractures; soft-tissue swelling
CT Size → management; fluid in fascial plane (soft-tissue window)
Ultrasound Hypoechoic space superficial to fascia; localise for drainage
MRI Best extent (avg 30 × 12 cm); acute: T1 low, T2 high · subacute: T1 + T2 high with capsule low on both

Not to do for MLLMRI + core biopsy (sarcoma work-up), CT chest / abdomen / pelvis (metastasis work-up), admit for antibiotics (abscess)

5Management

Morel-Lavallée lesion
  • Small (< 50 cm³)→compression ± percutaneous drainage + drain
  • Large (> 50 cm³) / failed nonop→open I&D + drain
    • overlies fracture incision→dual-incision I&D, same sitting as fixation
  • Chronic pseudocyst→open debridement + capsule resection

Operative criteria

Treatment Indication Outcome
Compression (ace wraps, bike shorts) < 50 cm³ Needs compliance
Percutaneous drainage + drain (US-guided, 1–2 cm incision, irrigate) < 50 cm³ Inferior to open (can't debride necrotic tissue); needle aspiration → high recurrence
Single-incision I&D > 50 cm³ or failed nonop; not in fracture approach 75% resolution
Dual-incision I&D Lesion overlies fracture approach / found intra-op Higher infection; serial I&D
Open debridement + capsule resection Chronic pseudocyst Often multiple surgeries

Chronic lesion — open debridement & drain

Large symptomatic lesion at 1 monthopen I&D + drain via limited approach (protect compromised subdermal plexus)
✗ Wrong options: needle decompression · biopsy · antibiotics

Trochanteric fracture + MLL (TO)fix fracture + incision, open debridement at same time
✗ Wrong options: delay fixation · observe · fix + ambulate only

Techniquescrub-brush / Cobb debridement · ≥ 15 Fr drain exiting away, remove at < 20–30 mL/day · primary vs delayed closure controversial (VAC + repeat I&D at 48–72 h)

Dual-incisionproximal + distal ends of lesion; close proximal primarily, distal: VAC → repeat I&D 48–72 h

6Complications

Complication Fact
Recurrence Most common — up to 56% nonop, 15–20% after open → repeat I&D + drain, VAC, sclerotherapy (talc / doxycycline)
Pseudocyst Chronic untreated → resect capsule
Skin necrosis Delay, repeated I&D → skin graft
SSI after pelvic / acetabular surgery MLL = independent risk factor

Prognosisbetter if small, acute, away from incisions

Differentiation from necrotising fasciitis (LRINEC)

LRINEC (TO)CRP, WBC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose; ≥ 6 = high risk · not included: SGPT (ALT)

X vs Y

Morel-Lavallée Haematoma / seroma
Plane Subcutaneous fat ↔ deep fascia Intramuscular / dermis
Skin Hypermobile, fluctuant Not hypermobile

"Plane of fluid collection?"deep to subcutaneous fat, superficial to deep fascia

"Trochanteric fracture + thigh fullness (TO)?"fixation combined with incision + open debridement

"Large fluctuant lesion 1 month after crush?"open I&D + drain

"NOT in LRINEC (TO)?"SGPT
