Trauma · 39 / 67

1Basics

Definition & risk factors

Necrotising fasciitislife-threatening infection spreading rapidly along fascial planes; overlying cellulitis ± (early skin deceptively benign)

Immune suppressiondiabetes (commonest comorbidity, 71%), AIDS / HIV, cancer, obesity, alcohol

Bacterial entryIV drug use, injections, insect bites, skin abrasions (turf), abdominal / perineal surgery

Microbiology & empiric antibiotics (polymicrobial vs group A strep)

Type Organisms Setting
1 — polymicrobial (80–90%) 4–5 species: non-group A strep, anaerobes (Clostridia), facultative anaerobes, gram-negative enteric bacilli (Enterobacteriaceae); synergy Diabetics, cancer, post-op abdominal / perineal
2 — monomicrobial (5%) Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus (commonest monomicrobial) Healthy, extremities
3 Vibrio vulnificus (gram-negative rods) Marine exposure
4 Fungal —

Commonest overallpolymicrobial · commonest single isolate — group A strep (Fontes, Wong)
✗ Wrong options: GAS · MRSA · S. aureus

Polymicrobial culture most likely indiabetic with necrotising soft-tissue infection
✗ Wrong options: chronic PJI (CoNS) · nail through shoe (Pseudomonas) · neonate hip (GBS) · acute PJI (S. aureus)

MRSAnot the commonest monomicrobial cause

3Presentation

Earlyrapidly progressing cellulitis / abscess, minimal swelling, no discoloration

Latesevere pain (out of proportion), high fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension

Skinbullae (purple / haemorrhagic), ischaemic patches, cutaneous gangrene, induration, subcutaneous emphysema (gas only 13%)

Red flagworsening despite IV antibiotics + systemic toxicity

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Imagingnot required; CT / MRI delay surgery (only show oedema / thickening) · gas → urgent debridement

Frozen section1 × 1 × 1 cm, bedside or OR; confirms early cases; never delay surgery · histology: fascial necrosis, organisms in fascia, PMNs, fibrinous thrombi + vessel wall necrosis

Diagnosis — LRINEC score & laboratory markers

LRINEC component Points
CRP ≥ 150 mg/L 4 (largest)
WBC 15–25 · > 25 × 10⁹/L 1 · 2
Hb 11–13.5 · < 11 g/dL 1 · 2
Na < 135 mmol/L 2
Creatinine > 141 µmol/L 2
Glucose > 10 mmol/L 1

Scoremax 13; ≥ 6 → high risk; original PPV 92% · later sens 68%, spec 85%

NOT in LRINECESR, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, SGPT / ALT

Missing value given CRP, WBC, glucose, Cr, Nahaemoglobin

Most valuable lab (with Na 130, CRP > 200)WBC > 25 → emergent debridement ± amputation
✗ Wrong options: ESR · MRI

5Management

Suspected necrotising fasciitis
  • Resuscitate + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately
  • Emergent radical debridement (skin, fat, fascia, muscle) — don't wait for imaging / ICU / culture
    • life-threatening→amputation
  • Serial debridements; hyperbaric O₂ if anaerobes

Emergent surgical debridement

Worsening despite cefazolin, hypotensionurgent aggressive debridement of skin, fat + fascia
✗ Wrong options: triple antibiotics alone · ICU + ID consult · gentle closure · HBO / IVIG first

Diabetic, bullae, CRP > 200, WBC 25k, Na 127emergent debridement ± amputation
✗ Wrong options: vascular exploration · ICU + escalate antibiotics · MRI · CT

IVDU / HIV hand, CRP 178, WBC 29kemergent debridement

Neonatal Forearm Compartment Syndrome

Trauma · 40 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Rarecase reports; largest series 24 cases / 20 yr

Whenfirst 24 h of life, present at birth

Whereforearm, wrist, hand; unilateral; R = L; dorsum > volar

Risk factor Type
Hypercoagulable — polycythaemia Intrinsic
Prematurity, multiple gestation —
Oligohydramnios Extrinsic
Maternal diabetes, abnormal lie, neonatal respiratory distress —

Pathophysiology

Commonestidiopathic

Extrinsic (compression)fetal posture, oligohydramnios, umbilical cord loops, amniotic bands, birth trauma

Intrinsic (clotting)hypercoagulable state → arterial / venous thrombosis

3Presentation

Pathognomonicskin lesion in ALL: bullae, erythema, ulcers, eschar, distal hand / digit oedema, fingertip gangrene

Nervesradial + PIN > ulnar = median; ↓ spontaneous movement

Usually missed → found only after complications

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Radiographsskeletal changes late: physeal distortion (widening, flaring, premature closure, angulation), shortening, LLD

MRIlate cases with full-thickness necrosis + contracture (fasciotomy futile) → map necrosis, guide debridement

LabsCBC, ESR, CRP normal (vs infection)

Compartment pressure — NOT measuredno neonatal Δp standards; DBP at birth < 40 mmHg → small rise impairs perfusion

Differential

Condition Distinguishing feature
Cellulitis Mother well, cultures negative
Necrotising fasciitis Most easily confused; skin + subcutaneous only → excision, not fasciotomy; confirmed at surgery
Vascular injury Absent pulses / Doppler; with brachial plexus lesions

Neonatal forearm compartment syndrome
  • Diagnosed < 24 h→emergency fasciotomy (volar, dorsal, mobile wad + carpal tunnel) ± STSG
  • Hypercoagulable→anticoagulants / thrombolytics
  • Late→salvage (debride, neurolysis, release, lengthening, angular correction, tendon reconstruction)

Best outcomefasciotomy within first 24 h · salvage inferior

6-h-old, 34 wk, oligohydramnios, polycythaemia, bullaeneonatal compartment syndrome → fasciotomy
✗ Wrong options: cellulitis + antibiotics · NF debridement / HBO · needle manometry

6Complications

Complication Treatment
Ischaemic muscle contracture Debridement + release
Fingertip gangrene —
Physeal distortion Lengthening, angular correction
Nerve dysfunction Neurolysis

Prognosismissed diagnosis = worst; early fasciotomy = best

"Neonate with bullous forearm, oligohydramnios, polycythaemia?"neonatal compartment syndrome; fasciotomy

Olecranon Fractures

Trauma · 41 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence12 / 100,000 / yr · ~10% of upper-limb fractures · mean age ~57; bimodal

Mechanismdirect blow → comminuted · indirect (FOOSH) → transverse / oblique

Transolecranon fracture-dislocationsevere axial load; distal humerus driven through olecranon = anterior dislocation; PRUJ intact (vs Monteggia)

Anatomy

Greater sigmoid (semilunar) notcholecranon + coronoid; articulates with trochlea (flexion-extension + stability)

Tricepsinserts posterior proximal ulna, blends with periosteum (radial nerve, C7) · anconeus — lateral olecranon (radial nerve)

3Presentation

Painposterior elbow · palpable gap → displaced / comminuted

Can't extend elbowextensor (triceps) mechanism discontinuous

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

True lateralessential for fracture pattern · radiocapitellar view → radial head / capitellum · CT → comminuted planning

Classifications

Colton Description
Nondisplaced Displacement doesn't increase with flexion
Avulsion Displaced
Oblique / transverse Displaced
Comminuted Displaced
Fracture-dislocation Transolecranon
Schatzker Pattern
A Simple transverse
B Transverse impacted
C Oblique
D Comminuted
E More distal, extra-articular
F Fracture-dislocation
AO Pattern
A Extra-articular
B Intra-articular
C Intra-articular radial head + olecranon

Mayocomminution, displacement, fracture-dislocation

5Management

Olecranon fracture
  • Nondisplaced, extensor intact→cast 45–90°, motion at 1 wk
  • Displaced, transverse, no comminution→tension band (or IM screw)
  • Comminuted / oblique past coronoid / Monteggia / fracture-dislocation→plate
  • Elderly low-demand→nonop or excision + triceps advancement (< 50% joint)

Operative criteria

Implant Indication
Tension band / IM screw Transverse, no comminution, through midpoint of trochlear notch, proximal to coronoid
Plate Comminution, oblique extending distal to coronoid, coronoid involvement, Monteggia, fracture-dislocation, articular impaction, open
Excision + triceps advancement Elderly osteoporotic, < 50% of joint, too comminuted / small, nonunion; no instability
Nonop cast Nondisplaced + intact extensor; displaced in low-demand elderly

Tension band wiring — indications & biomechanics

Mechanismconverts triceps distraction (tension) into articular compression
✗ Wrong options: neutralisation · shear · bending

Best fortransverse fracture through midpoint of trochlear notch
✗ Wrong options: comminuted · coronoid · Monteggia · oblique distal

TechniqueK-wires engaging anterior cortex (↓ migration) but no over-penetration; 18-gauge wire / thick suture figure-of-8 through drill hole

Conshardware removal 40–80%; no axial stability in comminution; can narrow sigmoid notch if comminuted

Relative TBW indicationstip fractures, transverse, osteoporotic, displaced

Plate fixation — comminution, fracture-dislocation & open fractures

Comminutionthe indication for plate over TBW
✗ Wrong options: displacement · intra-articular · obliquity alone

Comminuted, past coronoid (24-yr)plate + screws
✗ Wrong options: IMN · TBW + IM screw · triceps advancement · TEA

Bridge platingcomminuted, non-reconstructable, young / active (45-yr)
✗ Wrong options: osteotomy fixation · simple transverse · 91-yr osteoporotic (excise) · child apophysis

Transolecranon fracture-dislocation (open or closed)plate → best function
✗ Wrong options: TBW / IM screw (need cortical contact) · excision (anterior instability) · cast

Techniquedorsal (tension) side; lag screws for oblique; ⅓ tubular too weak for comminution; triceps advanced over plate; removal ~20%

Elderly low-demand — nonoperative or excision with triceps advancement

✗ Wrong options: 45° × 8 wk (stiffness) · pinning · TBW · locking plate

✗ Wrong options: IM screw · TBW · TEA · lag + plate

Excision ideal85-yr, comminuted, < 50% of proximal joint
✗ Wrong options: young · > 50% · coronoid-level oblique

Fracture Transverse, simple Comminuted, oblique past coronoid, dislocation

Trauma · 42 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence30.7 / 100,000 / yr · average age 45

Associated injuries30% · compartment syndrome still possible with an open wound

Key radiology findings

Radiographsjoint above + below · CT — periarticular injury, knee arthrotomy (intra-articular air)

Classification & scoring (Gustilo, Ganga, AO soft tissue)

Gustilo (TO) Wound Soft tissue
I < 1 cm, clean Minimal
II 1–10 cm, moderate No periosteal stripping
IIIA Any size (high energy) Local coverage possible
IIIB — Periosteal stripping + exposed bone → flap needed
IIIC — Arterial injury needing repair

6 × 4 cm dirty crush wound, distal tibia, exposed bone + periosteal stripping (TO)IIIB

Automatically type III (TO)gunshot, farm injury

Gustilo drawbacks (TO)many modifications, wide IIIB spectrum, wound-size based, doesn't address salvage, poor interobserver reliability

Ganga Hospital Open Injury Score (TO) Points
Covering (skin + fascia) 1–5 (circumferential skin loss = 5)
Skeletal (bone + joint) 1–5 (bone loss ≥ 4 cm = 5)
Functional (musculotendinous + nerve) 1–5 (loss of ≥ 2 compartments / subtotal amputation = 5)
Comorbidities — 2 each Debridement > 12 h, age > 65, sewage / farm contamination, SBP < 90, compartment syndrome / other major injury same limb, DM / cardiorespiratory, polytrauma ISS > 25 / fat embolism

Ganga facts (TO)designed for IIIB; scored AFTER debridement (not in ED before); max 29; better reliability than Gustilo; doesn't predict survival of polytrauma

Ganga thresholds (TO)≤ 14 → salvage · 15–16 = grey zone · ≥ 17 → amputation · ("≥ 14 amputation threshold" in another TO item — read the options)

AO soft-tissue (TO)extensive closed degloving = IC4 (IC closed vs IO open)

Open fracture
  • ED: IV antibiotics (ASAP, < 1–3 h), tetanus, splint, saline dressing
  • OR: debridement (< 24 h; IIIB tibia < 12 h; gross contamination 6–12 h) + low-pressure saline / soap

  • Definitive fixation + coverage < 7 days→bone defect: Masquelet / fibula / transport

First thing to do (grade III tibia)IV antibiotics
✗ Wrong options: bedside I&D · splint · CTA · OR first

Host Typical site

Diabetes Foot, decubitus ulcers
Adult haematogenous Vertebrae (commonest)

Mechanism

Route Fact
Haematogenous Commonest in children; vertebrae in adults; S. aureus
Contiguous Surgery, trauma, wounds, poor vascularity; bacterial > mycobacterial / fungal

Age / setting Organism
Neonate (< 4 mo) S. aureus, Enterobacter, GAS + GBS
4 mo–4 yr S. aureus, GAS, Kingella kingae, Enterobacter
4 yr–adult S. aureus (80%), GAS, H. influenzae
Adult S. aureus ± Enterobacter / Strep

✗ Wrong options: H. influenzae · Strep viridans · Pseudomonas

Biofilm & bacterial growth stages

Stage Fact
Planktonic Free-floating bacteria attach to inert substrate + apoptosis → biofilm matrix
Sessile Quorum sensing → matures; no-growth state; virulence genes; antibiotic resistant
Dispersion Releases planktonic bacteria

Biofilmextracellular polymeric substance / exopolysaccharide (glycocalyx); poor antibiotic penetration + ↓ metabolism · PJI > 4 wk → explant

Metaphyseal osteomyelitis & joint spread

Intracapsular metaphyses (TO)proximal radius, proximal humerus, proximal femur, distal tibia / fibula → septic arthritis · NOT head of ulna

Symptomspain; fever (acute); sepsis signs

Draining sinuschronic; probe to bone → chronic osteomyelitis (diabetic ulcer probing bone = osteomyelitis, not Charcot — improves with elevation)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Fact
Radiographs Lag ~2 wk; need 50% bone loss; chronic: sequestrum (dead bone, nidus), involucrum (new bone around), Brodie abscess, sclerosis, periosteal reaction
CT Necrotic bone, planning (hardware artifact)
MRI Best for early diagnosis + localisation; negative rules out; may overestimate extent; T2 oedema
Penumbra sign (T1) Bright rim (vascularised membrane) around dark abscess, dark sclerotic outer rim → intraosseous abscess → surgery
Tc bone scan Normal X-ray + no MRI; sensitive, not specific; negative rules out
Gallium Diabetic foot / no MRI; cellulitis false positive

Genes & lab markers

Test Fact
WBC Raised in only ⅓ of acute
ESR Raised ~90%; fall = favourable
CRP Most sensitive (97%); falls faster than ESR
Blood cultures Often negative; guide haematogenous cases
Sinus tract culture Unreliable (contaminants)
Bone culture Gold standard for antibiotics (off antibiotics)

Histologyacute: live osteocytes + neutrophils · chronic: empty lacunae, marrow fibrosis, lymphocytes + plasma cells (plasma cell = chronic)

Most accurate diagnosis vs Ewing (TO)bone biopsy · "biopsy all infections, culture all tumours"
✗ Wrong options: indium scan · MRI (next step) · LDH

✗ Wrong options: ACHA (old view) · axillary · profunda

ACHAanterolateral branch → arcuate artery (main GT supply); 1990 study: supplies whole head except posteroinferior GT + head · disrupted in ~80% of fractures yet AVN infrequent → PCHA dominant

Pseudosubluxation Inferior head (haemarthrosis + atony)

Proximal Third Tibia Fracture

Trauma · 49 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence5–11% of tibial shaft fractures (~10%)

Mechanismlow energy: torsion → spiral oblique (indirect) · high energy: direct

Associatedcompartment syndrome, soft-tissue injury (muscle injury severity → amputation need)

Characteristic deformity — valgus & procurvatum and its causes

Force Effect
Patellar tendon Proximal fragment extends → apex anterior (procurvatum)
Gastrocnemius Distal fragment flexes
Pes anserinus Proximal fragment varus (per note)
Anterior compartment Valgus

Classic malunion after IMNvalgus + procurvatum (apex anterior) + anterior translation of proximal fragment
✗ Wrong options: varus · recurvatum · rotation

Causeswide metaphysis (no canal fit), eccentric / medial start, deforming muscles, knee hyperflexion, nail Herzog curve ("wedge effect")

Malalignment rate20–60% (Orthobullets) · 58% proximal ⅓ (Freedman; vs 7% middle, 8% distal) · up to 84% (OB)

Other fractures' typical malunionshumeral shaft: varus, shortening, IR · distal femur: varus, shortening, recurvatum · distal ⅓ tibia + intact fibula: varus + rotation · subtroch: flexion, abduction, ER

3Presentation

Examcontusions, blisters, open wounds, compartments (passive toe stretch ± pressures) · DPN, SPN, sural, tibial, saphenous; DP + PT pulses

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP + lateral tibia + knee + ankle · findings: proximal fragment extended, apex anterior, varus; distal fragment flexed

CTintra-articular extension (differential: plateau fracture, knee dislocation)

AO 42 Pattern
A Simple
B Wedge
C Comminuted

5Management

Proximal ⅓ tibia fracture
  • Closed low energy, acceptable alignment → long leg cast (10–20° flexion)→brace at 4 wk
  • Soft-tissue compromise / polytrauma→ex-fix (convert to IMN 7–21 d)
  • ≥ 5–6 cm proximal bone for 2 locking screws→IMN + anti-deformity tricks
  • Very proximal / inadequate nail fixation→percutaneous locking plate

Operative criteria

Acceptable for cast Limit
Varus / valgus < 5°
AP angulation < 10°
Cortical apposition > 50%
Shortening < 1 cm (hardest to control)
Rotation < 10°
Option Indication / fact
Ex-fix Soft-tissue compromise, polytrauma; circular frame for very proximal; more malalignment than IMN
IMN ≥ 5–6 cm proximal bone (2 locking screws); static locking proximal + distal; ≥ 2 proximal screws, oblique screws help
Percutaneous locking plate Extreme proximal, transverse / oblique, good soft tissue; lateral safer; lateral plate + medial comminution → varus collapse; ↑ infection vs IMN in open

Nailing technique — lateral start point, semi-extended / suprapatellar nailing, unicortical plate

Start pointjust medial to lateral tibial spine (AP) + proximal, anterior to articular margin (lateral) → lateral start prevents valgus
✗ Wrong options: medial start → valgus · distal + medial → anterior cortex cut-out

Approachlateral parapatellar (needs mobile patella) helps lateral start · medial parapatellar → valgus

Semi-extended / suprapatellar nailingneutralises extensor pull → prevents procurvatum · suprapatellar does NOT affect valgus (coronal)
✗ Wrong options: hyperflexion (worsens) · radiolucent triangle

Suprapatellar vs infrapatellarinfrapatellar → more anterior knee pain; ROM, union, PF joint same

Unicortical plateshort ⅓-tubular plate anterior / anteromedial / posteromedial, 2 unicortical screws each side → holds reduction (prevents procurvatum + anterior translation)

Universal / femoral distractorSchanz pins medial, parallel to joint (can double as blocking pins)

Prevent apex anterior — all EXCEPTanterior blocking screw (posterior blocking screw, posterior starting hole, semi-extended interlocking, anteriorly directed nail all help)

Preserve reduction — EXCEPTcountersinking the nail (loses aperture fixation)
✗ Wrong options: oblique proximal screws · blocking screws · lateral eminence start · unicortical plate

Valgus prevention — NOT shown forsuprapatellar portal

Nail choiceHerzog curve proximal to fracture (distal curve → anterior translation)

Lockingstatic; no acute dynamisation

Blocking (Poller) screws — position & function

Ruleplace in the concavity of the deformity, in the proximal (metaphyseal) fragment → narrows canal, redirects nail

Screw Prevents
Posterior to nail, proximal fragment (coronal screw) Procurvatum (counters patellar tendon + gastrocnemius)
Lateral to nail, proximal fragment (sagittal screw) Valgus
Anterior Worsens procurvatum
Medial Worsens valgus

Radial Head Fractures

Trauma · 50 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence1–4% of adult fractures · 20–30% of elbow fractures (commonest) · mean age ~45 (85% 30–60) · F:M 3:2

MechanismFOOSH with elbow extended + forearm pronated

Associated (30%)LCL injury (commonest, up to 80% on MRI), MCL, Essex-Lopresti, coronoid, olecranon, Monteggia, terrible triad, scaphoid

Anatomy

Head15° offset from neck · anterolateral third lacks subchondral bone (fractures here) · 40° concave dish

Safe zone (non-articular)90–110° arc between radial styloid + Lister's tubercle (straight lateral in neutral) · ~25% of head doesn't articulate with ulna

Radiocapitellar joint60% of elbow load

Ligament Role
LUCL (supinator crest) Varus + ER (hypersupination); deficiency → PLRI
RCL Into annular ligament
Annular Holds head to lesser sigmoid notch; interposition → irreducible
MCL anterior bundle Primary valgus stabiliser (radial head 2nd)

Radial head rolessecondary valgus restraint (key if MCL deficient) · longitudinal stability (with IOM + DRUJ)

Longitudinal instability (Essex-Lopresti) — radial head as buttress, excision contraindicated

Essex-Loprestiradial head fracture + IOM disruption + DRUJ injury → proximal radial migration, ulnocarpal impaction
✗ Wrong options: distal radius fracture

Single best answer (TO)interosseous membrane injury; IOM gives > 70% axial stability (TO)

Primary buttress against proximal migrationradial head (then IOM) (OB) — read the options · TFCC (triangular fibrocartilage complex) also maintains length

Excision in Essex-Lopresti (TO)if ever, delay 3 weeks (IOM heals)

Clueswrist / DRUJ tenderness, ballottement +, ulnar styloid base fracture, radius pull test > 3 mm (intra-op), DRUJ translation > 50% vs other side

Late presentationonly 20% satisfactory vs 80% if acute

3Presentation

Examlateral tenderness; mechanical block to motion (normal flexion 0–150°, pronation 75°, supination 85°) → aspirate haematoma + intra-articular lidocaine · PIN + ulnar nerve · pivot shift / posterolateral drawer (LUCL), valgus stress (MCL) · palpate wrist + IOM

Pain limits exam at 1 wkintra-articular lidocaine + re-examine
✗ Wrong options: CT · MRI · splint 2–3 wk · EUA

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Fact
AP + lateral elbow, forearm + wrist —
Radiocapitellar (Greenspan) Oblique lateral, 45° cephalad → head without coronoid overlap
Fat pads Haemarthrosis; posterior fat pad more sensitive
CT Comminution, fracture-dislocations (3D planning)
MRI Ligaments; rarely changes management
Dynamic CT Subtle DRUJ instability

Mason classification (Hotchkiss / Broberg-Morrey)

Type Description
I < 2 mm, no block
II > 2 mm / angulated, possible block
III Comminuted, displaced, block
IV + elbow dislocation

OTA 2R1A extra-articular · B partial articular · C complete articular · high interobserver variability

5Management

Radial head fracture
  • No block (Mason I / II)→sling 2–7 d + early ROM
  • Block / displaced, ≤ 3 fragments, young→ORIF (headless screws ± plate in safe zone)
  • > 3 fragments / dislocation / Essex-Lopresti / unstable→radial head arthroplasty (+ LCL repair)
  • Low-demand, no instability→fragment excision (< 25–30%) or resection (never if unstable)

Nonoperative vs ORIF — mechanical block & lidocaine test

Mason I (violinist, no block)sling ~2 days → active motion · good 85–95% · Mason II without block: early failure up to 12%
✗ Wrong options: cast ≥ 1 wk (worse function)

Displaced partial articular + block (20–30° / 45–65° arcs)ORIF via ECU / anconeus (Kocher) with plate or screws
✗ Wrong options: excision > 30% · medial approach · arthroplasty (older / ≥ 3 fragments)

Mason II on CT, youngORIF
✗ Wrong options: cast · excision (< 25%) · CRPP (none in adults) · replacement

✗ Wrong options: 4-part young → arthroplasty · resection in young Mason III · arthroplasty for minimally comminuted 3-part · excision with ulnar styloid / DRUJ injury

Operative criteria

Treatment Indication
Nonop Mason I; Mason II without block
ORIF Mason II with block; Mason III / IV if feasible (≤ 3 fragments); open; complex elbow injury
Arthroplasty > 3 fragments (≥ 3, OB), fracture-dislocation (> 30% articular), Essex-Lopresti, terrible triad, plastic deformity, malunion / nonunion
Fragment excision Low demand, no instability, fragment < 25% (Orthobullets) · < 30% (OB)
Resection Sedentary, delayed isolated fracture, salvage · not with IOM injury (pull > 3 mm), coronoid fracture, MCL deficiency

ORIF outcomes> 3 fragments → > 50% unsatisfactory · isolated vs complex similar at 4 yr · fixation fails more than arthroplasty if elbow unstable

Epidemiology

Whomen 10–20 yr, women > 60 yr

Mechanismhigh energy (direct blow, MVA, fall from height, sport) · low-energy both-bone → suspect wrist / elbow injury

Rotation axisradial head → ulnar fovea; radius rotates around ulna

IOMoblique radius → ulna; load passes distal radius → proximal ulna · distal fibres tight in supination, central in neutral

IOM ligaments (5) Note
Central band Key load-bearer; reconstruct this
Accessory band, distal oblique bundle, proximal oblique cord, dorsal oblique accessory cord —
NOT part of IOM Annular ligament

Adult both-bone forearm fracture (> 10 yr)

  • Bone loss→graft (< 5 cm) · vascularised fibula / Masquelet (large)

Option Indication Fact
Cast / brace (Muenster, above elbow) Rare — non-displaced, non-surgical candidates > 50° rotation loss in 30%, high nonunion
ORIF Nearly all ≥ 10 yr; Gustilo I–IIIA primary ORIF > 95% union compression · 88% bridge plating
Ex-fix Gustilo IIIB Distal pins 2nd + 3rd MC, ≤ 4 mm
IMN Very poor soft tissue only No rotational / axial control, can't keep bow, high nonunion · flexible nails contraindicated in length-unstable adult fractures

Trauma · 52 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence30–45% of pelvic ring injuries; bimodal (young high energy · elderly low-energy / insufficiency)

Sacrum5 fused vertebrae; 4 foramina; load from S1 → iliac wings → acetabulum

2 Angulated + incomplete translation
3 Complete translation + displacement

  • > 1 cm / soft-tissue compromise / failed nonop / displacement→fixation

Nonoperative Operative
< 1 cm displacement, no deficit Displacement > 1 cm

Scapula Fractures

Trauma · 53 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence< 1% of fractures, 3–5% of shoulder girdle · age 25–50, M > F · mortality 2–5%

Locationbody / spine 45–50% · glenoid 35% (neck 25%, fossa / rim 10%) · acromion 8% · coracoid 7%

Mechanismhigh energy 80–90% (MVC > 70%) · FOOSH · dislocation: anterior → anterior rim, posterior (seizure, shock) → posterior rim

Associated injuries (rib / chest injury, ISS)

Associated injuries80–95% · ↑ Injury Severity Score
✗ Wrong options: ↑ mortality · LOS · ICU

Injury Rate
Chest injury (commonest) 80% — pneumo / haemothorax > 30%, contusion > 40%
Rib fractures (commonest fracture) 52–53%
Head injury 35–50%
Ipsilateral limb 50% (clavicle 25%)
Spine 26–30%
Pelvis / acetabulum 15%
Vascular (subclavian / axillary) 11%
Brachial plexus 5–13% (75% resolve)

CT chestconsider for ribs + lung injury

Anatomy

Body18 muscles; spine separates supra- / infraspinatus; spinoglenoid notch → infraspinatus only · scapular notch → supra + infraspinatus

Glenoidpear-shaped, 1–5° retroversion, 15° superior tilt; labrum deepens 50%

Acromionpre- (tip), meso- (mid), meta- (base) acromion · os acromiale (unfused meso / meta) ≠ fracture

Coracoidossification centres open to ~25 yr (angle, tip); conjoint tendon, pectoralis minor; CC ligaments ~25 mm from tip

SSSC (superior shoulder suspensory complex)distal clavicle, acromion, coracoid, glenoid + AC + CC ligaments · double disruption = unstable ("floating shoulder")

Axillary nerveinferior to glenoid · motion ⅓ scapulothoracic, ⅔ glenohumeral

3Presentation

Often missed with distracting injuries · diffuse pain, dyspnoea, chest pain · passive ROM only · check axillary, radial, median, ulnar, pulses

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Measurement
True AP, Grashey, scapular Y, axillary; CXR Pneumothorax; medial border–spine > 1 cm → scapulothoracic dissociation
Glenopolar angle (Grashey) Normal 30–45°; < 20–22° → poor / operative
Lateral border offset Medialisation
Angulation Scapular Y
CT (3D) Intra-articular, displacement > 1 cm, thoracic / spine injuries
MRI SSSC ligament injury

Classifications

Ideberg (glenoid, Goss) Fracture
Ia Anterior rim
Ib Posterior rim
II Fossa → exits inferiorly
III Fossa → exits superiorly
IV Fossa → exits medially through body
Va / Vb / Vc II + IV · III + IV · II + III + IV
VI Severe comminution

AO-OTA glenoid (more reliable)14F0 extra-articular (neck) · 14F1 simple intra-articular (rim, transverse) · 14F2 multifragmentary · 14B body extension

Kuhn (acromion) Fracture
I Non / minimally displaced
II Displaced, subacromial space OK
III Displaced → narrows subacromial space
Ogawa (coracoid) Fracture
I Proximal to CC ligaments
II Tip (distal)

5Management

Scapula fracture
  • Most (90% minimally displaced)→sling 2–3 wk + early motion (weekly X-ray × 3 wk)
  • Glenoid: step-off > 4 mm or > 20–25% rim with subluxation→ORIF
  • Body / neck: medialisation > 20 mm, angulation > 40°, GPA < 20–22°, translation > 1 cm→ORIF (Judet)
  • Floating shoulder (SSSC double disruption)→fix (clavicle ± scapula)

Operative indications — glenoid neck displacement, SSSC double disruption, scapular spine

Fracture ORIF if
Body Medialisation > 20 mm, GPA < 20–22°, angulation > 40° (> 45°, OB), medialisation > 15 mm + angulation > 35°
Neck Angulation > 40°, translation > 1 cm, GPA < 20–22°, SSSC double disruption
Glenoid > 20–25% anterior / posterior rim + subluxation; step-off > 4 mm (> 5 mm OB · > 3–4 mm OB)
Acromion Kuhn III, painful nonunion, impingement, double disruption
Coracoid > 1 cm, nonunion, Ogawa I into body, double disruption (✗ Wrong options: Ogawa II tip (nonop even > 1 cm))
Any Open fracture

Neck: medial 3 mm, angulated 20°sling 2 wk + PT
✗ Wrong options: ORIF

Displaced lateral scapular spine, weak abductionORIF (poor deltoid lever, impingement)
✗ Wrong options: stimulator · brace · acromioplasty · excision

✗ Wrong options: sling · fix one only

✗ Wrong options: plexus injury (75% resolve) · LC1 pelvis · pneumothorax · 2 rib fractures

✗ Wrong options: labrum, supraspinatus, transverse scapular ligament, coracohumeral ligament

Nonop outcomesunion 6–8 wk; near-normal function; may displace in first 3 wk (rib fractures, SSSC injury) · poor if GPA < 20°

Floating shoulder

Definition (TO)ipsilateral clavicle + scapular neck fracture LATERAL to coracoid (anatomical neck) · surgical neck (medial to coracoid) + clavicle + CA + CC ligament disruption also counts — TO explanation calls both correct

Modified Judetinfraspinatus (suprascapular n.) ↔ teres minor (axillary n.)
✗ Wrong options: supra / infraspinatus · teres minor / major (axillary / lower subscapular) · deltopectoral

Incisionalong spine + down vertebral border ("L" / boomerang); detach posterior deltoid

At riskposterior branch axillary nerve (teres minor retracted inferiorly), suprascapular nerve + artery (infraspinatus superiorly), circumflex scapular + posterior humeral circumflex vessels

Other approachesstraight posterior (isolated neck / lateral border) · deltopectoral (anterior glenoid, Ideberg II; axillary + musculocutaneous risk; subscapularis failure) · lateral mid-axial (inferior glenoid) · posterior over spine (acromion)

Fixation2.7 / 3.5 mm plates (locking on thin border) · rim: screws / arthroscopic anchors · acromion: lag + recon plate / tension band · coracoid: 2.7 / 3.5 mm screws

Septic Arthritis - Adult

Trauma · 55 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Joints (descending)knee (~50%) > hip > shoulder > elbow > ankle > sternoclavicular (IV drug users)

Risk factorsage > 80, diabetes, RA, cirrhosis, HIV, crystal arthropathy, endocarditis / recent bacteraemia, IV drug use, recent joint surgery, prosthetic implant

Pathophysiology

Seedingbacteraemia · direct inoculation (trauma, surgery) · contiguous spread (adjacent osteomyelitis)

Cartilage destructionirreversible; begins by 8 hours · proteolytic enzymes from PMNs

S. aureus vs gonococcus — joint destructionS. aureus → greater WBC influx (> 50,000)
✗ Wrong options: filamentous appendages (that is gonococcal adhesion; S. aureus uses MSCRAMMs) · IL-1 inhibitors / endotoxin (both organisms induce IL-1 + have endotoxin activity) · penicillin sensitivity

Organisms

Organism Setting
Staphylococcus aureus Commonest (> 50%) in all patients, including IV drug users · gram +ve cocci in grape-like clusters
Neisseria gonorrhoeae ~20% · commonest in healthy sexually active adolescents / young adults · intracellular + extracellular gram −ve diplococci
Gram −ve bacilli (E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) 10–20% · neonates, IV drug users, elderly, immunocompromised diabetics
Streptococcus (Group A pyogenes commonest; Group B agalactiae) Gram +ve cocci in chains · Group B → infants, elderly, diabetics
Pseudomonas aeruginosa IV drug abuse (commonest SC organism in the 1980s)
Propionibacterium acnes Shoulder surgery
Salmonella / Strep. pneumoniae Sickle cell disease
Bartonella henselae HIV
Pasteurella multocida Dog / cat bite
Eikenella corrodens Human bite
Fungal / Candida Immunocompromised

Sternoclavicular septic arthritis

Frequency~1% of septic joints · IV drug users, diabetes, renal insufficiency / haemodialysis, immunocompromise, alcoholism, HIV

OrganismS. aureus — even in IV drug users · gonococcal, fungal, candida in HIV
✗ Wrong options: Pseudomonas (↑ incidence but not commonest) · Strep. pneumoniae · S. epidermidis · P. acnes · gonococcus

Presenting symptomchest wall tenderness
✗ Wrong options: shoulder pain (much less often)

ImagingCT / MRI routinely before surgery → retrosternal abscess, chest wall phlegmon, extent of osteomyelitis (may need general / cardiothoracic surgeon) · MRI better; CT if MRI unavailable

TreatmentI&D + antibiotics; aspiration alone ineffective · with medial clavicular osteolysis (osteomyelitis) → resection of SC joint (best outcome, lowest recurrence)
✗ Wrong options: antibiotics alone · repeat aspiration · hyperbaric O₂ · simple I&D (high recurrence)

Septic olecranon / prepatellar bursitis

OrganismS. aureus ~80% → gram +ve cocci in pairs and clusters · mixed flora common
✗ Wrong options: chains (Strep) · branching bacilli (Nocardia / Actinomyces) · gram −ve diplococci (Neisseria) · thin rods (E. coli)

Routedirect inoculation (poor bursal blood supply) · middle-aged men

3Presentation

Symptomsjoint pain · fever in only 60% · may look toxic

Examerythema, effusion, warmth, tenderness · can't bear weight, can't tolerate PROM · limb held in position of maximum joint volume → hip in FABER

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
Radiographs (AP + lateral) Joint space widening / effusion, periarticular osteopenia
Ultrasound Confirms effusion in large joints (hip); guides aspiration
MRI Effusion + adjacent osteomyelitis
CT Intra-articular air (traumatic arthrotomy adjunct) · SC joint abscess

Diagnostic criteria

Test Septic value
Serum WBC > 10,000 with left shift
ESR > 30 mm/h · may be normal early; rises in 2 days, may rise 3–5 days after antibiotics, normal by 3–4 wk
CRP > 1 mg/dL · most helpful · rises within hours, normalises within 1 wk → best to monitor treatment
Synovial WBC > 50,000 (native joint) = diagnostic · lower counts still infected if gram stain / culture +ve
Synovial PMN High (e.g. 90%)
Gram stain Identifies organism only ⅓ of the time
Glucose < 60% of serum
Viscosity Negative "string" sign (low viscosity)

Aspirationgold standard; send cell count + differential, gram stain, culture, glucose, crystals

Antibiotics within 24 h before arthrocentesis↓ synovial WBC → false negative

Crystals + septiccoexist in < 5% · crystals do NOT exclude infection

Septic shockhypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg + lactate > 2 mmol/L despite fluids → mortality > 40% · aspirate, then immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics

Diagnosis — aspiration & coexisting crystals

Red, hot 1st MTP, ↑ ESR / CRPjoint aspiration first (septic vs gout)
✗ Wrong options: I&D before diagnosis · oral antibiotics · indomethacin before aspiration · MRI

IV drug user, ankle WBC 95,000 + negatively birefringent crystalsurgent I&D · gout / pseudogout does not remove need for surgery
✗ Wrong options: await culture · 24 h IV antibiotics then reassess · analgesia · ESR / CRP / urate

Diabetic bacteraemia → septic knee, septic shockS. aureus
✗ Wrong options: gonococcus · gram −ve bacilli · Strep. pyogenes · Pseudomonas

Traumatic arthrotomy — saline load test

Saline into knee Sensitivity (1 cm inferolateral wound)
100 mL < 75% — insufficient
110 mL 75%
145 mL 90%
155 mL 95%
175 mL 99%

Technique18 G needle, saline with passive ROM · egress through wound = positive (arthrotomy)

Trapsmethylene blue does NOT ↑ sensitivity · exam alone performs worse than SLT · CT → intra-articular air (adjunct; ✗ Wrong options: MRI routinely)

100 mL, no egress, wound near patellainject at least another 55 mL
✗ Wrong options: close + discharge · arthroscopy yet · MRI · secondary intention

Positivesurgical I&D (open / arthroscopic) to prevent septic arthritis

Differential

Crystal arthropathy (gout, pseudogout) · cellulitis · bursitis (prepatellar)

5Management

Suspected native-joint septic arthritis
  • Aspirate first (cell count, gram, culture, glucose, crystals)
  • WBC > 50,000 / organisms→urgent open or arthroscopic I&D + IV antibiotics
    (crystals present → still I&D)
  • Gonococcal→aspiration / arthroscopic drainage + ceftriaxone
    • not responding→open I&D
  • SC joint with osteolysis→CT / MRI, then joint resection

Emergencyorthopaedic surgical emergency; damage within 8 hours

Empirical antibioticsyoung healthy: S. aureus + N. gonorrhoeae · immunocompromised: S. aureus + Pseudomonas → switch to culture-directed

Monitoringserum WBC, ESR, CRP

Techniqueopen or arthroscopic · remove all pus, irrigate · synovectomy as needed · fluid + tissue for culture

Gonococcal arthritis

Antibioticceftriaxone (3rd-gen cephalosporin; or cefotaxime / ceftizoxime) · fluoroquinolones if sensitive · + doxycycline where chlamydia common
✗ Wrong options: penicillin · tetracycline (high resistance) · erythromycin · vancomycin

Formsarthritis-dermatitis syndrome (~60%) · localised purulent arthritis (~40%) · bacteraemic infection; newborns + adolescents

Disseminated (polyarthralgia + trunk rash, gram −ve diplococci)serial aspiration + antibiotics
✗ Wrong options: open I&D first (reserved for non-responders / severe) · I&D without antibiotics · colchicine · observation

Workupscreen for HIV, syphilis, chlamydia · response → fever, pain, leucocytosis resolve

Clueyoung, sexually active, new vaginal discharge → take sexual history

Criterion (1 point each) (TO) In original Kocher?

CRP No — added later by Caird

✗ Wrong options: blood cultures + antibiotics · US-guided aspiration + antibiotics · antibiotics alone

4-yr, fever, ↑ ESR / CRP, hip collection on US (TO)answer key not provided by the source

Metaphyseal osteomyelitis & joint spread (TO)

Intracapsular metaphyses (TO)proximal radius, proximal humerus, proximal femur, distal tibia + fibula → osteomyelitis decompresses into joint → septic arthritis

EXCEPT (TO)head (distal end) of ulna

Tuberculosis of joints (TO)

Rice / millet / melon seed bodies (TO)tuberculous synovitis / tenosynovitis
✗ Wrong options: PVNS · RA · Madura foot

First radiographic sign of healing (TO)remineralisation of bone (trabecular pattern, ↓ osteopenia) · spine: + sharpened disc margins, ↓ paravertebral shadow, fusion
✗ Wrong options: joint space reappears · sequestrum removal · bony ankylosis

TB hip (TO)second commonest osteoarticular TB · usually ends in fibrous ankylosis · advanced → FADIR usually; complete iliofemoral ligament resorption → FABER

Other TB hip classifications (TO)Babhulkar + Pande 2002 (clinico-radiological) · Tuli modification · Moon 2012: stable — Perthes, atrophic, protrusio · unstable — travelling acetabulum, mortar + pestle, dislocating

Osteomyelitis Contiguous spread

Sternoclavicular Dislocation

Trauma · 57 / 67

1Basics

Types

Traumaticanterior (commoner) · posterior → mediastinal structures at risk · high energy (MVA, contact sport)

Atraumatic subluxationyounger, generalised ligamentous laxity; with overhead elevation, reduces on lowering arm

Medial clavicle physisfirst bone to ossify, last physis to close (20–25 yr) · under 20–25 yr "dislocation" is usually a physeal fracture · closure ~25 yr (OB)

Stabilisers — posterior capsular ligament

SC jointdiarthrodial saddle joint, incongruous (~50% contact), fibrocartilage, intra-articular disc · stability is ligamentous

Structure Function
Posterior capsular (SC) ligament Most important — primary restraint to anterior-posterior stability
Anterior SC ligament Primary restraint to superior displacement of medial clavicle
Costoclavicular (rhomboid) — anterior fasciculus Resists superior rotation + lateral displacement
Costoclavicular — posterior fasciculus Resists inferior rotation + medial displacement
Intra-articular disc ligament Prevents medial displacement; secondary restraint to superior displacement

Prevents posterior dislocationposterior SC joint capsule
✗ Wrong options: first rib · disc ligament · costoclavicular · interclavicular

3Presentation

Anteriorpalpable bump; prominence ↑ with abduction + elevation

Posteriordyspnoea, dysphagia, tachypnoea, stridor worse supine · paraesthesia in arm · venous congestion (unilateral jugular engorgement) / ↓ pulse · ↓ arm ROM · turning head to affected side relieves pain

Posterior complicationsearly: pneumothorax, great vessel laceration / erosion / occlusion, oesophageal rupture, brachial plexus compression, respiratory distress, myocardial conduction abnormality · late: tracheo-oesophageal fistula, stridor, dysphagia

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
AP chest Hard to see; often read as normal
Serendipity view (40° cephalic tilt) Anterior → clavicle above contralateral · posterior → clavicle below
CT (axial) Study of choice — direction, mediastinal injury, distinguishes physeal fracture
MRI Adds nothing; delays treatment (avoid)

Sternoclavicular dislocation
  • Atraumatic subluxation→observation / reassurance
  • Chronic anterior (> 3 wk), mildly symptomatic→sling, symptomatic
  • Acute (< 3 wk) anterior or posterior→closed reduction under GA in OR ± thoracic back-up
    • stable→immobilise
    • unstable→accept deformity (anterior) / open reduction + reconstruction
  • Posterior, failed closed reduction or chronic→open reduction + soft-tissue reconstruction

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
Atraumatic subluxation Reassurance, symptomatic
Chronic anterior, minimally symptomatic (> 3 wk) Sling, unrestricted activity by 3 months
Acute anterior / posterior (< 3 wk) Closed reduction under GA ± thoracic back-up
Acute posterior, failed closed reduction (dysphagia, dyspnoea, ↓ pulses) Open reduction + soft-tissue reconstruction
Chronic anterior / posterior, persistently symptomatic Open reduction + reconstruction
Chronic posterior (> 3 wk) with dysphagia Open reduction in OR + thoracic back-up (✗ Wrong options: sling (avoid late mediastinal problems))

Posterior dislocation — reduction in OR with thoracic backup

Posterior + ↓ pulses (16-yr)reduction in OR with thoracic surgery back-up
✗ Wrong options: sling · ED reduction · ORIF + pinning of physis

Closed reduction failsin up to 75% → open reduction

✗ Wrong options: observation · open first · ORIF · allograft reconstruction first

After closed reductionimmobilisation 4 wk (OB) · Velpeau bandage 6 wk (Orthobullets) — read the options · elbow exercises at 3 wk · sport at 3 months

✗ Wrong options: midshaft clavicle ORIF · distal clavicle excision · SC joint I&D · Judet scapula

NeverED reduction (mediastinal injury), compression plating across SC joint, K-wires (migration)

Closed reduction techniquesupine, arm at table edge, abduct + extend with axial traction, direct posterior pressure over medial clavicle · towel clip / fingers pull medial clavicle

Open reduction & reconstruction

Figure-of-8 tendon graft2 drill holes in manubrium + 2 in medial clavicle, 1 cm apart · gracilis or semitendinosus · don't disrupt SCM sheath; clean capsulotomy for repair

Medial clavicle excisionoutdated · resect < 15 mm to preserve costoclavicular ligaments (repair if injured) · Wirth + Rockwood: costoclavicular reconstruction ± medial head resection for unstable injuries

Fixation hazards — pin migration

Highest life-threatening complicationspercutaneous pins (K-wires / Steinmann) → migrate to heart, pulmonary artery, aorta
✗ Wrong options: cannulated screws · cerclage · Balser plate · locking plate

Anterior dislocation — natural history

Anterior dislocation — truerarely symptomatic when left unreduced · surgery mainly cosmetic
✗ Wrong options: stable after reduction (persistent instability common) · tracheal injury on reduction · fusion · acute medial clavicle excision

Atraumatic spontaneous subluxation

Diagnosisno trauma, lump at base of neck, worse overhead · settles in 4–6 wk nonoperatively
✗ Wrong options: unreduced posterior · hypoplasia · arthritis · hyperostosis

Beighton-Horan ≥ 5 / 9 = hypermobility · treatment → observation
✗ Wrong options: figure-of-8 brace · resection · reconstruction · arthrodesis

Type III SC instability (TO)non-structural, abnormal muscle patterning (inappropriate pectoralis major, EMG) → biofeedback physiotherapy · surgery only if structural abnormality
✗ Wrong options: closed reduction + sling · open reduction + reconstruction · open reduction + sling

Complication Fact
Cosmetic deformity Anterior — usually well tolerated
Mediastinal injury Posterior — great vessels, trachea, oesophagus
Pin migration Heart, pulmonary artery, aorta → avoid K-wires

Epidemiology

Lateraleversion of plantarflexed foot; anterior process of calcaneus = fulcrum for anterolateral talus

Type Features Image

Lateral More often open, more associated fractures, higher energy · locked in pronation · fractures: cuboid, anterior calcaneus, lateral process of talus, fibula
Anterior Rare —
Posterior Rare —

Type Description Image

Major (4 of 5 needed) Minor (optional)

Localised periosteal / endosteal thickening of lateral cortex —

5Management

Subtrochanteric fracture
  • Non-ambulatory, unfit for surgery→observation + analgesia (limited role)
  • Most→cephalomedullary IM nail (reamed, statically locked)
  • Fixed-angle plate→femoral neck fracture, narrow canal, shaft deformity, preference
    • 95° blade plate / condylar screw (not sliding hip screw)
  • Symptomatic impending AFF (lateral cortical stress line)→prophylactic IM nail

Implant choice — cephalomedullary nail vs plate

Implant Fact
Cephalomedullary nail Load-sharing, preserves vascularity, stronger in unstable patterns · reamed + statically locked → highest union (✗ Wrong options: unreamed (reaming ↑ vascularity + union without ↑ pulmonary / transfusion risk))
95° blade plate / condylar screw Load-bearing; lateral approach (split / elevate vastus lateralis, profunda perforators) · tension band · devitalises fragments, weaker in comminution
135° sliding hip screw Contraindicated → loss of fixation, malunion, distal fragment displaces medially + proximally, proximal rotates on single screw

CMN vs SHSCMN: lower revision, less pain, better mobility, higher QoL + satisfaction (EXCEPT; ✗ Wrong options: "higher pain")

Failed 135° plate (reverse obliquity nonunion) — would have preventedcephalomedullary nail
✗ Wrong options: longer plate · autograft · strut allograft · derotation screw

Tension band principleseccentric loading + implant on tensile side + opposite cortex resists compression → subtrochanteric femur
✗ Wrong options: comminuted tibia / humerus / olecranon distal to coronoid · valgus impacted proximal humerus

Anterior distal femoral cortex perforationnail with greater radius of curvature (straighter) than femoral bow

Nailing technique

Position Advantages
Lateral Easier reduction of distal to flexed proximal fragment, easier entry (piriformis), vastus retraction
Supine Protects injured spine, access in polytrauma, easier fluoroscopy, easier to judge rotation, shorter set-up

Lateral disadvantagesharder imaging, rotation hard to judge, impractical in polytrauma · supine: harder start point

Reductionreduce before + during nail passage (nail can't reduce) · percutaneous aids / open clamp · evaluate proximal fragment before guidewire

Entrypiriformis nail may avoid malreduction from the valgus proximal bend of trochanteric nails

Causeprolonged bisphosphonate (> 5 yr) · low-energy fall · prodromal pain
✗ Wrong options: acute trauma · metastasis · fibrous cortical defect · osteomyelitis

✗ Wrong options: observe · physio · MRI · THA

✗ Wrong options: both · bone scan · oncology

✗ Wrong options: 2 yr · Caucasian · valgus · female sex

Fixation of AFF Risk
IM nail ↑ iatrogenic fracture (brittle, thick cortices; canal–nail mismatch) · ↑ nonunion → revision
Plate ↑ hardware failure (varus, intramembranous healing inhibited) · no ↑ iatrogenic fracture

Main complicationdelayed healing + nonunion · anatomic reduction = best predictor of union
✗ Wrong options: LLD · metastasis · femoral head AVN · occult neck fracture

✗ Wrong options: vitamin D (gut uptake) · ATP analogues (non-nitrogen bisphosphonates) · mevalonate pathway (nitrogen bisphosphonates) · RANKL antibody (denosumab)

Nonunion Lowest with reamed statically locked IMN · treat with plating (corrects varus)

Talus5 articular surfaces, ~70% cartilage, no muscle / tendon attachments → direct extraosseous blood supply (artery of tarsal canal main; deltoid artery to body)

Lateral processarticulates with posterior facet of calcaneus + lateral malleolus (lateral margin of talofibular joint) · "lateral facet of calcaneus" (OB) — not medial facet

Posterior processmedial + lateral tubercles separated by FHL groove · os trigonum in up to 50% — don't call it a fracture

Anterior Most important — valgus + PMRI restraint · inserts sublime tubercle (anteromedial facet of coronoid), 18.4 mm dorsal to tip (✗ Wrong options: 3 mm distal to tip · radial tuberosity)

Mechanismfall on extended arm, forearm supinated → valgus + axial + posterolateral rotatory forces → posterolateral dislocation · ~60% of complex dislocations from standing-height fall (TO)

Regan-Morrey Coronoid height Fixation
I Tip (< 10%) Not needed — no stability conferred (cadaver)
II ≤ 50% Usually not — fix MCL first if unstable
III > 50% Fix

Biomechanics> 50% fractured → ↑ posterior axial displacement at all flexion angles incl. 30° · < 50% (I + II) → no significant change · anteromedial facet → PMRI
✗ Wrong options: 25% → displacement

✗ Wrong options: displacement > 5 mm · comminution · age

✗ Wrong options: brachialis attachment · HO prevention · LUCL isometric point

Terrible triad (after reduction)
  • Rare: concentric, small coronoid, radial head non-surgical, stable→splint 90° 7–10 d, early ROM

    • 3 LCL repair to humerus→4 MCL repair if still unstable
    • 5 hinged ex-fix if still unstable

Radial head ORIF Non-comminuted, < 40% articular · 2-part > 30% → ORIF

Epidemiology

Incidence5–10% of tibia fractures (Orthobullets) · 5–7% (TO) · < 10% of lower-limb injuries · age 35–45, M > F

Associatedfibula fracture 75% (commonest association, TO) · ipsilateral limb injury 30% · open 20% · bilateral 5–10% · syndesmotic injury ~3.4%

Fracture anatomy & patterns (Chaput fragment)

Mechanismhigh-energy axial load (talus driven into plafond → articular impaction + metaphyseal comminution) · fall from height, MVC · low-energy rotation (skiing) less common

Posterior pilonrotation + axial impaction (plantarflexed foot) → large posterior malleolus fragment, posteromedial comminution, double-density sign → ORIF

Fragment (ligament attached) Position
Medial malleolar Deltoid

Wagstaffe Fibular (anterior tubercle) — other end of AITFL

3 fragments typical (intact ligaments) · 4 classic on X-ray: medial, anterior (Chaput), lateral (Wagstaffe), posterior (Volkmann)

AO/OTA 43 Pattern Subtypes (TO)

Pilon fracture
  • Non-displaced / unfit / high skin risk→long leg cast 6 wk

  • Simple articular extension→percutaneous screws + IM nail
  • Non-reconstructable / elderly / labourer→primary arthrodesis (rare)

Sequencesplint → spanning ex-fix → CT → delayed ORIF

✗ Wrong options: ORIF · percutaneous · cast · arthrodesis · CT / MRI first

✗ Wrong options: immediate tibia · splint + ORIF at 1 wk · Ilizarov + limited fixation

✗ Wrong options: splint → cast · ORIF · Blair fusion

✗ Wrong options: fibula only · walking cast · dynamise · fusion in young

Tibial Shaft Fractures

Trauma · 65 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest long-bone fracture17% of lower-limb fractures · 4% of Medicare fractures · M > F, bimodal · proximal ⅓ = 5–10% of shaft fractures · open ~20%

Mechanism Pattern Fibula Soft tissue
Low energy, torsion Spiral Different level Less · posterior malleolus with spiral distal ⅓
High energy, direct Wedge / short oblique, comminuted Same level Severe (Tscherne II / III, open)

Amputation predictorseverity of muscle / soft-tissue injury

Shafttriangular · proximal canal centred laterally (start point) · subcutaneous anteromedial crest · tubercle ~3 cm below joint · tibia carries 80–85% of load

Compartment Contents
Anterior Tibialis anterior, EDL, EHL · deep peroneal n.
Lateral Peroneus longus + brevis · superficial peroneal n.
Superficial posterior Gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris
Deep posterior Popliteus, tibialis posterior, FDL, FHL · tibial n.

✗ Wrong options: MRI knee / hip · CT knee · calcaneal view · CT chest · arterial duplex

Not associatedvertical medial malleolus shear, Chaput, talus, Tillaux, knee dislocation · PITFL intact with posterior malleolus fracture

Compartment syndromediaphyseal 8.1% (proximal 1.6%, distal 1.4%) · occurs in open fractures too · check all 4

Floating kneeantegrade tibial nail + retrograde femoral nail

5Management

Tibial shaft fracture
  • Closed, low energy, acceptable alignment → long leg cast→PTB brace ~4 wk
  • Most→reamed, statically locked IM nail
    • proximal ⅓→lateral start, semi-extended / suprapatellar, blocking screws
    • distal ⅓→fibular plating, center-center guidewire
  • Open→antibiotics < 3 h, I&D < 12–24 h, nail or ex-fix
  • Polytrauma / contaminated → ex-fix→nail when resuscitated (ideally < 7 d)

RTSGCS + SBP + RR codes · most widely used pre-hospital triage tool · lower score = more severe · RTS < 4 → transfer to trauma centre

RTS — true (TO)improves appropriateness of treatment
✗ Wrong options: improves diagnostic / investigation error rate (no difference) · higher score = more severe · includes respiratory effort + capillary refill (those were in the old Trauma Score, removed in RTS)

Injury Severity Score calculation (ISS, MISS)

AIS grade Severity
1 Minor (laceration, contusion)
2 Moderate (large joint dislocation)
3 Severe, not life-threatening (femoral shaft, open pelvic fracture)
4 Severe, life-threatening, survival probable
5 Critical, survival uncertain (crushed larynx)
6 Maximal / unsurvivable (crushed head)

ISSsum of squares of the highest AIS in the 3 most severely injured body regions (A² + B² + C²) · range 1–75 · any AIS 6 → 75 · first anatomical scoring system

Body regions6 (TO; OB: head, face, chest, abdomen, extremities + pelvis, external) · 9 anatomic regions (Orthobullets) — read the options

Only the highest AIS per regionbilateral femur fractures count once → NISS fixes this

Polytrauma thresholdISS > 15 (major trauma; 10% mortality) (Orthobullets, TO, OB) · ISS ≥ 18 polytrauma / transfer (OB) — read the options

Worked example ISS
Chest 4, liver 4, open tibia 3, radius 2, scalp 1 (TO) 16 + 16 + 9 = 41
Open chest 4, colon 4, femur 3, shoulder 2, thyroid 1 41
Subdural 4, spleen 4, pelvis / femur 3, nose 2, ribs 2 41
Bilateral femur 3 + abdomen 3 + face 2 + lung 2 9 + 9 + 4 = 22

NISS3 highest AIS regardless of region → better for severe single-region injury; more predictive of complications + mortality

ISS limitshard to calculate in resus · misses multiple injuries in one region

MISS (paediatric)5 regions (neurological, face / neck, chest, abdomen / pelvic contents, extremities / pelvic girdle) · graded 1–5 · same sum-of-squares · MISS < 40 → no deaths; > 40 → 50%; > 50 → 75%

MISS examplechest 3 + abdomen 2 + face / neck 4 (GCS 14 → neuro grade 1, excluded) → 9 + 4 + 16 = 29

Wound & Hardware Infection

Trauma · 67 / 67

1Basics

Epidemiology

Commonest complication of orthopaedic trauma surgeryup to 16% after fracture (Orthobullets) · ≥ 10% after severe injury, < 2% after closed elective surgery (TO) · SSI 11.8 / 100 patients (TO)

Risk factorshost immunodeficiency, extremes of age, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, tobacco, steroids, malnutrition, radiation, vascular insufficiency

Biofilm — glycocalyx & quorum sensing

Seedingsoft-tissue, vessel + periosteal disruption lets bacteria evade defences · direct seeding of implant · haematogenous

Biofilmdepends on exopolysaccharide glycocalyx · forms within ~4 weeks · resists antibiotics → chronic (> 4 wk) → explant + antibiotics
✗ Wrong options: osteoclast differentiation (RANK-RANKL) · metastasis · endochondral / intramembranous bone

Biofilm stage Mechanism
1 Adhesion Individual bacteria attach to substrate (adhesins)
2 Maturation Quorum sensing (cell-to-cell signalling) → activates virulence-factor genes, ↑ resistance (✗ Wrong options: creates planktonic bacteria · mediates adhesion · ↓ resistance)

Planktonic bacteriaindividual free-floating

Shoulder surgery infection — C. acnes

Indolent infection after arthroscopic acromioplasty + mini-open cuff repairPropionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes · arthroscopy fluid may dilute skin prep before mini-open
✗ Wrong options: E. coli · Strep. viridans · Enterococcus

3Presentation

Historysoft-tissue + bone injury, hardware, previous surgery / infection at site

Symptomspain at old fracture site (infected nonunion) ± fever, chills, night sweats

Examerythema, drainage / purulence, tenderness · gross motion = nonunion

Surgical site infection — definition & time window (TO)

SSI (TO)infection within 30 days of surgery, or within 1 year with an implant, at incision or deep tissue

NOT an SSI (TO)no instrumentation, 3 months
✗ Wrong options: implant at 3 or 6 months · no implant at 1 month (all are SSIs)

SSI type (TO) Features
Superficial incisional Pus from superficial incision; pain, swelling, redness, heat
Deep incisional / organ-space 30 d (1 yr with implant) · pus from deep incision, spontaneous dehiscence, fever > 38 °C

HAI (TO)not present / incubating on admission; most appear > 48 h after admission · up to 7% (developed) / 10% (developing) of inpatients

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Study Finding
X-ray (biplanar ± 45° obliques) Normal early · subacute / chronic: peri-implant lucency, involucrum (reactive new bone), sequestrum (dead infected bone)
CT Pre-operative planning
MRI Extent, abscess · 98% sensitive, 78% specific · metal artefact
WBC-labelled scan Infection around hardware (MRI artefact) · distinguishes mimics

Labs & cultures

WBCmay be normal (chronic, indolent)

ESRstays ↑ for months after injury / surgery without infection · normalises slowly — poor marker of cure · normal: men < 50 yr 0–15, women 0–20 mm/h · ↑ pregnancy, renal disease, cancer, anaemia · ↓ sickle cell, leukaemia, CHF, hyperviscosity

Culturesin-office swabs / sinus-tract aspirates unreliable · intra-operative deep cultures (multiple sites) most reliable

CRP / ESR kinetics after surgery & infection

CRP after fracture fixationpeaks by 48 h (day 2), then falls · rising / not falling after 48 h → infection or haematoma · most predictive marker in first post-op week (> erythema, serous drainage, serial ESR)
✗ Wrong options: 24 h · 96 h · 7 d

Cure after treated wound infectionnormal CRP (< 3 mg/L) even if ESR still raised (CRP 1, ESR 25 ✓) · CRP tracks clinical response

5Management

Infection after fixation
  • Early (< ~4 wk), deep, fracture unhealed, implant stable→I&D + retain implant + culture-specific antibiotics until union
  • Unfit for surgery / unhealed, high surgical risk→antibiotic suppression (32% fail)
  • Chronic (> 4 wk biofilm) or healed fracture→debride + remove hardware + antibiotics
  • Loose / failed implant→remove, stabilise (ex-fix), staged revision

Early postoperative infection — debridement with implant retention

Purulent drainage probing to plate, 4 wk after ankle ORIFI&D + keep fixation + culture-specific antibiotics until union
✗ Wrong options: oral / IV suppression without surgery · remove implants + cast (instability, malunion / nonunion) · office culture + suppression

Success71% for early acute post-op infection with debridement + antibiotics · failure risk: IM nail, open fracture

Debridementany active infection · keep hardware if removal threatens stability · thorough excision · deep bone samples for culture + histology

Irrigationlow-pressure normal saline may be best during debridement (Orthobullets) · povidone-iodine before closure; saline not recommended for SSI prevention (TO, WHO) — read the options

Suppressionwhen surgical risk > benefit (immunosuppressed, elderly) or infected unhealed fracture · monitor ESR + CRP · 32% persist / worsen

SSI prevention (TO, WHO)

Measure Recommendation
Skin prep Chlorhexidine-alcohol, concentric circles outward
Hair Don't remove; if needed clippers, never shave
Antibiotic prophylaxis Within 120 min before incision (ideally 30–60 min)
Temperature Warm — hypothermia < 36 °C; start ≥ 30 min before induction (NICE)
Glucose / fluids Tight perioperative glucose · goal-directed normovolaemia
Drapes Woven or non-woven; plastic adhesive incise drapes not recommended
Laminar flow Not recommended for arthroplasty SSI prevention
Wound Sterile dressing 48 h; advanced dressings not better · drains out when indicated
Elective surgery Postpone if remote-site infection
